**Surat al-Mu'minun** has one hundred and eighteen verses (some count one hundred and nineteen) and is Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14] ﴿Then indeed, after that, you are to die.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 15] ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 16] ﴿And We have certainly created above you seven heavens, and We are never unaware of creation.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 17] ﴿And We sent down from the sky water in measure, and We settled it in the earth, and indeed, We are able to remove it.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 18] ﴿Then We produced for you thereby gardens of palm trees and grapevines, in which you have much fruit, and from which you eat.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 19] ﴿And a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai, which grows with oil and a condiment for those who eat.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20] ﴿And indeed, in livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you drink from what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 21] ﴿And upon them and upon ships you are carried.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 22] ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. (p. 393) *al-Sulalah* (extract): the pattern *fu'alah* from *salaltu al-shay' min al-shay'*, meaning "I extracted the thing from the thing." Umayyah said:

*He created mankind from an extract of a stinking fluid, and to that extract they will all return.*

A child is called the *sulalah* of its father, as though it has slipped out from its father's back. The poet said:

*She brought him forth, a lion-like, thick-skinned, strong one, the offspring of a weak womb.*

This form indicates paucity, like *qulamah* (nail-parings) and *nuhatah* (filings).

*Sina'* and *Sinin*: two names for one place. Most Arabs pronounce the *sin* of *Sina'* with a fatha, so its alif is for feminine marking, like *sahra'*, and it is therefore not inflected with tanwin, due to the permanent feminine marker. The tribe of Kinanah pronounces the *sin* with a kasra, and so, according to the Kufans, it is also not inflected due to the permanent feminine marker, because they maintain that the hamzah of *fa'la'* can be a feminine marker. According to the Basrans, it is not inflected due to being a proper noun (*'alamiyyah*) together with foreignness (*'ujmah*), or due to being a proper noun together with feminine marking, because the alif of *fa'la'* is not, in their view, a feminine marker but an augmentation (*ilhaq*), like *'ilba'* and *darha'*. It is said that it is the mountain of Palestine. It is also said that it lies between Egypt and Aylah.

*Al-Duhn* (oil): the extract of olives, almonds, and similar things that contain fat. *Al-Dahn* with a fatha on the *dal* means rubbing a thing with oil.

*Hayhat* (far, far): a verbal particle (*ism fi'l*) that indicates remoteness; its meaning is "it has become distant." It has many dialects, which we have mentioned in the book *al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil*, and some of them will come, God willing, in what has been read with it.

*Al-Ghutha'* (debris): the foam and what rises on a torrent and similar things that are of no use. This is what Abu 'Ubayd said. Al-Akhfash said: *al-ghuthaʾ* and *al-jufaʾ* are the same, and it is what the flood carries of filth and foam. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the withered leaves of trees, which when the flood passes mix with its foam, end quote. Its *thaʾ* may be doubled or single, and its plural is *aghthaʾ* irregularly. Al-Ghuthaʾ, whether with single or double *thaʾ*, is a collective noun. (In his narration of the verse of Imru' al-Qays: *min al-sayl*.)

*Tatra* (one after another): one following another. Al-Asma'i said: between them there is an interval. Others said: *al-mutawatirah* is consecutive without interval. Its *ta'* is substituted from a *waw* contrary to analogy, since its root is *al-watar*, like the *ta'* of *tawlaj* and *taywqur*, whose original forms are *wawlaj* and *wayqur*, because it derives from *al-wulukh* (entering) and *al-waqar* (dignity). Most Arabs do not give it tanwin, so it is not inflected due to the permanent feminine marker. The tribe of Kinanah gives it tanwin. The alif in it should then be an augmentation, as in *'alqan* with tanwin, and writing it with a *ya'* indicates this. Whoever claims that its tanwin is like that of *sabran* and *nasran* is mistaken, because then its pattern would be *fa'lan*, and the case ending on the *ra'* would not be preserved, so one would say *tatrun* in the nominative and *tatrin* in the genitive. However, the augmenting alif in a verbal noun is rare, and it is not necessary that a parallel exist. It is also said that *tatra* is a collective noun like *asra* and *shatta*.

*Al-Ma'in* (flowing water): the *mim* in it is augmentative, and its pattern is *maf'ul*, like *makhit*. It is water whose flow is seen with the eye. You say *'anahu*, meaning he reached it with his eye, like your saying *kabadahu*, meaning he struck his liver. Al-Khalil included it under the root '-y-n. It is also said that the *mim* is original, from the root *ma'ana*, meaning the thing increased, so its pattern is *fa'il*. Al-Farra' permitted both views. Jarir said:

*Indeed, those who departed with your heart left behind a trickle in your eye that still flows.*

*Al-Ghamrah* (confusion): ignorance. A *ghamr* man is heedless, one who has not tested affairs. Its root is covering. From it comes *al-ghamr* for resentment, because it covers the heart, and *al-ghamr* for abundant water, because it covers the earth. *Al-Ghamrah* is water that covers a man's height. *Al-Ghamarat* are hardships. A *ghamir* man is one who throws himself into perils, and one "enters the throng of people," meaning into their crowd.

*Al-Juʾar* (crying out): like *al-khuwar*. *Ja'ara al-thawr yaju'u* means it cried out. *Ja'ara al-rajul ila Allah* means he humbled himself in supplication. Al-Jawhari said this. The poet said:

*He alternates among the prayers to the King: sometimes prostrating, and sometimes crying out.*

It is also said that *al-juʾar* is a cry for help. He said: *ja'ara sa'at al-niyam li-rabbih* (he cried out to his Lord during the hours of the sleepers).

*Al-Samir* (night talk): a singular noun with the meaning of a plural. One says *qawm samir* and *sumar*. Its meaning is staying up at night, derived from *al-samar*, which is the light of the moon that falls on trees. They used to sit and converse in moonlight. *Al-samir* is also a companion in the night who stays awake, and he is also called *al-sammar*. It is said, "I will not do it as long as the two sons of Samir stay (*ma asmar*)," and *al-samir* also means time, whose two sons are night and day.

*Nakaba 'an al-tariq* (he deviated from the road), and *nakkaba* with doubling of the *kaf* means that he turned away from it.

*Al-lajaj fi al-shay'* (obstinacy regarding a thing): persisting in it.

Its *ta'* is substituted from a *waw* contrary to analogy, since its root is *al-watar*, like the *ta'* of *tawlaj* and *taywqur*, whose original forms are *wawlaj* and *wayqur*, because it derives from *al-wulukh* (entering) and *al-waqar* (dignity). Most Arabs do not give it tanwin, so it is not inflected due to the permanent feminine marker. The tribe of Kinanah gives it tanwin. The alif in it should then be an augmentation, as in *'alqan* with tanwin, and writing it with a *ya'* indicates this. Whoever claims that its tanwin is like that of *sabran* and *nasran* is mistaken, because then its pattern would be *fa'lan*, and the case ending on the *ra'* would not be preserved, so one would say *tatrun* in the nominative and *tatrin* in the genitive. However, the augmenting alif in a verbal noun is rare, and it is not necessary that a parallel exist. It is also said that *tatra* is a collective noun like *asra* and *shatta*.

*Al-Ma'in* (flowing water): the *mim* in it is augmentative, and its pattern is *maf'ul*, like *makhit*. It is water whose flow is seen with the eye. You say *'anahu*, meaning he reached it with his eye, like your saying *kabadahu*, meaning he struck his liver. Al-Khalil included it under the root '-y-n. It is also said that the *mim* is original, from the root *ma'ana*, meaning the thing increased, so its pattern is *fa'il*. Al-Farra' permitted both views. Jarir said:

*Indeed, those who departed with your heart left behind a trickle in your eye that still flows.*

*Al-Ghamrah* (confusion): ignorance. A *ghamr* man is heedless, one who has not tested affairs. Its root is covering. From it comes *al-ghamr* for resentment, because it covers the heart, and *al-ghamr* for abundant water, because it covers the earth. *Al-Ghamrah* is water that covers a man's height. *Al-Ghamarat* are hardships. A *ghamir* man is one who throws himself into perils, and one "enters the throng of people," meaning into their crowd.

*Al-Juʾar* (crying out): like *al-khuwar*. *Ja'ara al-thawr yaju'u* means it cried out. *Ja'ara al-rajul ila Allah* means he humbled himself in supplication. Al-Jawhari said this. The poet said:

*He alternates among the prayers to the King: sometimes prostrating, and sometimes crying out.*

It is also said that *al-juʾar* is a cry for help. He said: *ja'ara sa'at al-niyam li-rabbih* (he cried out to his Lord during the hours of the sleepers).

*Al-Samir* (night talk): a singular noun with the meaning of a plural. One says *qawm samir* and *sumar*. Its meaning is staying up at night, derived from *al-samar*, which is the light of the moon that falls on trees. They used to sit and converse in moonlight. *Al-samir* is also a companion in the night who stays awake, and he is also called *al-sammar*. It is said, "I will not do it as long as the two sons of Samir stay (*ma asmar*)," and *al-samir* also means time, whose two sons are night and day.

*Nakaba 'an al-tariq* (he deviated from the road), and *nakkaba* with doubling of the *kaf* means that he turned away from it.

*Al-lajaj fi al-shay'* (obstinacy regarding a thing): persisting in it.

So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14] ﴿Then indeed, after that, you are to die.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 15] ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 16] ﴿And We have certainly created above you seven heavens, and We are never unaware of creation.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 17] ﴿And We sent down from the sky water in measure, and We settled it in the earth, and indeed, We are able to remove it.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 18] ﴿Then We produced for you thereby gardens of palm trees and grapevines, in which you have much fruit, and from which you eat.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 19] ﴿And a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai, which grows with oil and a condiment for those who eat.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20] ﴿And indeed, in livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you drink from what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 21] ﴿And upon them and upon ships you are carried.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 22] ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 23] ﴿So the chiefs who disbelieved among his people said, "This is none but a man like you who wants to make himself superior to you. And if Allah had willed, He would have sent down angels. We have not heard of this among our forefathers, the earlier ones.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24] ﴿He is not but a man possessed by madness, so wait for him for a time.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 25] ﴿He said, "My Lord, support me, for they have denied me."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 26] ﴿So We revealed to him, "Construct the ship under Our observation and Our inspiration. And when Our command comes and the oven overflows, then load into it two of each kind, and your family, except those against whom the word has already preceded. And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 27] ﴿And when you have boarded the ship, you and those with you, then say, "All praise is due to Allah, who has saved us from the wrongdoing people."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 28] ﴿And say, "My Lord, let me land at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 29] ﴿Indeed, in that are signs, and indeed, We were ever testing.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 30] ﴿Then We produced after them another generation.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 31] ﴿And We sent among them a messenger from themselves, saying, "Worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 32] ﴿And the chiefs of his people who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, and whom We had given luxury in the worldly life, said, "This is none but a man like you; he eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 33] ﴿And if you obey a man like yourselves, you will then be losers.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 34] ﴿Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought out?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 35] ﴿Far, far is that which you are promised.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 36] ﴿There is none but our worldly life; we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 37] ﴿He is not but a man who has invented a lie against Allah, and we are not believers in him.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 38] ﴿He said, "My Lord, support me, for they have denied me."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 39] ﴿He said, "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 40] ﴿So the blast seized them in truth, and We made them as debris. So away with the wrongdoing people.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 41] ﴿Then We produced after them other generations.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 42] ﴿No nation can precede its term, nor can they delay.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 43] ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession. Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him, so We followed some of them with others and made them into tales. So away with a people who do not believe.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 44] ﴿Then We sent Moses and his brother Aaron with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 45] ﴿to Pharaoh and his establishment, but they were arrogant and were a haughty people.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 46] ﴿They said, "Shall we believe two men like ourselves, while their people are servants to us?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 47] ﴿So they denied them, and they became among those destroyed.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 48] ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book, that they might be guided.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 49] ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign, and We gave them refuge on a high ground, with settled security and flowing water.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50] ﴿O messengers, eat from the good things and act righteously. Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 51] ﴿And indeed, this your community is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 52] ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves into sects, each faction rejoicing in what they have.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 53] ﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 54] ﴿Do they think that what We provide them with of wealth and children﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55] ﴿is Us hastening to them with good? Rather, they do not perceive.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 56] ﴿Indeed, those who are apprehensive out of fear of their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 57] ﴿and those who believe in the signs of their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 58] ﴿and those who do not associate anything with their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 59] ﴿and who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60] ﴿those hasten to good deeds, and they are foremost in them.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 61] ﴿And We do not burden a soul except within its capacity, and with Us is a record which speaks with truth, and they will not be wronged.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 62] ﴿But their hearts are in confusion about this, and they have deeds other than that which they are doing.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 63] ﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment, they will cry out in supplication.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 64] ﴿Do not cry out today; indeed, you will not be helped by Us.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 65] ﴿My verses were recited to you, but you turned back on your heels﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 66] ﴿arrogant, speaking nonsense about it at night, talking idly.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 67] ﴿Have they not reflected upon the word, or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers, the earlier ones?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 68] ﴿Or did they not recognize their messenger, so they reject him?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 69] ﴿Or do they say, "He has madness"? Rather, he brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 70] ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Rather, We have brought them their reminder, but they, from their reminder, are turning away.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 71] ﴿Or do you ask them for payment? But the payment of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 72] ﴿And indeed, you invite them to a straight path.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 73] ﴿And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 74] ﴿And even if We had mercy on them and removed what afflicts them of adversity, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 75]

(p. 393) *al-Sulalah* (extract): the pattern *fu'alah* from *salaltu al-shay' min al-shay'*, meaning "I extracted the thing from the thing." Umayyah said:

*He created mankind from an extract of a stinking fluid, and to that extract they will all return.*

A child is called the *sulalah* of its father, as though it has slipped out from its father's back. The poet said:

*She brought him forth, a lion-like, thick-skinned, strong one, the offspring of a weak womb.*

This form indicates paucity, like *qulamah* (nail-parings) and *nuhatah* (filings).

*Sina'* and *Sinin*: two names for one place. Most Arabs pronounce the *sin* of *Sina'* with a fatha, so its alif is for feminine marking, like *sahra'*, and it is therefore not inflected with tanwin, due to the permanent feminine marker. The tribe of Kinanah pronounces the *sin* with a kasra, and so, according to the Kufans, it is also not inflected due to the permanent feminine marker, because they maintain that the hamzah of *fa'la'* can be a feminine marker. According to the Basrans, it is not inflected due to being a proper noun (*'alamiyyah*) together with foreignness (*'ujmah*), or due to being a proper noun together with feminine marking, because the alif of *fa'la'* is not, in their view, a feminine marker but an augmentation (*ilhaq*), like *'ilba'* and *darha'*. It is said that it is the mountain of Palestine. It is also said that it lies between Egypt and Aylah.

*Al-Duhn* (oil): the extract of olives, almonds, and similar things that contain fat. *Al-Dahn* with a fatha on the *dal* means rubbing a thing with oil.

*Hayhat* (far, far): a verbal particle (*ism fi'l*) that indicates remoteness; its meaning is "it has become distant." It has many dialects, which we have mentioned in the book *al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil*, and some of them will come, God willing, in what has been read with it.

*Al-Ghutha'* (debris): the foam and what rises on a torrent and similar things that are of no use. This is what Abu 'Ubayd said. Al-Akhfash said: *al-ghuthaʾ* and *al-jufaʾ* are the same, and it is what the flood carries of filth and foam. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the withered leaves of trees, which when the flood passes mix with its foam, end quote. Its *thaʾ* may be doubled or single, and its plural is *aghthaʾ* irregularly. Al-Ghuthaʾ, whether with single or double *thaʾ*, is a collective noun. (In his narration of the verse of Imru' al-Qays: *min al-sayl*.)

*Al-Ma'in* (flowing water): the *mim* in it is augmentative, and its pattern is *maf'ul*, like *makhit*. It is water whose flow is seen with the eye. You say *'anahu*, meaning he reached it with his eye, like your saying *kabadahu*, meaning he struck his liver. Al-Khalil included it under the root '-y-n. It is also said that the *mim* is original, from the root *ma'ana*, meaning the thing increased, so its pattern is *fa'il*. Al-Farra' permitted both views. Jarir said:

*Indeed, those who departed with your heart left behind a trickle in your eye that still flows.*

*Al-Ghamrah* (confusion): ignorance. A *ghamr* man is heedless, one who has not tested affairs. Its root is covering. From it comes *al-ghamr* for resentment, because it covers the heart, and *al-ghamr* for abundant water, because it covers the earth. *Al-Ghamrah* is water that covers a man's height. *Al-Ghamarat* are hardships. Rather, he brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 70] ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Rather, We have brought them their reminder, but they, from their reminder, are turning away.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 71] ﴿Or do you ask them for payment? But the payment of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 72] ﴿And indeed, you invite them to a straight path.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 73] ﴿And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 74] ﴿And even if We had mercy on them and removed what afflicts them of adversity, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 75]

(p. 393) *al-Sulalah* (extract): the pattern *fu'alah* from *salaltu al-shay' min al-shay'*, meaning "I extracted the thing from the thing." Umayyah said:

*He created mankind from an extract of a stinking fluid, and to that extract they will all return.*

A child is called the *sulalah* of its father, as though it has slipped out from its father's back. The poet said:

*She brought him forth, a lion-like, thick-skinned, strong one, the offspring of a weak womb.*

This form indicates paucity, like *qulamah* (nail-parings) and *nuhatah* (filings).

*Sina'* and *Sinin*: two names for one place. Most Arabs pronounce the *sin* of *Sina'* with a fatha, so its alif is for feminine marking, like *sahra'*, and it is therefore not inflected with tanwin, due to the permanent feminine marker. The tribe of Kinanah pronounces the *sin* with a kasra, and so, according to the Kufans, it is also not inflected due to the permanent feminine marker, because they maintain that the hamzah of *fa'la'* can be a feminine marker. According to the Basrans, it is not inflected due to being a proper noun (*'alamiyyah*) together with foreignness (*'ujmah*), or due to being a proper noun together with feminine marking, because the alif of *fa'la'* is not, in their view, a feminine marker but an augmentation (*ilhaq*), like *'ilba'* and *darha'*. It is said that it is the mountain of Palestine. It is also said that it lies between Egypt and Aylah.

*Al-Duhn* (oil): the extract of olives, almonds, and similar things that contain fat. *Al-Dahn* with a fatha on the *dal* means rubbing a thing with oil.

*Hayhat* (far, far): a verbal particle (*ism fi'l*) that indicates remoteness; its meaning is "it has become distant." It has many dialects, which we have mentioned in the book *al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil*, and some of them will come, God willing, in what has been read with it.

*Al-Ghutha'* (debris): the foam and what rises on a torrent and similar things that are of no use. This is what Abu 'Ubayd said. Al-Akhfash said: *al-ghuthaʾ* and *al-jufaʾ* are the same, and it is what the flood carries of filth and foam. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the withered leaves of trees, which when the flood passes mix with its foam, end quote. Its *thaʾ* may be doubled or single, and its plural is *aghthaʾ* irregularly. Al-Ghuthaʾ, whether with single or double *thaʾ*, is a collective noun. (In his narration of the verse of Imru' al-Qays: *min al-sayl*.)

*Tatra* (one after another): one following another. Al-Asma'i said: between them there is an interval. Others said: *al-mutawatirah* is consecutive without interval. Its *ta'* is substituted from a *waw* contrary to analogy, since its root is *al-watar*, like the *ta'* of *tawlaj* and *taywqur*, whose original forms are *wawlaj* and *wayqur*, because it derives from *al-wulukh* (entering) and *al-waqar* (dignity). Most Arabs do not give it tanwin, so it is not inflected due to the permanent feminine marker. The tribe of Kinanah gives it tanwin. The alif in it should then be an augmentation, as in *'alqan* with tanwin, and writing it with a *ya'* indicates this. Whoever claims that its tanwin is like that of *sabran* and *nasran* is mistaken, because then its pattern would be *fa'lan*, and the case ending on the *ra'* would not be preserved, so one would say *tatrun* in the nominative and *tatrin* in the genitive. However, the augmenting alif in a verbal noun is rare, and it is not necessary that a parallel exist. It is also said that *tatra* is a collective noun like *asra* and *shatta*.

*Al-Ma'in* (flowing water): the *mim* in it is augmentative, and its pattern is *maf'ul*, like *makhit*. It is water whose flow is seen with the eye. You say *'anahu*, meaning he reached it with his eye, like your saying *kabadahu*, meaning he struck his liver. Al-Khalil included it under the root '-y-n. It is also said that the *mim* is original, from the root *ma'ana*, meaning the thing increased, so its pattern is *fa'il*. Al-Farra' permitted both views. Jarir said:

*Indeed, those who departed with your heart left behind a trickle in your eye that still flows.*

*Al-Ghamrah* (confusion): ignorance. A *ghamr* man is heedless, one who has not tested affairs. Its root is covering. From it comes *al-ghamr* for resentment, because it covers the heart, and *al-ghamr* for abundant water, because it covers the earth. *Al-Ghamrah* is water that covers a man's height. *Al-Ghamarat* are hardships. A *ghamir* man is one who throws himself into perils, and one "enters the throng of people," meaning into their crowd.

*Al-Juʾar* (crying out): like *al-khuwar*. *Ja'ara al-thawr yaju'u* means it cried out. *Ja'ara al-rajul ila Allah* means he humbled himself in supplication. Al-Jawhari said this. The poet said:

*He alternates among the prayers to the King: sometimes prostrating, and sometimes crying out.*

It is also said that *al-juʾar* is a cry for help. He said: *ja'ara sa'at al-niyam li-rabbih* (he cried out to his Lord during the hours of the sleepers).

*Al-Samir* (night talk): a singular noun with the meaning of a plural. One says *qawm samir* and *sumar*. Its meaning is staying up at night, derived from *al-samar*, which is the light of the moon that falls on trees. They used to sit and converse in moonlight. *Al-samir* is also a companion in the night who stays awake, and he is also called *al-sammar*. It is said, "I will not do it as long as the two sons of Samir stay (*ma asmar*)," and *al-samir* also means time, whose two sons are night and day.

*Nakaba 'an al-tariq* (he deviated from the road), and *nakkaba* with doubling of the *kaf* means that he turned away from it.

*Al-lajaj fi al-shay'* (obstinacy regarding a thing): persisting in it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 23, verse 5–11 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 2] ﴿and who turn away from ill speech﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3] ﴿and who are active in giving zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] ﴿and who guard their private parts﴾ ﴿except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy﴾ ﴿but whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors﴾ ﴿and who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾ ﴿and who guard their prayers﴾ ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws; therein they will abide forever﴾ ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12] ﴿then We placed him as a drop of semen in a firm lodging﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 13] ﴿then We made the drop a clinging clot, then We made the clot a lump, then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14] ﴿Then indeed, after that, you are to die﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 15] ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be resurrected﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 16].

(p-395) This surah is Meccan without dispute. In the Sahih of al-Hakim it is reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever observes them will enter Paradise," then he recited ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] up to the ten verses. Its connection to the end of the surah before it is evident, because He, exalted is He, addressed the believers with His saying ﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], up to the verse in which is ﴿that you may succeed﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], and that is in the manner of expressing hope. So His saying ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] corresponds to it, as an announcement of the attainment of the success they had hoped for.

Talha ibn Musarrif and Amr ibn Ubayd read ﴿Uflih al-mu'minun﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the lam, in the passive voice, and its meaning is "enter into success." It may be that it is from falaha (intransitive), or that aflaha comes both transitively and intransitively. Talha also read it with a fatha on the hamza and the lam and a damma on the ha'. Isa ibn Umar said: I heard Talha ibn Musarrif reading "qad aflahu al-mu'minun" (with a waw), so I said to him: Do you make a grammatical error? He said: Yes, just as my companions made errors, end of quote. He means that his basis in recitation is what was transmitted, and it is not a grammatical error, since it is according to the dialect of "akaluni al-baraghith" (the fleas have eaten me). Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is by way of vagueness and explanation. Ibn Atiyya said: it is a rejected reading. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh it is written with a waw after the ha', and in al-Lawami' the waw of the plural was omitted after the ha' because the two came together in continuous speech, and the writing was conformed to the connected form, like ﴿wa-yamhu Allahu al-batil﴾ [al-Shura: 24]. Al-Zamakhshari said: And from him, i.e. from Talha, ﴿aflah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] with a single damma without a waw, dispensing with it by it, as in the saying of the poet:
"Fa-law anna al-atibba' kanu hawli" (If only the physicians were around me)
End of quote. This is not good, because the waw in ﴿aflaha﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] was omitted for the meeting of two unvocalized letters, whereas here it was omitted out of necessity, so it is not like it. Al-Zamakhshari said: it may require it, since it affirms what is expected and negates what is expected, and there is no doubt that the believers were expecting such glad tidings, namely the announcement of the lasting of success for them, so they were addressed with what indicates the lasting of what they had anticipated, end of quote.

Khushu' linguistically means humility and abasement. The exegetes have several statements about it here. Amr ibn Dinar said: it is stillness and good bearing. Mujahid said: lowering the gaze and lowering the wing. Muslim ibn Yasar and Qatadah said: lowering the head. Al-Hasan said: fear. Al-Dahhak said: placing the right hand upon the left. From Ali: abandoning turning around in prayer. From Abu al-Darda': magnifying the station, sincerity of speech, complete certainty, and gathering of attention. In a hadith: "he (peace and blessings be upon him) used to pray raising his gaze to the sky, and when this verse was revealed he cast his gaze toward his place of prostration." Among khushu' is that one observes the etiquettes: avoiding folding the garment, fidgeting with one's body and clothes, turning around, stretching, yawning, closing the eyes, covering the mouth, wrapping (the garment over the shoulders), cracking the knuckles, interlacing the fingers, shortening (the prayer), and shuffling pebbles. In al-Tahrir it is said: there is disagreement about khushu': is it among the obligations of prayer or among its virtues and completions, according to two opinions; the correct one is the first, and its place is the heart, and it is the first knowledge to be lifted from people, as stated by Ubadah ibn al-Samit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): why is the prayer attributed to them? (I say): because prayer is shared between the one who prays and the one to whom it is prayed. The one who prays is the one who benefits from it alone, and it is his provision and treasure, so it is "his prayer." As for the one to whom it is prayed, He is self-sufficient and exalted above need for it and benefit from it.

﴿Al-laghw﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3] is what does not concern you of speech or action, such as play and frivolity, and what good manners require one to discard. He means that they have such seriousness that it occupies them from frivolity. When He described them with khushu' in prayer, He followed it with the description of turning away from idle talk, so as to combine for them the two difficult acts upon the self, which are the foundations of the building of obligation, end of quote. When the object of an active participle precedes it, it may be permissible to strengthen its transitivity with the preposition lam as with the verb, and likewise when it comes after; but with its preceding it is more common, which is why ﴿li-l-zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] came with lam; had it come in the accusative it would have been correct Arabic. As for zakah: if by it is meant the purifying (tazkiyah), then attributing the act to it is valid, since whatever proceeds may be said of it "was done." If by zakah is meant the amount that comes out of wealth for the poor (p-396), then it is by ellipsis, i.e. "for the payment of zakah," ﴿active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4], since acts cannot be attributed to the physical objects from the payer; or "active" is taken to include the meaning of "paying." Al-Tibrizi explained it this way. It was said that ﴿li-l-zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] means "for good deeds," as in His saying ﴿better than him in purity (zakah)﴾ [al-Kahf: 81], i.e. a righteous deed; this was said by Abu Muslim. It was also said that "zakah" here means growth and increase, the lam is the lam of cause, and the object of ﴿active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] is omitted; the estimate is: ﴿and who﴾ for the sake of achieving growth and increase ﴿are active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4]: the good. It was said: what is spent is not called zakah until it reaches the hand of the poor. It was said: the extracted amount is not called zakah, so the expression by the act of its extraction is preferable to expressing it by "payment." In this there is a refutation of some of the heretics of the non-Arabs who were far from the taste of Arabic, in his saying: "Did he not say 'mu'addun' (payers)?" In al-Tahrir wa-l-Tahbir he said: this is what is said of "neither reason nor transmission," and the Noble Book was revealed in the most eloquent and sound of languages without dispute. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt has said:
"Al-mut'imuna al-ta'ama fi al-sanati al-azmah / wa-l-fa'iluna li-l-zakawat" (Those who feed the food in the year of famine, and those who are active for the zakawat)
No eloquent Arab replied to him, nor did the scholars of Arabic criticize it; rather, all of them cite it as proof and evidence, end of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: interpreting the verse in this way is more correct, because the word is plural in it, i.e. if zakah is meant as the amount, it is by omission of a noun, namely "for the payment of zakawat." He justified this by its being plural, meaning: when it is meant as the amount, its plural is valid; and when it is meant as the purifying, it is not pluralized, because purifying is a verbal noun and verbal nouns are not pluralized. This is not accepted; rather, some words from it have come in the plural, such as ʿulum, hulum, and ashghal. As for when they differ, most grammarians permit their pluralization, and here they differ according to their objects: paying cash is not paying livestock, and not paying plants. The zakah in Umayyah's verse is among the verbal nouns that came in the plural, so its interpretation as the amount is not exceeded merely because of its plural.

*Hafiza* does not take ʿala as its complement. It was said: ʿala here means min, i.e. "except from their wives," as min is used in the sense of ʿala in His saying ﴿and We helped him against (min) the people﴾ [al-Anbiya': 77], i.e. ʿala the people; this was said by al-Farra', and Ibn Malik and others followed him. The better view is that it is by way of implicit transitivity: ﴿hafizun﴾ is taken to include the meaning "restraining" or "confining," and both of these take ʿala, as in His saying ﴿keep your wife for yourself﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. Al-Zamakhshari here strained over several explanations. He said: ﴿ʿala azwajihim﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e. "except being in charge over their wives or being their custodians," from your saying: "So-and-so was over so-and-so, then she died leaving him and he married her," and similar to it: "Ziyad was over Basra," i.e. governing it. From this the saying "so-and-so is under so-and-so" comes, and for this reason a woman was called a bed (firash). Or ʿala is attached to an omitted element indicated by "not blameworthy," as if it were said: "they are blamed," ﴿except over their wives﴾, i.e. they are blamed for every intercourse except what has been permitted to them, ﴿for then they are not blameworthy﴾ for it; or he makes it a complement of ﴿hafizun﴾ from your saying "guard for me the rein of my horse," by implicitly giving it the meaning of negation, just as "I adjure you by God, except that you do it" is implicitly given the meaning "I did not ask of you anything except your doing it," end of quote. He means that ﴿hafizun﴾ has the form of an affirmative while its meaning is negative, i.e. "and those who have not guarded their private parts except over their wives," so the exception is a restricted exception, with ʿala attached to what precedes it, as he illustrated with "I adjure you," whose form is that of an affirmative while its meaning is negation: "I did not ask of you." These explanations he mentioned are far-fetched, and foreignness is evident in them.

His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ is intended as a category, as in His saying ﴿marry what is good for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is intended from the class of rational beings what is treated like non-rational beings, namely females, end of quote. His saying "namely females" is not good, because the word hum (they) is specific to males; he should have said "and it is females" in agreement with ma, or "they are females" in agreement with the meaning of ma. This exception is a limit at which one must stop. Concubinage is specific to men and is not permitted to women by consensus; so if a woman was married to a slave and she then owned him and freed him while owning him, the marriage is annulled according to the jurists of the regions. Al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, and Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah said: the two remain in their marriage. In His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ there is an indication of the generalization of sexual intercourse with what is owned by the right hand, and it is specific (p-397) to females by consensus, so it is as if it were said: "or what their right hands possess" of women. Regarding combining two sisters from ownership by the right hand, and between a female slave and her paternal or maternal aunt, there is disagreement. It is also specified in the verse as prohibiting intercourse with a menstruating woman, a slave woman who has been married, and one who has been subjected to zihar until he makes expiation. His saying "beyond that" includes fornication, sodomy, bestiality, and masturbation. The meaning of "beyond that" is beyond this limit which has been defined concerning wives and female slaves, and its position is as object of ibtaghā, i.e. "contrary to that." It was said: wara' here cannot be except with an omitted element, its estimate being "what is beyond that."

The majority of scholars hold that masturbation (called al-istimna', also known as al-khadkhada and jald 'Umayra; they use 'Umayra as a euphemism for the penis) is forbidden. Ahmad ibn Hanbal permitted it, reasoning that it is a surplus substance in the body, so it is permissible to expel it when there is need, like phlebotomy (al-fasd) and cupping (al-hijama). Harmala ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz asked Malik about this, and he recited this verse. A discussion took place on this matter with the chief judge Abu al-Fath Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Muti' al-Qushayri, known as Ibn Daqiq al-'Id, who argued for its prohibition with the same evidence Malik had used, namely His saying: ﴿But whoever seeks beyond that﴾. I said to him: That phrase came in the manner of what the Arabs used to do of fornication and boasting about it in their poetry, and this was so common among them that among their prostitutes there were those who bore banners, and they did not disapprove of it. As for jald 'Umayra, it was not familiar among them, and none of them mentioned it in their poetry as far as we know; so it is not included in His saying ﴿beyond that﴾. Do you not see that the place of what is permitted, which is their women, is by marriage or concubinage, so what lies beyond that is of the same kind as what is made lawful for them, namely women, and so nothing of them is lawful to them except by marriage or concubinage? And it is apparent that temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'a) does not fall under His saying ﴿whoever seeks beyond that﴾, because the term "spouse" applies to it. Al-Zuhri asked al-Qasim ibn Muhammad about temporary marriage, and he said: It is forbidden in the Book of Allah, and he recited: ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ ... the verse; and the prohibition does not clearly appear in this verse.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, read ﴿li-amanatihim﴾ in the singular, while the rest of the seven read it in the plural. The apparent meaning is the generality of trusts, so it includes whatever Allah entrusted to the servant of speech, action and belief, and so it includes all obligations, both of acts and of abstentions, and what the human being was entrusted with before; it is also possible that it is restricted to the trusts of people. The amanah is the thing entrusted, and observing it means attending to it by guarding it until it is delivered. Amanah is also used as a verbal noun, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [an-Nisa: 58]. What is delivered (al-mu'addá) is the specific entrusted object, or the statement if what is entrusted is a statement and not the verbal noun.

Al-Akhawan read ﴿'ala salatihim﴾ in the singular, while the rest of the seven read it in the plural. Humility (al-khushu') and guarding (al-muhafaza) are distinct. He began first with humility, which encompasses inner vigilance of the heart and humbling oneself through bodily acts, and then followed it with guarding, which is performing the prayer at its time with its conditions: the purity of the one praying, his clothing, and his place, and performing its pillars in the best of their forms, and this being his constant practice at every time. Al-Zamakhshari said: It was made singular first so that humility is conveyed toward the category of prayer, whatever prayer it is, and it was made plural at the end so that guarding is conveyed over its numbers, which are: the five daily prayers, the witr, the sunnah prayers attached to each prayer, the Friday prayer, the two 'Id prayers, the funeral prayer, the prayer for rain, the prayers of the eclipses, the Duha prayer, the tahajjud, the prayer of tasbih, the prayer of need, and other voluntary prayers.

﴿Those﴾, that is, those who combine these qualities, ﴿are the inheritors﴾, deserving of being called inheritors to the exclusion of others. Then he described the inheritors with His saying: ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws﴾; thus he came with a majesty and eloquence in their inheritance that is not hidden from the observer. The meaning of inheritance is what passed in Surat Maryam. The discussion has ended. And the discussion of al-Firdaws has already preceded at the end of al-Kahf.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 23, verse 5–11 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 2] ﴿and who turn away from ill speech﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3] ﴿and who are active in giving zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] ﴿and who guard their private parts﴾ ﴿except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy﴾ ﴿but whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors﴾ ﴿and who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾ ﴿and who guard their prayers﴾ ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws; therein they will abide forever﴾ ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12] ﴿then We placed him as a drop of semen in a firm lodging﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 13] ﴿then We made the drop a clinging clot, then We made the clot a lump, then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14] ﴿Then indeed, after that, you are to die﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 15] ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be resurrected﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 16].

(p-395) This surah is Meccan without dispute. In the Sahih of al-Hakim it is reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever observes them will enter Paradise," then he recited ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] up to the ten verses. Its connection to the end of the surah before it is evident, because He, exalted is He, addressed the believers with His saying ﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], up to the verse in which is ﴿that you may succeed﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], and that is in the manner of expressing hope. So His saying ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] corresponds to it, as an announcement of the attainment of the success they had hoped for.

Talha ibn Musarrif and Amr ibn Ubayd read ﴿Uflih al-mu'minun﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the lam, in the passive voice, and its meaning is "enter into success." It may be that it is from falaha (intransitive), or that aflaha comes both transitively and intransitively. Talha also read it with a fatha on the hamza and the lam and a damma on the ha'. Isa ibn Umar said: I heard Talha ibn Musarrif reading "qad aflahu al-mu'minun" (with a waw), so I said to him: Do you make a grammatical error? He said: Yes, just as my companions made errors, end of quote. He means that his basis in recitation is what was transmitted, and it is not a grammatical error, since it is according to the dialect of "akaluni al-baraghith" (the fleas have eaten me). Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is by way of vagueness and explanation. Ibn Atiyya said: it is a rejected reading. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh it is written with a waw after the ha', and in al-Lawami' the waw of the plural was omitted after the ha' because the two came together in continuous speech, and the writing was conformed to the connected form, like ﴿wa-yamhu Allahu al-batil﴾ [al-Shura: 24]. Al-Zamakhshari said: And from him, i.e. from Talha, ﴿aflah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] with a single damma without a waw, dispensing with it by it, as in the saying of the poet:
"Fa-law anna al-atibba' kanu hawli" (If only the physicians were around me)
End of quote. This is not good, because the waw in ﴿aflaha﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] was omitted for the meeting of two unvocalized letters, whereas here it was omitted out of necessity, so it is not like it. Al-Zamakhshari said: it may require it, since it affirms what is expected and negates what is expected, and there is no doubt that the believers were expecting such glad tidings, namely the announcement of the lasting of success for them, so they were addressed with what indicates the lasting of what they had anticipated, end of quote.

Khushu' linguistically means humility and abasement. The exegetes have several statements about it here. Amr ibn Dinar said: it is stillness and good bearing. Mujahid said: lowering the gaze and lowering the wing. Muslim ibn Yasar and Qatadah said: lowering the head. Al-Hasan said: fear. Al-Dahhak said: placing the right hand upon the left. From Ali: abandoning turning around in prayer. From Abu al-Darda': magnifying the station, sincerity of speech, complete certainty, and gathering of attention. In a hadith: "he (peace and blessings be upon him) used to pray raising his gaze to the sky, and when this verse was revealed he cast his gaze toward his place of prostration." Among khushu' is that one observes the etiquettes: avoiding folding the garment, fidgeting with one's body and clothes, turning around, stretching, yawning, closing the eyes, covering the mouth, wrapping (the garment over the shoulders), cracking the knuckles, interlacing the fingers, shortening (the prayer), and shuffling pebbles. In al-Tahrir it is said: there is disagreement about khushu': is it among the obligations of prayer or among its virtues and completions, according to two opinions; the correct one is the first, and its place is the heart, and it is the first knowledge to be lifted from people, as stated by Ubadah ibn al-Samit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): why is the prayer attributed to them? (I say): because prayer is shared between the one who prays and the one to whom it is prayed. The one who prays is the one who benefits from it alone, and it is his provision and treasure, so it is "his prayer." As for the one to whom it is prayed, He is self-sufficient and exalted above need for it and benefit from it.

﴿Al-laghw﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3] is what does not concern you of speech or action, such as play and frivolity, and what good manners require one to discard. He means that they have such seriousness that it occupies them from frivolity. When He described them with khushu' in prayer, He followed it with the description of turning away from idle talk, so as to combine for them the two difficult acts upon the self, which are the foundations of the building of obligation, end of quote. When the object of an active participle precedes it, it may be permissible to strengthen its transitivity with the preposition lam as with the verb, and likewise when it comes after; but with its preceding it is more common, which is why ﴿li-l-zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] came with lam; had it come in the accusative it would have been correct Arabic. As for zakah: if by it is meant the purifying (tazkiyah), then attributing the act to it is valid, since whatever proceeds may be said of it "was done." If by zakah is meant the amount that comes out of wealth for the poor (p-396), then it is by ellipsis, i.e. "for the payment of zakah," ﴿active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4], since acts cannot be attributed to the physical objects from the payer; or "active" is taken to include the meaning of "paying." Al-Tibrizi explained it this way. It was said that ﴿li-l-zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] means "for good deeds," as in His saying ﴿better than him in purity (zakah)﴾ [al-Kahf: 81], i.e. a righteous deed; this was said by Abu Muslim. It was also said that "zakah" here means growth and increase, the lam is the lam of cause, and the object of ﴿active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] is omitted; the estimate is: ﴿and who﴾ for the sake of achieving growth and increase ﴿are active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4]: the good. It was said: what is spent is not called zakah until it reaches the hand of the poor. It was said: the extracted amount is not called zakah, so the expression by the act of its extraction is preferable to expressing it by "payment." In this there is a refutation of some of the heretics of the non-Arabs who were far from the taste of Arabic, in his saying: "Did he not say 'mu'addun' (payers)?" In al-Tahrir wa-l-Tahbir he said: this is what is said of "neither reason nor transmission," and the Noble Book was revealed in the most eloquent and sound of languages without dispute. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt has said:
"Al-mut'imuna al-ta'ama fi al-sanati al-azmah / wa-l-fa'iluna li-l-zakawat" (Those who feed the food in the year of famine, and those who are active for the zakawat)
No eloquent Arab replied to him, nor did the scholars of Arabic criticize it; rather, all of them cite it as proof and evidence, end of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: interpreting the verse in this way is more correct, because the word is plural in it, i.e. if zakah is meant as the amount, it is by omission of a noun, namely "for the payment of zakawat." He justified this by its being plural, meaning: when it is meant as the amount, its plural is valid; and when it is meant as the purifying, it is not pluralized, because purifying is a verbal noun and verbal nouns are not pluralized. This is not accepted; rather, some words from it have come in the plural, such as ʿulum, hulum, and ashghal. As for when they differ, most grammarians permit their pluralization, and here they differ according to their objects: paying cash is not paying livestock, and not paying plants. The zakah in Umayyah's verse is among the verbal nouns that came in the plural, so its interpretation as the amount is not exceeded merely because of its plural.

*Hafiza* does not take ʿala as its complement. It was said: ʿala here means min, i.e. "except from their wives," as min is used in the sense of ʿala in His saying ﴿and We helped him against (min) the people﴾ [al-Anbiya': 77], i.e. ʿala the people; this was said by al-Farra', and Ibn Malik and others followed him. The better view is that it is by way of implicit transitivity: ﴿hafizun﴾ is taken to include the meaning "restraining" or "confining," and both of these take ʿala, as in His saying ﴿keep your wife for yourself﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. Al-Zamakhshari here strained over several explanations. He said: ﴿ʿala azwajihim﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e. "except being in charge over their wives or being their custodians," from your saying: "So-and-so was over so-and-so, then she died leaving him and he married her," and similar to it: "Ziyad was over Basra," i.e. governing it. From this the saying "so-and-so is under so-and-so" comes, and for this reason a woman was called a bed (firash). Or ʿala is attached to an omitted element indicated by "not blameworthy," as if it were said: "they are blamed," ﴿except over their wives﴾, i.e. they are blamed for every intercourse except what has been permitted to them, ﴿for then they are not blameworthy﴾ for it; or he makes it a complement of ﴿hafizun﴾ from your saying "guard for me the rein of my horse," by implicitly giving it the meaning of negation, just as "I adjure you by God, except that you do it" is implicitly given the meaning "I did not ask of you anything except your doing it," end of quote. He means that ﴿hafizun﴾ has the form of an affirmative while its meaning is negative, i.e. "and those who have not guarded their private parts except over their wives," so the exception is a restricted exception, with ʿala attached to what precedes it, as he illustrated with "I adjure you," whose form is that of an affirmative while its meaning is negation: "I did not ask of you." These explanations he mentioned are far-fetched, and foreignness is evident in them.

His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ is intended as a category, as in His saying ﴿marry what is good for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is intended from the class of rational beings what is treated like non-rational beings, namely females, end of quote. His saying "namely females" is not good, because the word hum (they) is specific to males; he should have said "and it is females" in agreement with ma, or "they are females" in agreement with the meaning of ma. This exception is a limit at which one must stop. Concubinage is specific to men and is not permitted to women by consensus; so if a woman was married to a slave and she then owned him and freed him while owning him, the marriage is annulled according to the jurists of the regions. Al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, and Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah said: the two remain in their marriage. In His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ there is an indication of the generalization of sexual intercourse with what is owned by the right hand, and it is specific (p-397) to females by consensus, so it is as if it were said: "or what their right hands possess" of women. Regarding combining two sisters from ownership by the right hand, and between a female slave and her paternal or maternal aunt, there is disagreement. It is also specified in the verse as prohibiting intercourse with a menstruating woman, a slave woman who has been married, and one who has been subjected to zihar until he makes expiation. His saying "beyond that" includes fornication, sodomy, bestiality, and masturbation. The meaning of "beyond that" is beyond this limit which has been defined concerning wives and female slaves, and its position is as object of ibtaghā, i.e. "contrary to that." It was said: wara' here cannot be except with an omitted element, its estimate being "what is beyond that."

The majority of scholars hold that masturbation (called al-istimna', also known as al-khadkhada and jald 'Umayra; they use 'Umayra as a euphemism for the penis) is forbidden. Ahmad ibn Hanbal permitted it, reasoning that it is a surplus substance in the body, so it is permissible to expel it when there is need, like phlebotomy (al-fasd) and cupping (al-hijama). Harmala ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz asked Malik about this, and he recited this verse. A discussion took place on this matter with the chief judge Abu al-Fath Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Muti' al-Qushayri, known as Ibn Daqiq al-'Id, who argued for its prohibition with the same evidence Malik had used, namely His saying: ﴿But whoever seeks beyond that﴾. I said to him: That phrase came in the manner of what the Arabs used to do of fornication and boasting about it in their poetry, and this was so common among them that among their prostitutes there were those who bore banners, and they did not disapprove of it. As for jald 'Umayra, it was not familiar among them, and none of them mentioned it in their poetry as far as we know; so it is not included in His saying ﴿beyond that﴾. Do you not see that the place of what is permitted, which is their women, is by marriage or concubinage, so what lies beyond that is of the same kind as what is made lawful for them, namely women, and so nothing of them is lawful to them except by marriage or concubinage? And it is apparent that temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'a) does not fall under His saying ﴿whoever seeks beyond that﴾, because the term "spouse" applies to it. Al-Zuhri asked al-Qasim ibn Muhammad about temporary marriage, and he said: It is forbidden in the Book of Allah, and he recited: ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ ... the verse; and the prohibition does not clearly appear in this verse.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, read ﴿li-amanatihim﴾ in the singular, while the rest of the seven read it in the plural. The apparent meaning is the generality of trusts, so it includes whatever Allah entrusted to the servant of speech, action and belief, and so it includes all obligations, both of acts and of abstentions, and what the human being was entrusted with before; it is also possible that it is restricted to the trusts of people. The amanah is the thing entrusted, and observing it means attending to it by guarding it until it is delivered. Amanah is also used as a verbal noun, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [an-Nisa: 58]. What is delivered (al-mu'addá) is the specific entrusted object, or the statement if what is entrusted is a statement and not the verbal noun.

Al-Akhawan read ﴿'ala salatihim﴾ in the singular, while the rest of the seven read it in the plural. Humility (al-khushu') and guarding (al-muhafaza) are distinct. He began first with humility, which encompasses inner vigilance of the heart and humbling oneself through bodily acts, and then followed it with guarding, which is performing the prayer at its time with its conditions: the purity of the one praying, his clothing, and his place, and performing its pillars in the best of their forms, and this being his constant practice at every time. Al-Zamakhshari said: It was made singular first so that humility is conveyed toward the category of prayer, whatever prayer it is, and it was made plural at the end so that guarding is conveyed over its numbers, which are: the five daily prayers, the witr, the sunnah prayers attached to each prayer, the Friday prayer, the two 'Id prayers, the funeral prayer, the prayer for rain, the prayers of the eclipses, the Duha prayer, the tahajjud, the prayer of tasbih, the prayer of need, and other voluntary prayers.

﴿Those﴾, that is, those who combine these qualities, ﴿are the inheritors﴾, deserving of being called inheritors to the exclusion of others. Then he described the inheritors with His saying: ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws﴾; thus he came with a majesty and eloquence in their inheritance that is not hidden from the observer. The meaning of inheritance is what passed in Surat Maryam. The discussion has ended. And the discussion of al-Firdaws has already preceded at the end of al-Kahf.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 23, verse 5–11 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 2] ﴿and who turn away from ill speech﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3] ﴿and who are active in giving zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] ﴿and who guard their private parts﴾ ﴿except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy﴾ ﴿but whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors﴾ ﴿and who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾ ﴿and who guard their prayers﴾ ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws; therein they will abide forever﴾ ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12] ﴿then We placed him as a drop of semen in a firm lodging﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 13] ﴿then We made the drop a clinging clot, then We made the clot a lump, then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14] ﴿Then indeed, after that, you are to die﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 15] ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be resurrected﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 16].

In the Sahih of al-Hakim it is reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever observes them will enter Paradise," then he recited ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] up to the ten verses. Its connection to the end of the surah before it is evident, because He, exalted is He, addressed the believers with His saying ﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], up to the verse in which is ﴿that you may succeed﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], and that is in the manner of expressing hope. In His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ there is an indication of the generalization of sexual intercourse with what is owned by the right hand, and it is specific (p-397) to females by consensus, so it is as if it were said: "or what their right hands possess" of women. Regarding combining two sisters from ownership by the right hand, and between a female slave and her paternal or maternal aunt, there is disagreement. It is also specified in the verse as prohibiting intercourse with a menstruating woman, a slave woman who has been married, and one who has been subjected to zihar until he makes expiation. His saying "beyond that" includes fornication, sodomy, bestiality, and masturbation. The meaning of "beyond that" is beyond this limit which has been defined concerning wives and female slaves, and its position is as object of ibtaghā, i.e. "contrary to that." It was said: wara' here cannot be except with an omitted element, its estimate being "what is beyond that."

The majority of scholars hold that masturbation (called al-istimna', also known as al-khadkhada and jald 'Umayra; they use 'Umayra as a euphemism for the penis) is forbidden. Ahmad ibn Hanbal permitted it, reasoning that it is a surplus substance in the body, so it is permissible to expel it when there is need, like phlebotomy (al-fasd) and cupping (al-hijama). Harmala ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz asked Malik about this, and he recited this verse. A discussion took place on this matter with the chief judge Abu al-Fath Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Muti' al-Qushayri, known as Ibn Daqiq al-'Id, who argued for its prohibition with the same evidence Malik had used, namely His saying: ﴿But whoever seeks beyond that﴾. I said to him: That phrase came in the manner of what the Arabs used to do of fornication and boasting about it in their poetry, and this was so common among them that among their prostitutes there were those who bore banners, and they did not disapprove of it. As for jald 'Umayra, it was not familiar among them, and none of them mentioned it in their poetry as far as we know; so it is not included in His saying ﴿beyond that﴾. Do you not see that the place of what is permitted, which is their women, is by marriage or concubinage, so what lies beyond that is of the same kind as what is made lawful for them, namely women, and so nothing of them is lawful to them except by marriage or concubinage? And it is apparent that temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'a) does not fall under His saying ﴿whoever seeks beyond that﴾, because the term "spouse" applies to it. Al-Zuhri asked al-Qasim ibn Muhammad about temporary marriage, and he said: It is forbidden in the Book of Allah, and he recited: ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ ... the verse; and the prohibition does not clearly appear in this verse.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, read ﴿li-amanatihim﴾ in the singular, while the rest of the seven read it in the plural. The apparent meaning is the generality of trusts, so it includes whatever Allah entrusted to the servant of speech, action and belief, and so it includes all obligations, both of acts and of abstentions, and what the human being was entrusted with before; it is also possible that it is restricted to the trusts of people. The amanah is the thing entrusted, and observing it means attending to it by guarding it until it is delivered. Amanah is also used as a verbal noun, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [an-Nisa: 58]. What is delivered (al-mu'addá) is the specific entrusted object, or the statement if what is entrusted is a statement and not the verbal noun.

Al-Akhawan read ﴿'ala salatihim﴾ in the singular, while the rest of the seven read it in the plural. Humility (al-khushu') and guarding (al-muhafaza) are distinct. He began first with humility, which encompasses inner vigilance of the heart and humbling oneself through bodily acts, and then followed it with guarding, which is performing the prayer at its time with its conditions: the purity of the one praying, his clothing, and his place, and performing its pillars in the best of their forms, and this being his constant practice at every time. Al-Zamakhshari said: It was made singular first so that humility is conveyed toward the category of prayer, whatever prayer it is, and it was made plural at the end so that guarding is conveyed over its numbers, which are: the five daily prayers, the witr, the sunnah prayers attached to each prayer, the Friday prayer, the two 'Id prayers, the funeral prayer, the prayer for rain, the prayers of the eclipses, the Duha prayer, the tahajjud, the prayer of tasbih, the prayer of need, and other voluntary prayers.

﴿Those﴾, that is, those who combine these qualities, ﴿are the inheritors﴾, deserving of being called inheritors to the exclusion of others. Then he described the inheritors with His saying: ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws﴾; thus he came with a majesty and eloquence in their inheritance that is not hidden from the observer. The meaning of inheritance is what passed in Surat Maryam. The discussion has ended. And the discussion of al-Firdaws has already preceded at the end of al-Kahf.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 23, verse 5–11 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 2] ﴿and who turn away from ill speech﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3] ﴿and who are active in giving zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] ﴿and who guard their private parts﴾ ﴿except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy﴾ ﴿but whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors﴾ ﴿and who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾ ﴿and who guard their prayers﴾ ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws; therein they will abide forever﴾ ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12] ﴿then We placed him as a drop of semen in a firm lodging﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 13] ﴿then We made the drop a clinging clot, then We made the clot a lump, then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14] ﴿Then indeed, after that, you are to die﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 15] ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be resurrected﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 16].

(p-395) This surah is Meccan without dispute. In the Sahih of al-Hakim it is reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever observes them will enter Paradise," then he recited ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] up to the ten verses. Its connection to the end of the surah before it is evident, because He, exalted is He, addressed the believers with His saying ﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], up to the verse in which is ﴿that you may succeed﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], and that is in the manner of expressing hope. So His saying ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] corresponds to it, as an announcement of the attainment of the success they had hoped for.

Talha ibn Musarrif and Amr ibn Ubayd read ﴿Uflih al-mu'minun﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the lam, in the passive voice, and its meaning is "enter into success." It may be that it is from falaha (intransitive), or that aflaha comes both transitively and intransitively. Talha also read it with a fatha on the hamza and the lam and a damma on the ha'. Isa ibn Umar said: I heard Talha ibn Musarrif reading "qad aflahu al-mu'minun" (with a waw), so I said to him: Do you make a grammatical error? He said: Yes, just as my companions made errors, end of quote. He means that his basis in recitation is what was transmitted, and it is not a grammatical error, since it is according to the dialect of "akaluni al-baraghith" (the fleas have eaten me). Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is by way of vagueness and explanation. Ibn Atiyya said: it is a rejected reading. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh it is written with a waw after the ha', and in al-Lawami' the waw of the plural was omitted after the ha' because the two came together in continuous speech, and the writing was conformed to the connected form, like ﴿wa-yamhu Allahu al-batil﴾ [al-Shura: 24]. Al-Zamakhshari said: And from him, i.e. from Talha, ﴿aflah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] with a single damma without a waw, dispensing with it by it, as in the saying of the poet:
"Fa-law anna al-atibba' kanu hawli" (If only the physicians were around me)
End of quote. This is not good, because the waw in ﴿aflaha﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] was omitted for the meeting of two unvocalized letters, whereas here it was omitted out of necessity, so it is not like it. Al-Zamakhshari said: it may require it, since it affirms what is expected and negates what is expected, and there is no doubt that the believers were expecting such glad tidings, namely the announcement of the lasting of success for them, so they were addressed with what indicates the lasting of what they had anticipated, end of quote.

Khushu' linguistically means humility and abasement. The exegetes have several statements about it here. Amr ibn Dinar said: it is stillness and good bearing. Mujahid said: lowering the gaze and lowering the wing. Muslim ibn Yasar and Qatadah said: lowering the head. Al-Hasan said: fear. Al-Dahhak said: placing the right hand upon the left. From Ali: abandoning turning around in prayer. From Abu al-Darda': magnifying the station, sincerity of speech, complete certainty, and gathering of attention. In a hadith: "he (peace and blessings be upon him) used to pray raising his gaze to the sky, and when this verse was revealed he cast his gaze toward his place of prostration." Among khushu' is that one observes the etiquettes: avoiding folding the garment, fidgeting with one's body and clothes, turning around, stretching, yawning, closing the eyes, covering the mouth, wrapping (the garment over the shoulders), cracking the knuckles, interlacing the fingers, shortening (the prayer), and shuffling pebbles. In al-Tahrir it is said: there is disagreement about khushu': is it among the obligations of prayer or among its virtues and completions, according to two opinions; the correct one is the first, and its place is the heart, and it is the first knowledge to be lifted from people, as stated by Ubadah ibn al-Samit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): why is the prayer attributed to them? (I say): because prayer is shared between the one who prays and the one to whom it is prayed. The one who prays is the one who benefits from it alone, and it is his provision and treasure, so it is "his prayer." As for the one to whom it is prayed, He is self-sufficient and exalted above need for it and benefit from it.

﴿Al-laghw﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3] is what does not concern you of speech or action, such as play and frivolity, and what good manners require one to discard. He means that they have such seriousness that it occupies them from frivolity. When He described them with khushu' in prayer, He followed it with the description of turning away from idle talk, so as to combine for them the two difficult acts upon the self, which are the foundations of the building of obligation, end of quote. When the object of an active participle precedes it, it may be permissible to strengthen its transitivity with the preposition lam as with the verb, and likewise when it comes after; but with its preceding it is more common, which is why ﴿li-l-zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] came with lam; had it come in the accusative it would have been correct Arabic. As for zakah: if by it is meant the purifying (tazkiyah), then attributing the act to it is valid, since whatever proceeds may be said of it "was done." If by zakah is meant the amount that comes out of wealth for the poor (p-396), then it is by ellipsis, i.e. "for the payment of zakah," ﴿active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4], since acts cannot be attributed to the physical objects from the payer; or "active" is taken to include the meaning of "paying." Al-Tibrizi explained it this way. It was said that ﴿li-l-zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] means "for good deeds," as in His saying ﴿better than him in purity (zakah)﴾ [al-Kahf: 81], i.e. a righteous deed; this was said by Abu Muslim. It was also said that "zakah" here means growth and increase, the lam is the lam of cause, and the object of ﴿active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] is omitted; the estimate is: ﴿and who﴾ for the sake of achieving growth and increase ﴿are active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4]: the good. It was said: what is spent is not called zakah until it reaches the hand of the poor. It was said: the extracted amount is not called zakah, so the expression by the act of its extraction is preferable to expressing it by "payment." In this there is a refutation of some of the heretics of the non-Arabs who were far from the taste of Arabic, in his saying: "Did he not say 'mu'addun' (payers)?" In al-Tahrir wa-l-Tahbir he said: this is what is said of "neither reason nor transmission," and the Noble Book was revealed in the most eloquent and sound of languages without dispute. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt has said:
"Al-mut'imuna al-ta'ama fi al-sanati al-azmah / wa-l-fa'iluna li-l-zakawat" (Those who feed the food in the year of famine, and those who are active for the zakawat)
No eloquent Arab replied to him, nor did the scholars of Arabic criticize it; rather, all of them cite it as proof and evidence, end of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: interpreting the verse in this way is more correct, because the word is plural in it, i.e. if zakah is meant as the amount, it is by omission of a noun, namely "for the payment of zakawat." He justified this by its being plural, meaning: when it is meant as the amount, its plural is valid; and when it is meant as the purifying, it is not pluralized, because purifying is a verbal noun and verbal nouns are not pluralized. This is not accepted; rather, some words from it have come in the plural, such as ʿulum, hulum, and ashghal. As for when they differ, most grammarians permit their pluralization, and here they differ according to their objects: paying cash is not paying livestock, and not paying plants. The zakah in Umayyah's verse is among the verbal nouns that came in the plural, so its interpretation as the amount is not exceeded merely because of its plural.

*Hafiza* does not take ʿala as its complement.
