The better view is that it is by way of implicit transitivity: ﴿hafizun﴾ is taken to include the meaning "restraining" or "confining," and both of these take ʿala, as in His saying ﴿keep your wife for yourself﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. Al-Zamakhshari here strained over several explanations. He said: ﴿ʿala azwajihim﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e. "except being in charge over their wives or being their custodians," from your saying: "So-and-so was over so-and-so, then she died leaving him and he married her," and similar to it: "Ziyad was over Basra," i.e. governing it. From this the saying "so-and-so is under so-and-so" comes, and for this reason a woman was called a bed (firash). Or ʿala is attached to an omitted element indicated by "not blameworthy," as if it were said: "they are blamed," ﴿except over their wives﴾, i.e. they are blamed for every intercourse except what has been permitted to them, ﴿for then they are not blameworthy﴾ for it; or he makes it a complement of ﴿hafizun﴾ from your saying "guard for me the rein of my horse," by implicitly giving it the meaning of negation, just as "I adjure you by God, except that you do it" is implicitly given the meaning "I did not ask of you anything except your doing it," end of quote. He means that ﴿hafizun﴾ has the form of an affirmative while its meaning is negative, i.e. "and those who have not guarded their private parts except over their wives," so the exception is a restricted exception, with ʿala attached to what precedes it, as he illustrated with "I adjure you," whose form is that of an affirmative while its meaning is negation: "I did not ask of you." These explanations he mentioned are far-fetched, and foreignness is evident in them.

His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ is intended as a category, as in His saying ﴿marry what is good for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is intended from the class of rational beings what is treated like non-rational beings, namely females, end of quote. His saying "namely females" is not good, because the word hum (they) is specific to males; he should have said "and it is females" in agreement with ma, or "they are females" in agreement with the meaning of ma. This exception is a limit at which one must stop. Concubinage is specific to men and is not permitted to women by consensus; so if a woman was married to a slave and she then owned him and freed him while owning him, the marriage is annulled according to the jurists of the regions. When He described them with khushu' in prayer, He followed it with the description of turning away from idle talk, so as to combine for them the two difficult acts upon the self, which are the foundations of the building of obligation, end of quote. When the object of an active participle precedes it, it may be permissible to strengthen its transitivity with the preposition lam as with the verb, and likewise when it comes after; but with its preceding it is more common, which is why ﴿li-l-zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] came with lam; had it come in the accusative it would have been correct Arabic. As for zakah: if by it is meant the purifying (tazkiyah), then attributing the act to it is valid, since whatever proceeds may be said of it "was done." If by zakah is meant the amount that comes out of wealth for the poor (p-396), then it is by ellipsis, i.e. "for the payment of zakah," ﴿active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4], since acts cannot be attributed to the physical objects from the payer; or "active" is taken to include the meaning of "paying." Al-Tibrizi explained it this way. It was said that ﴿li-l-zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] means "for good deeds," as in His saying ﴿better than him in purity (zakah)﴾ [al-Kahf: 81], i.e. a righteous deed; this was said by Abu Muslim. It was also said that "zakah" here means growth and increase, the lam is the lam of cause, and the object of ﴿active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] is omitted; the estimate is: ﴿and who﴾ for the sake of achieving growth and increase ﴿are active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4]: the good. It was said: what is spent is not called zakah until it reaches the hand of the poor. It was said: the extracted amount is not called zakah, so the expression by the act of its extraction is preferable to expressing it by "payment." In this there is a refutation of some of the heretics of the non-Arabs who were far from the taste of Arabic, in his saying: "Did he not say 'mu'addun' (payers)?" In al-Tahrir wa-l-Tahbir he said: this is what is said of "neither reason nor transmission," and the Noble Book was revealed in the most eloquent and sound of languages without dispute. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt has said:
"Al-mut'imuna al-ta'ama fi al-sanati al-azmah / wa-l-fa'iluna li-l-zakawat" (Those who feed the food in the year of famine, and those who are active for the zakawat)
No eloquent Arab replied to him, nor did the scholars of Arabic criticize it; rather, all of them cite it as proof and evidence, end of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: interpreting the verse in this way is more correct, because the word is plural in it, i.e. if zakah is meant as the amount, it is by omission of a noun, namely "for the payment of zakawat." He justified this by its being plural, meaning: when it is meant as the amount, its plural is valid; and when it is meant as the purifying, it is not pluralized, because purifying is a verbal noun and verbal nouns are not pluralized. This is not accepted; rather, some words from it have come in the plural, such as ʿulum, hulum, and ashghal. As for when they differ, most grammarians permit their pluralization, and here they differ according to their objects: paying cash is not paying livestock, and not paying plants. The zakah in Umayyah's verse is among the verbal nouns that came in the plural, so its interpretation as the amount is not exceeded merely because of its plural.

*Hafiza* does not take ʿala as its complement. It was said: ʿala here means min, i.e. "except from their wives," as min is used in the sense of ʿala in His saying ﴿and We helped him against (min) the people﴾ [al-Anbiya': 77], i.e. ʿala the people; this was said by al-Farra', and Ibn Malik and others followed him. The better view is that it is by way of implicit transitivity: ﴿hafizun﴾ is taken to include the meaning "restraining" or "confining," and both of these take ʿala, as in His saying ﴿keep your wife for yourself﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. Al-Zamakhshari here strained over several explanations. He said: ﴿ʿala azwajihim﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e. "except being in charge over their wives or being their custodians," from your saying: "So-and-so was over so-and-so, then she died leaving him and he married her," and similar to it: "Ziyad was over Basra," i.e. governing it. From this the saying "so-and-so is under so-and-so" comes, and for this reason a woman was called a bed (firash). Or ʿala is attached to an omitted element indicated by "not blameworthy," as if it were said: "they are blamed," ﴿except over their wives﴾, i.e. they are blamed for every intercourse except what has been permitted to them, ﴿for then they are not blameworthy﴾ for it; or he makes it a complement of ﴿hafizun﴾ from your saying "guard for me the rein of my horse," by implicitly giving it the meaning of negation, just as "I adjure you by God, except that you do it" is implicitly given the meaning "I did not ask of you anything except your doing it," end of quote. He means that ﴿hafizun﴾ has the form of an affirmative while its meaning is negative, i.e. "and those who have not guarded their private parts except over their wives," so the exception is a restricted exception, with ʿala attached to what precedes it, as he illustrated with "I adjure you," whose form is that of an affirmative while its meaning is negation: "I did not ask of you." These explanations he mentioned are far-fetched, and foreignness is evident in them.

His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ is intended as a category, as in His saying ﴿marry what is good for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is intended from the class of rational beings what is treated like non-rational beings, namely females, end of quote. His saying "namely females" is not good, because the word hum (they) is specific to males; he should have said "and it is females" in agreement with ma, or "they are females" in agreement with the meaning of ma. This exception is a limit at which one must stop. Concubinage is specific to men and is not permitted to women by consensus; so if a woman was married to a slave and she then owned him and freed him while owning him, the marriage is annulled according to the jurists of the regions. Al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, and Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah said: the two remain in their marriage. In His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ there is an indication of the generalization of sexual intercourse with what is owned by the right hand, and it is specific (p-397) to females by consensus, so it is as if it were said: "or what their right hands possess" of women. Regarding combining two sisters from ownership by the right hand, and between a female slave and her paternal or maternal aunt, there is disagreement. It is also specified in the verse as prohibiting intercourse with a menstruating woman, a slave woman who has been married, and one who has been subjected to zihar until he makes expiation. His saying "beyond that" includes fornication, sodomy, bestiality, and masturbation. The meaning of "beyond that" is beyond this limit which has been defined concerning wives and female slaves, and its position is as object of ibtaghā, i.e. "contrary to that." It was said: wara' here cannot be except with an omitted element, its estimate being "what is beyond that."

The majority of scholars hold that masturbation (called al-istimna', also known as al-khadkhada and jald 'Umayra; they use 'Umayra as a euphemism for the penis) is forbidden. Ahmad ibn Hanbal permitted it, reasoning that it is a surplus substance in the body, so it is permissible to expel it when there is need, like phlebotomy (al-fasd) and cupping (al-hijama). Harmala ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz asked Malik about this, and he recited this verse. A discussion took place on this matter with the chief judge Abu al-Fath Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Muti' al-Qushayri, known as Ibn Daqiq al-'Id, who argued for its prohibition with the same evidence Malik had used, namely His saying: ﴿But whoever seeks beyond that﴾. I said to him: That phrase came in the manner of what the Arabs used to do of fornication and boasting about it in their poetry, and this was so common among them that among their prostitutes there were those who bore banners, and they did not disapprove of it. As for jald 'Umayra, it was not familiar among them, and none of them mentioned it in their poetry as far as we know; so it is not included in His saying ﴿beyond that﴾. Do you not see that the place of what is permitted, which is their women, is by marriage or concubinage, so what lies beyond that is of the same kind as what is made lawful for them, namely women, and so nothing of them is lawful to them except by marriage or concubinage? And it is apparent that temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'a) does not fall under His saying ﴿whoever seeks beyond that﴾, because the term "spouse" applies to it. Al-Zuhri asked al-Qasim ibn Muhammad about temporary marriage, and he said: It is forbidden in the Book of Allah, and he recited: ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ ... the verse; and the prohibition does not clearly appear in this verse.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, read ﴿li-amanatihim﴾ in the singular, while the rest of the seven read it in the plural. The apparent meaning is the generality of trusts, so it includes whatever Allah entrusted to the servant of speech, action and belief, and so it includes all obligations, both of acts and of abstentions, and what the human being was entrusted with before; it is also possible that it is restricted to the trusts of people. The amanah is the thing entrusted, and observing it means attending to it by guarding it until it is delivered. Amanah is also used as a verbal noun, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [an-Nisa: 58]. What is delivered (al-mu'addá) is the specific entrusted object, or the statement if what is entrusted is a statement and not the verbal noun.

Al-Akhawan read ﴿'ala salatihim﴾ in the singular, while the rest of the seven read it in the plural. Humility (al-khushu') and guarding (al-muhafaza) are distinct. He began first with humility, which encompasses inner vigilance of the heart and humbling oneself through bodily acts, and then followed it with guarding, which is performing the prayer at its time with its conditions: the purity of the one praying, his clothing, and his place, and performing its pillars in the best of their forms, and this being his constant practice at every time. Al-Zamakhshari said: It was made singular first so that humility is conveyed toward the category of prayer, whatever prayer it is, and it was made plural at the end so that guarding is conveyed over its numbers, which are: the five daily prayers, the witr, the sunnah prayers attached to each prayer, the Friday prayer, the two 'Id prayers, the funeral prayer, the prayer for rain, the prayers of the eclipses, the Duha prayer, the tahajjud, the prayer of tasbih, the prayer of need, and other voluntary prayers.

﴿Those﴾, that is, those who combine these qualities, ﴿are the inheritors﴾, deserving of being called inheritors to the exclusion of others. Then he described the inheritors with His saying: ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws﴾; thus he came with a majesty and eloquence in their inheritance that is not hidden from the observer. The meaning of inheritance is what passed in Surat Maryam. The discussion has ended. And the discussion of al-Firdaws has already preceded at the end of al-Kahf.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 23, verse 5–11 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 2] ﴿and who turn away from ill speech﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3] ﴿and who are active in giving zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] ﴿and who guard their private parts﴾ ﴿except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy﴾ ﴿but whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors﴾ ﴿and who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾ ﴿and who guard their prayers﴾ ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws; therein they will abide forever﴾ ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12] ﴿then We placed him as a drop of semen in a firm lodging﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 13] ﴿then We made the drop a clinging clot, then We made the clot a lump, then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14] ﴿Then indeed, after that, you are to die﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 15] ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be resurrected﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 16].

(p-395) This surah is Meccan without dispute. In the Sahih of al-Hakim it is reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever observes them will enter Paradise," then he recited ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] up to the ten verses. Its connection to the end of the surah before it is evident, because He, exalted is He, addressed the believers with His saying ﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], up to the verse in which is ﴿that you may succeed﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], and that is in the manner of expressing hope. So His saying ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] corresponds to it, as an announcement of the attainment of the success they had hoped for.

Talha ibn Musarrif and Amr ibn Ubayd read ﴿Uflih al-mu'minun﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the lam, in the passive voice, and its meaning is "enter into success." It may be that it is from falaha (intransitive), or that aflaha comes both transitively and intransitively. Talha also read it with a fatha on the hamza and the lam and a damma on the ha'. Isa ibn Umar said: I heard Talha ibn Musarrif reading "qad aflahu al-mu'minun" (with a waw), so I said to him: Do you make a grammatical error? He said: Yes, just as my companions made errors, end of quote. He means that his basis in recitation is what was transmitted, and it is not a grammatical error, since it is according to the dialect of "akaluni al-baraghith" (the fleas have eaten me). Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is by way of vagueness and explanation. Ibn Atiyya said: it is a rejected reading. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh it is written with a waw after the ha', and in al-Lawami' the waw of the plural was omitted after the ha' because the two came together in continuous speech, and the writing was conformed to the connected form, like ﴿wa-yamhu Allahu al-batil﴾ [al-Shura: 24]. Al-Zamakhshari said: And from him, i.e. from Talha, ﴿aflah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] with a single damma without a waw, dispensing with it by it, as in the saying of the poet:
"Fa-law anna al-atibba' kanu hawli" (If only the physicians were around me)
End of quote. This is not good, because the waw in ﴿aflaha﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] was omitted for the meeting of two unvocalized letters, whereas here it was omitted out of necessity, so it is not like it. Al-Zamakhshari said: it may require it, since it affirms what is expected and negates what is expected, and there is no doubt that the believers were expecting such glad tidings, namely the announcement of the lasting of success for them, so they were addressed with what indicates the lasting of what they had anticipated, end of quote.

Khushu' linguistically means humility and abasement. The exegetes have several statements about it here. Amr ibn Dinar said: it is stillness and good bearing. Mujahid said: lowering the gaze and lowering the wing. Muslim ibn Yasar and Qatadah said: lowering the head. Al-Hasan said: fear. Al-Dahhak said: placing the right hand upon the left. From Ali: abandoning turning around in prayer. From Abu al-Darda': magnifying the station, sincerity of speech, complete certainty, and gathering of attention. In a hadith: "he (peace and blessings be upon him) used to pray raising his gaze to the sky, and when this verse was revealed he cast his gaze toward his place of prostration." Among khushu' is that one observes the etiquettes: avoiding folding the garment, fidgeting with one's body and clothes, turning around, stretching, yawning, closing the eyes, covering the mouth, wrapping (the garment over the shoulders), cracking the knuckles, interlacing the fingers, shortening (the prayer), and shuffling pebbles. In al-Tahrir it is said: there is disagreement about khushu': is it among the obligations of prayer or among its virtues and completions, according to two opinions; the correct one is the first, and its place is the heart, and it is the first knowledge to be lifted from people, as stated by Ubadah ibn al-Samit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): why is the prayer attributed to them? (I say): because prayer is shared between the one who prays and the one to whom it is prayed. The one who prays is the one who benefits from it alone, and it is his provision and treasure, so it is "his prayer." As for the one to whom it is prayed, He is self-sufficient and exalted above need for it and benefit from it.

﴿Those﴾, that is, those who combine these qualities, ﴿are the inheritors﴾, deserving of being called inheritors to the exclusion of others. Then he described the inheritors with His saying: ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws﴾; thus he came with a majesty and eloquence in their inheritance that is not hidden from the observer. The meaning of inheritance is what passed in Surat Maryam. The discussion has ended. And the discussion of al-Firdaws has already preceded at the end of al-Kahf.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 23, verse 5–11 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 2] ﴿and who turn away from ill speech﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3] ﴿and who are active in giving zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] ﴿and who guard their private parts﴾ ﴿except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy﴾ ﴿but whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors﴾ ﴿and who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾ ﴿and who guard their prayers﴾ ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws; therein they will abide forever﴾ ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12] ﴿then We placed him as a drop of semen in a firm lodging﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 13] ﴿then We made the drop a clinging clot, then We made the clot a lump, then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14] ﴿Then indeed, after that, you are to die﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 15] ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be resurrected﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 16].

(p-395) This surah is Meccan without dispute. In the Sahih of al-Hakim it is reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever observes them will enter Paradise," then he recited ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] up to the ten verses. Its connection to the end of the surah before it is evident, because He, exalted is He, addressed the believers with His saying ﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], up to the verse in which is ﴿that you may succeed﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], and that is in the manner of expressing hope. So His saying ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] corresponds to it, as an announcement of the attainment of the success they had hoped for.

Talha ibn Musarrif and Amr ibn Ubayd read ﴿Uflih al-mu'minun﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the lam, in the passive voice, and its meaning is "enter into success." It may be that it is from falaha (intransitive), or that aflaha comes both transitively and intransitively. Talha also read it with a fatha on the hamza and the lam and a damma on the ha'. Isa ibn Umar said: I heard Talha ibn Musarrif reading "qad aflahu al-mu'minun" (with a waw), so I said to him: Do you make a grammatical error? He said: Yes, just as my companions made errors, end of quote. He means that his basis in recitation is what was transmitted, and it is not a grammatical error, since it is according to the dialect of "akaluni al-baraghith" (the fleas have eaten me). Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is by way of vagueness and explanation. Ibn Atiyya said: it is a rejected reading. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh it is written with a waw after the ha', and in al-Lawami' the waw of the plural was omitted after the ha' because the two came together in continuous speech, and the writing was conformed to the connected form, like ﴿wa-yamhu Allahu al-batil﴾ [al-Shura: 24]. Al-Zamakhshari said: And from him, i.e. from Talha, ﴿aflah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] with a single damma without a waw, dispensing with it by it, as in the saying of the poet:
"Fa-law anna al-atibba' kanu hawli" (If only the physicians were around me)
End of quote. This is not good, because the waw in ﴿aflaha﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] was omitted for the meeting of two unvocalized letters, whereas here it was omitted out of necessity, so it is not like it. Al-Zamakhshari said: it may require it, since it affirms what is expected and negates what is expected, and there is no doubt that the believers were expecting such glad tidings, namely the announcement of the lasting of success for them, so they were addressed with what indicates the lasting of what they had anticipated, end of quote.

Khushu' linguistically means humility and abasement. The exegetes have several statements about it here. Amr ibn Dinar said: it is stillness and good bearing. Mujahid said: lowering the gaze and lowering the wing. Muslim ibn Yasar and Qatadah said: lowering the head. Al-Hasan said: fear. Al-Dahhak said: placing the right hand upon the left. From Ali: abandoning turning around in prayer. From Abu al-Darda': magnifying the station, sincerity of speech, complete certainty, and gathering of attention. In a hadith: "he (peace and blessings be upon him) used to pray raising his gaze to the sky, and when this verse was revealed he cast his gaze toward his place of prostration." Among khushu' is that one observes the etiquettes: avoiding folding the garment, fidgeting with one's body and clothes, turning around, stretching, yawning, closing the eyes, covering the mouth, wrapping (the garment over the shoulders), cracking the knuckles, interlacing the fingers, shortening (the prayer), and shuffling pebbles. In al-Tahrir it is said: there is disagreement about khushu': is it among the obligations of prayer or among its virtues and completions, according to two opinions; the correct one is the first, and its place is the heart, and it is the first knowledge to be lifted from people, as stated by Ubadah ibn al-Samit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): why is the prayer attributed to them? (I say): because prayer is shared between the one who prays and the one to whom it is prayed. The one who prays is the one who benefits from it alone, and it is his provision and treasure, so it is "his prayer." As for the one to whom it is prayed, He is self-sufficient and exalted above need for it and benefit from it.

﴿Al-laghw﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3] is what does not concern you of speech or action, such as play and frivolity, and what good manners require one to discard. He means that they have such seriousness that it occupies them from frivolity. When He described them with khushu' in prayer, He followed it with the description of turning away from idle talk, so as to combine for them the two difficult acts upon the self, which are the foundations of the building of obligation, end of quote. When the object of an active participle precedes it, it may be permissible to strengthen its transitivity with the preposition lam as with the verb, and likewise when it comes after; but with its preceding it is more common, which is why ﴿li-l-zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] came with lam; had it come in the accusative it would have been correct Arabic. As for zakah: if by it is meant the purifying (tazkiyah), then attributing the act to it is valid, since whatever proceeds may be said of it "was done." If by zakah is meant the amount that comes out of wealth for the poor (p-396), then it is by ellipsis, i.e. "for the payment of zakah," ﴿active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4], since acts cannot be attributed to the physical objects from the payer; or "active" is taken to include the meaning of "paying." Al-Tibrizi explained it this way. It was said that ﴿li-l-zakah﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] means "for good deeds," as in His saying ﴿better than him in purity (zakah)﴾ [al-Kahf: 81], i.e. a righteous deed; this was said by Abu Muslim. It was also said that "zakah" here means growth and increase, the lam is the lam of cause, and the object of ﴿active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4] is omitted; the estimate is: ﴿and who﴾ for the sake of achieving growth and increase ﴿are active﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4]: the good. It was said: what is spent is not called zakah until it reaches the hand of the poor. It was said: the extracted amount is not called zakah, so the expression by the act of its extraction is preferable to expressing it by "payment." In this there is a refutation of some of the heretics of the non-Arabs who were far from the taste of Arabic, in his saying: "Did he not say 'mu'addun' (payers)?" In al-Tahrir wa-l-Tahbir he said: this is what is said of "neither reason nor transmission," and the Noble Book was revealed in the most eloquent and sound of languages without dispute. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt has said:
"Al-mut'imuna al-ta'ama fi al-sanati al-azmah / wa-l-fa'iluna li-l-zakawat" (Those who feed the food in the year of famine, and those who are active for the zakawat)
No eloquent Arab replied to him, nor did the scholars of Arabic criticize it; rather, all of them cite it as proof and evidence, end of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: interpreting the verse in this way is more correct, because the word is plural in it, i.e. if zakah is meant as the amount, it is by omission of a noun, namely "for the payment of zakawat." He justified this by its being plural, meaning: when it is meant as the amount, its plural is valid; and when it is meant as the purifying, it is not pluralized, because purifying is a verbal noun and verbal nouns are not pluralized. This is not accepted; rather, some words from it have come in the plural, such as ʿulum, hulum, and ashghal. As for when they differ, most grammarians permit their pluralization, and here they differ according to their objects: paying cash is not paying livestock, and not paying plants. The zakah in Umayyah's verse is among the verbal nouns that came in the plural, so its interpretation as the amount is not exceeded merely because of its plural.

*Hafiza* does not take ʿala as its complement. It was said: ʿala here means min, i.e. "except from their wives," as min is used in the sense of ʿala in His saying ﴿and We helped him against (min) the people﴾ [al-Anbiya': 77], i.e. ʿala the people; this was said by al-Farra', and Ibn Malik and others followed him. The better view is that it is by way of implicit transitivity: ﴿hafizun﴾ is taken to include the meaning "restraining" or "confining," and both of these take ʿala, as in His saying ﴿keep your wife for yourself﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. Al-Zamakhshari here strained over several explanations. He said: ﴿ʿala azwajihim﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e. "except being in charge over their wives or being their custodians," from your saying: "So-and-so was over so-and-so, then she died leaving him and he married her," and similar to it: "Ziyad was over Basra," i.e. governing it. From this the saying "so-and-so is under so-and-so" comes, and for this reason a woman was called a bed (firash). Or ʿala is attached to an omitted element indicated by "not blameworthy," as if it were said: "they are blamed," ﴿except over their wives﴾, i.e. they are blamed for every intercourse except what has been permitted to them, ﴿for then they are not blameworthy﴾ for it; or he makes it a complement of ﴿hafizun﴾ from your saying "guard for me the rein of my horse," by implicitly giving it the meaning of negation, just as "I adjure you by God, except that you do it" is implicitly given the meaning "I did not ask of you anything except your doing it," end of quote. He means that ﴿hafizun﴾ has the form of an affirmative while its meaning is negative, i.e. "and those who have not guarded their private parts except over their wives," so the exception is a restricted exception, with ʿala attached to what precedes it, as he illustrated with "I adjure you," whose form is that of an affirmative while its meaning is negation: "I did not ask of you." These explanations he mentioned are far-fetched, and foreignness is evident in them.

His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ is intended as a category, as in His saying ﴿marry what is good for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is intended from the class of rational beings what is treated like non-rational beings, namely females, end of quote. His saying "namely females" is not good, because the word hum (they) is specific to males; he should have said "and it is females" in agreement with ma, or "they are females" in agreement with the meaning of ma. This exception is a limit at which one must stop. Concubinage is specific to men and is not permitted to women by consensus; so if a woman was married to a slave and she then owned him and freed him while owning him, the marriage is annulled according to the jurists of the regions. Al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, and Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah said: the two remain in their marriage. In His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ there is an indication of the generalization of sexual intercourse with what is owned by the right hand, and it is specific (p-397) to females by consensus, so it is as if it were said: "or what their right hands possess" of women. Regarding combining two sisters from ownership by the right hand, and between a female slave and her paternal or maternal aunt, there is disagreement. It is also specified in the verse as prohibiting intercourse with a menstruating woman, a slave woman who has been married, and one who has been subjected to zihar until he makes expiation. His saying "beyond that" includes fornication, sodomy, bestiality, and masturbation. The meaning of "beyond that" is beyond this limit which has been defined concerning wives and female slaves, and its position is as object of ibtaghā, i.e. "contrary to that." It was said: wara' here cannot be except with an omitted element, its estimate being "what is beyond that."

The majority of scholars hold that masturbation (called al-istimna', also known as al-khadkhada and jald 'Umayra; they use 'Umayra as a euphemism for the penis) is forbidden. Ahmad ibn Hanbal permitted it, reasoning that it is a surplus substance in the body, so it is permissible to expel it when there is need, like phlebotomy (al-fasd) and cupping (al-hijama). Harmala ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz asked Malik about this, and he recited this verse. A discussion took place on this matter with the chief judge Abu al-Fath Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Muti' al-Qushayri, known as Ibn Daqiq al-'Id, who argued for its prohibition with the same evidence Malik had used, namely His saying: ﴿But whoever seeks beyond that﴾. I said to him: That phrase came in the manner of what the Arabs used to do of fornication and boasting about it in their poetry, and this was so common among them that among their prostitutes there were those who bore banners, and they did not disapprove of it. As for jald 'Umayra, it was not familiar among them, and none of them mentioned it in their poetry as far as we know; so it is not included in His saying ﴿beyond that﴾. Do you not see that the place of what is permitted, which is their women, is by marriage or concubinage, so what lies beyond that is of the same kind as what is made lawful for them, namely women, and so nothing of them is lawful to them except by marriage or concubinage? And it is apparent that temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'a) does not fall under His saying ﴿whoever seeks beyond that﴾, because the term "spouse" applies to it. Al-Zuhri asked al-Qasim ibn Muhammad about temporary marriage, and he said: It is forbidden in the Book of Allah, and he recited: ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ ... the verse; and the prohibition does not clearly appear in this verse.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, read ﴿li-amanatihim﴾ in the singular, while the rest of the seven read it in the plural. The apparent meaning is the generality of trusts, so it includes whatever Allah entrusted to the servant of speech, action and belief, and so it includes all obligations, both of acts and of abstentions, and what the human being was entrusted with before; it is also possible that it is restricted to the trusts of people. The amanah is the thing entrusted, and observing it means attending to it by guarding it until it is delivered. Amanah is also used as a verbal noun, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [an-Nisa: 58]. What is delivered (al-mu'addá) is the specific entrusted object, or the statement if what is entrusted is a statement and not the verbal noun.

Al-Akhawan read ﴿'ala salatihim﴾ in the singular, while the rest of the seven read it in the plural. Humility (al-khushu') and guarding (al-muhafaza) are distinct. He began first with humility, which encompasses inner vigilance of the heart and humbling oneself through bodily acts, and then followed it with guarding, which is performing the prayer at its time with its conditions: the purity of the one praying, his clothing, and his place, and performing its pillars in the best of their forms, and this being his constant practice at every time. Al-Zamakhshari said: It was made singular first so that humility is conveyed toward the category of prayer, whatever prayer it is, and it was made plural at the end so that guarding is conveyed over its numbers, which are: the five daily prayers, the witr, the sunnah prayers attached to each prayer, the Friday prayer, the two 'Id prayers, the funeral prayer, the prayer for rain, the prayers of the eclipses, the Duha prayer, the tahajjud, the prayer of tasbih, the prayer of need, and other voluntary prayers.

﴿Those﴾, that is, those who combine these qualities, ﴿are the inheritors﴾, deserving of being called inheritors to the exclusion of others. Then he described the inheritors with His saying: ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws﴾; thus he came with a majesty and eloquence in their inheritance that is not hidden from the observer. The meaning of inheritance is what passed in Surat Maryam. The discussion has ended. And the discussion of al-Firdaws has already preceded at the end of al-Kahf.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 23, verses 12–16:

﴿Indeed, We created man﴾ (the verse), when Exalted God mentioned that those who possess these noble attributes are the ones who inherit the Paradise (al-Firdaws), this included the otherworldly return (al-ma'ad al-ukhrawi). He mentioned the first creation (al-nash'ah al-ula) so that it might serve as evidence for the soundness of the last creation (al-nash'ah al-akhirah). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is the beginning of a new discourse (ibtida' kalam), and the waw at its beginning is conjunctive, joining one statement to another, even though they differ in meaning." End of quote. We have explained the connection between them, and they do not differ in meaning in every respect. And ﴿al-insan﴾ here: Qatadah and others, and it is narrated from Salman and Ibn 'Abbas, that it means Adam, because he was drawn out (insall) from the clay.

﴿Then We made it﴾ refers back to the son of Adam, even though he was not mentioned, because the matter is well known and the meaning is suitable only for him. Its parallel is ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32]. Or, there is an elision of a modifier, meaning: "Then We made his offspring (naslahu)." It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that ﴿al-insan﴾ is the son of Adam, and ﴿a extract of clay﴾ (sulalah min tin) is the choice essence of water, meaning the seminal fluid (al-mani), which is a collective noun (ism jins). And "clay" (al-tin) is meant to refer to Adam, since his origin was from clay, just as the "vein of moisture" (irq al-tharā) is named; or it is made from clay because it is an extract (sulalah) of his two parents, who are nourished by what comes from clay. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He first created the substance of man as clay, then after that He made his substance a drop (nutfah)." End of quote. Thus he made al-insan a genus, by considering its two states and not by considering each individual descended from it. The first ﴿min﴾ (from) indicates the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah), and the second ﴿min﴾, Al-Zamakhshari said, is explanatory (lil-bayan), like His saying ﴿of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. End of quote. It is explanatory only on the assumption that the extract (al-sulalah) is the clay itself. But if we say that it is what was drawn out from the clay, then it indicates the starting point.

Al-qarar is the place of settlement, and what is meant here is the womb. Al-makin is the firmly established, and the settlement is described by it because it is firmly established in itself, such that no disorder befalls it, or because of the firm establishment of what dwells in it, so it is described thus figuratively, as in the saying "a traveled road" (tariq sa'ir), because it is traveled upon. The explanation of the nutfah (drop), the 'alaqah (clinging clot), and the mudghah (lump of flesh) has already been given.

The majority (al-jumhur) read ﴿'izaman﴾ and ﴿al-'izam﴾ with the plural form in both. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, and Aban, al-Fadl, al-Hasan, Qatadah also, al-A'raj, al-A'mash, Mujahid, and Ibn Muhaysin read the first in the singular and the second in the plural. Abu Raja', Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr, and Mujahid also read the first in the plural and the second in the singular, so the singular is meant as a genus. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The singular was placed in the position of the plural to eliminate ambiguity, because man has many bones." End of quote. This is not permissible according to Sibawayh and our companions (the Basran grammarians) except in cases of necessity (darurah), and they cited the verse:

"Eat in part of your belly, you will be chaste."

It is known that this does not cause ambiguity, because not all of them have one belly, and despite this they restricted its occurrence to cases of necessity.

﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd said: it is the breathing of the spirit (nafkh al-ruh) into him. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is his emergence into this world. A group said: the growth of his hair. Mujahid said: the completion of his youth. Ibn 'Abbas also said: his disposal of worldly affairs. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This specification has no basis; rather it is general in this and in other things, from the existence of speech and perception. Its first rank is from the time of breathing the spirit, and its last is his acquisition of intelligible concepts until he dies." End of quote, summarized. It is close to what al-'Awfi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and His saying after that supports it: ﴿Then indeed you, after that, will surely die﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said, in summary: ﴿another creation﴾ differs from the first creation with a difference that is extremely far, in that He made it a living being, speaking, hearing, seeing, and placed in every organ and every part of it wonders and marvels that cannot be grasped by description nor reached by explanation. Abu Hanifah has argued from His saying ﴿another creation﴾ that one who usurps an egg which then hatches with him is liable for the egg and does not return the chick. He said: ﴿We produced him﴾ means that the production of the spirit in him and the completion of his creation is considered a production of him. It has been said: in this there is a refutation of al-Nazzam in his claim that man is only the spirit, and God has shown that he is composed of these things; and a refutation of the philosophers in their claim that man is an indivisible thing. And ﴿tabaraka﴾ (blessed) is a past-tense verb that does not inflect, and its meaning is "exalted and sanctified." And ﴿the best of creators﴾ is an elative form (af'al al-tafdil). The disagreement concerning it, when it is annexed to a definite noun, is whether its annexation is pure (mahdah) or not pure (ghayr mahdah). Whoever says it is pure, parses ﴿the best﴾ as a modifier (sifah); whoever says it is not pure, parses it as an appositive (badal). It has also been said: it is the predicate of an elided subject, its estimate being "He is the best of creators." The meaning of ﴿al-khaliqin﴾ is "the ones who measure/determine" (al-muqaddirin), and it is a description that is applied to other than God Exalted, as Zuhayr said:

"Indeed you measure what you create, and some of the people create but do not measure."

Al-A'lam said: this is a proverb he (i.e., Zuhayr) coined. The creator (al-khaliq) is one who does not measure the leather and prepare it to be cut and sewn, and al-fary is cutting. The meaning is that when you prepare yourself for a matter, you proceed toward it, execute it, and do not fail in it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its meaning is "the craftsmen" (al-sani'in); it is said of one who makes something that he "created" it, and he cited Zuhayr's verse. He said: this term is not negated of human beings in the sense of making (al-sun'), it is only negated in the sense of bringing into existence (al-ikhtira'). Ibn Jurayj said: He said ﴿the creators﴾ because He permitted 'Isa to create. The specification of the elative form is elided because ﴿al-khaliqin﴾ indicates it, i.e., ﴿the best of creators﴾ in creation, that is, those who measure with measure.

It is narrated that when 'Umar heard ﴿Indeed, We created man﴾ up to its end, he said: ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾, and it was revealed. It is also narrated that the one who said it was Mu'adh. It has been said: it was 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, and this was the cause of his apostasy; then he embraced Islam again and his Islam was good.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿la-ma'itun﴾ with an alif, intending the occurrence of the attribute, so it is said: "You are about to die (ma'it) shortly, and dead (mayyit)," and "ma'it" is not said of one who has already died. Al-Farra' said: it is only said with reference to the future, and Ibn Malik said likewise. When the future is intended of a derived form from a triliteral root not of the pattern fa'il, it is returned to that root as long as the occurrence is not estimated. That is, it is not said of one who has died: "ma'it." Al-Zamakhshari said: The difference between mayyit and ma'it is that mayyit, like hayy (living), is a stable attribute, while ma'it indicates occurrence: you say, "Zayd is ma'it now and ma'it tomorrow," like your saying "yamutu" (he dies), and similar to it is "dayyiq" and "da'iq" in His saying: ﴿and your chest is constrained by it﴾ [Hud: 12]. End of quote. The reference in His saying after that, "after that," is to this development and production, ﴿another creation﴾, that is, and to the expiration of the term of your life.

﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be raised﴾. Exalted God alerted to the magnitude of His power by bringing into existence first, then by annihilation, then by re-creation. His mention of death and resurrection does not indicate the cessation of life in the grave, because the intent is to mention the three genera: the production, the causing of death, and the re-creation; the re-creation in the grave is of the same kind as the re-creation. The meaning of ﴿tub'athun﴾ (you will be raised) is for recompense. If you say: death is certain for everyone, and resurrection has been denied by groups and deemed unlikely, though it is certain from the standpoint of evidence, because it is possible in itself and the revelation has come with it, so it is necessary to affirm it with certainty; why then was the sentence about death emphasized with ﴿inna﴾ and the lam, while the sentence about resurrection was emphasized only with ﴿inna﴾? (The answer is): it was emphasized greatly as an alert to the human being that death should be before his eyes and he should not neglect to anticipate it, for his end is to it. So it is as if its sentence were emphasized three times for this meaning, because the human being in the worldly life strives in it to the utmost, and accumulates and hoards until it is as though he were immortal in it. So he is alerted by the mention of death, emphasized and intensified, so that he may shorten (his hopes), and know that his end is to annihilation, so that he may work for the abode of permanence. The sentence about resurrection was emphasized only with ﴿inna﴾, because it was presented in the form of something certain in which there is no room for dispute, and no denial is accepted; or because it is a decisive matter that must have its existence, so it did not need a second emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said, in summary: ﴿another creation﴾ differs from the first creation with a difference that is extremely far, in that He made it a living being, speaking, hearing, seeing, and placed in every organ and every part of it wonders and marvels that cannot be grasped by description nor reached by explanation. Abu Hanifah has argued from His saying ﴿another creation﴾ that one who usurps an egg which then hatches with him is liable for the egg and does not return the chick. He said: ﴿We produced him﴾ means that the production of the spirit in him and the completion of his creation is considered a production of him. It has been said: in this there is a refutation of al-Nazzam in his claim that man is only the spirit, and God has shown that he is composed of these things; and a refutation of the philosophers in their claim that man is an indivisible thing. And ﴿tabaraka﴾ (blessed) is a past-tense verb that does not inflect, and its meaning is "exalted and sanctified." And ﴿the best of creators﴾ is an elative form (af'al al-tafdil). The disagreement concerning it, when it is annexed to a definite noun, is whether its annexation is pure (mahdah) or not pure (ghayr mahdah). Whoever says it is pure, parses ﴿the best﴾ as a modifier (sifah); whoever says it is not pure, parses it as an appositive (badal). It has also been said: it is the predicate of an elided subject, its estimate being "He is the best of creators." The meaning of ﴿al-khaliqin﴾ is "the ones who measure/determine" (al-muqaddirin), and it is a description that is applied to other than God Exalted, as Zuhayr said:

"Indeed you measure what you create, and some of the people create but do not measure."

Al-A'lam said: this is a proverb he (i.e., Zuhayr) coined. The creator (al-khaliq) is one who does not measure the leather and prepare it to be cut and sewn, and al-fary is cutting. The meaning is that when you prepare yourself for a matter, you proceed toward it, execute it, and do not fail in it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its meaning is "the craftsmen" (al-sani'in); it is said of one who makes something that he "created" it, and he cited Zuhayr's verse. He said: this term is not negated of human beings in the sense of making (al-sun'), it is only negated in the sense of bringing into existence (al-ikhtira'). Ibn Jurayj said: He said ﴿the creators﴾ because He permitted 'Isa to create. The specification of the elative form is elided because ﴿al-khaliqin﴾ indicates it, i.e., ﴿the best of creators﴾ in creation, that is, those who measure with measure.

It is narrated that when 'Umar heard ﴿Indeed, We created man﴾ up to its end, he said: ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾, and it was revealed. It is also narrated that the one who said it was Mu'adh. It has been said: it was 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, and this was the cause of his apostasy; then he embraced Islam again and his Islam was good.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿la-ma'itun﴾ with an alif, intending the occurrence of the attribute, so it is said: "You are about to die (ma'it) shortly, and dead (mayyit)," and "ma'it" is not said of one who has already died. Al-Farra' said: it is only said with reference to the future, and Ibn Malik said likewise. When the future is intended of a derived form from a triliteral root not of the pattern fa'il, it is returned to that root as long as the occurrence is not estimated. That is, it is not said of one who has died: "ma'it." Al-Zamakhshari said: The difference between mayyit and ma'it is that mayyit, like hayy (living), is a stable attribute, while ma'it indicates occurrence: you say, "Zayd is ma'it now and ma'it tomorrow," like your saying "yamutu" (he dies), and similar to it is "dayyiq" and "da'iq" in His saying: ﴿and your chest is constrained by it﴾ [Hud: 12]. End of quote. The reference in His saying after that, "after that," is to this development and production, ﴿another creation﴾, that is, and to the expiration of the term of your life.

﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be raised﴾. Exalted God alerted to the magnitude of His power by bringing into existence first, then by annihilation, then by re-creation. His mention of death and resurrection does not indicate the cessation of life in the grave, because the intent is to mention the three genera: the production, the causing of death, and the re-creation; the re-creation in the grave is of the same kind as the re-creation. The meaning of ﴿tub'athun﴾ (you will be raised) is for recompense. If you say: death is certain for everyone, and resurrection has been denied by groups and deemed unlikely, though it is certain from the standpoint of evidence, because it is possible in itself and the revelation has come with it, so it is necessary to affirm it with certainty; why then was the sentence about death emphasized with ﴿inna﴾ and the lam, while the sentence about resurrection was emphasized only with ﴿inna﴾? (The answer is): it was emphasized greatly as an alert to the human being that death should be before his eyes and he should not neglect to anticipate it, for his end is to it. So it is as if its sentence were emphasized three times for this meaning, because the human being in the worldly life strives in it to the utmost, and accumulates and hoards until it is as though he were immortal in it. So he is alerted by the mention of death, emphasized and intensified, so that he may shorten (his hopes), and know that his end is to annihilation, so that he may work for the abode of permanence. The sentence about resurrection was emphasized only with ﴿inna﴾, because it was presented in the form of something certain in which there is no room for dispute, and no denial is accepted; or because it is a decisive matter that must have its existence, so it did not need a second emphasis. You had asked why the lam entered in His saying ﴿la-mayyitun﴾ and did not enter in ﴿tub'athun﴾; I answered: the lam makes the present tense (al-mudari') specifically for the present time in most cases, so it does not combine with the Day of Resurrection; because the operation of ﴿tub'athun﴾ on the future time (al-zarf al-mustaqbal) makes it specifically future, so the present is excluded. I said "in most cases" because it has come rarely with a future time, as in His saying, Exalted: ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Nahl: 124]. Moreover, it is possible to interpret this verse, and to maintain that the lam makes the present specifically present, by estimating an operator for "the Day of Resurrection."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 23, verses 12–16:

﴿Indeed, We created man﴾ (the verse), when Exalted God mentioned that those who possess these noble attributes are the ones who inherit the Paradise (al-Firdaws), this included the otherworldly return (al-ma'ad al-ukhrawi). He mentioned the first creation (al-nash'ah al-ula) so that it might serve as evidence for the soundness of the last creation (al-nash'ah al-akhirah). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is the beginning of a new discourse (ibtida' kalam), and the waw at its beginning is conjunctive, joining one statement to another, even though they differ in meaning." End of quote. We have explained the connection between them, and they do not differ in meaning in every respect. And ﴿al-insan﴾ here: Qatadah and others, and it is narrated from Salman and Ibn 'Abbas, that it means Adam, because he was drawn out (insall) from the clay.

﴿Then We made it﴾ refers back to the son of Adam, even though he was not mentioned, because the matter is well known and the meaning is suitable only for him. Its parallel is ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32]. Or, there is an elision of a modifier, meaning: "Then We made his offspring (naslahu)." It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that ﴿al-insan﴾ is the son of Adam, and ﴿a extract of clay﴾ (sulalah min tin) is the choice essence of water, meaning the seminal fluid (al-mani), which is a collective noun (ism jins). And "clay" (al-tin) is meant to refer to Adam, since his origin was from clay, just as the "vein of moisture" (irq al-tharā) is named; or it is made from clay because it is an extract (sulalah) of his two parents, who are nourished by what comes from clay. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He first created the substance of man as clay, then after that He made his substance a drop (nutfah)." End of quote. Thus he made al-insan a genus, by considering its two states and not by considering each individual descended from it. The first ﴿min﴾ (from) indicates the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah), and the second ﴿min﴾, Al-Zamakhshari said, is explanatory (lil-bayan), like His saying ﴿of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. End of quote. It is explanatory only on the assumption that the extract (al-sulalah) is the clay itself. But if we say that it is what was drawn out from the clay, then it indicates the starting point.

Al-qarar is the place of settlement, and what is meant here is the womb. Al-makin is the firmly established, and the settlement is described by it because it is firmly established in itself, such that no disorder befalls it, or because of the firm establishment of what dwells in it, so it is described thus figuratively, as in the saying "a traveled road" (tariq sa'ir), because it is traveled upon. The explanation of the nutfah (drop), the 'alaqah (clinging clot), and the mudghah (lump of flesh) has already been given.

The majority (al-jumhur) read ﴿'izaman﴾ and ﴿al-'izam﴾ with the plural form in both. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, and Aban, al-Fadl, al-Hasan, Qatadah also, al-A'raj, al-A'mash, Mujahid, and Ibn Muhaysin read the first in the singular and the second in the plural. Abu Raja', Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr, and Mujahid also read the first in the plural and the second in the singular, so the singular is meant as a genus. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The singular was placed in the position of the plural to eliminate ambiguity, because man has many bones." End of quote. This is not permissible according to Sibawayh and our companions (the Basran grammarians) except in cases of necessity (darurah), and they cited the verse:

"Eat in part of your belly, you will be chaste."

It is known that this does not cause ambiguity, because not all of them have one belly, and despite this they restricted its occurrence to cases of necessity.

﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd said: it is the breathing of the spirit (nafkh al-ruh) into him. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is his emergence into this world. A group said: the growth of his hair. Mujahid said: the completion of his youth. Ibn 'Abbas also said: his disposal of worldly affairs. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This specification has no basis; rather it is general in this and in other things, from the existence of speech and perception. Its first rank is from the time of breathing the spirit, and its last is his acquisition of intelligible concepts until he dies." End of quote, summarized. It is close to what al-'Awfi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and His saying after that supports it: ﴿Then indeed you, after that, will surely die﴾.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned the beginning of the creation of man and the end of his affair, He reminded him of His blessings. [p. 400] As for ﴿seven paths﴾, these are the heavens. They were called "paths" (ṭarāʾiq) because they are layered one upon another. It is said: ṭāraqa al-naʿl (he placed one sandal upon another), and ṭāraqa bayna thawbayn (he wore one of two garments over the other). This was stated by al-Khalil, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, in the same sense as His saying: ﴿layers﴾ [al-Mulk: 3]. It is also said: they are called paths because they are the paths of the angels in their ascent. It is said: because there are paths for the stars in their courses. It is said: because each heaven has a path and a form different from the other. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is also possible that the "paths" means "spread out" things, from ṭaraqtu al-shay' (I spread out the thing).

﴿And We were not unaware of the creation﴾: He, the Exalted, negated heedlessness regarding His creation, which means what He created. He is the Guardian of the heavens from falling, and the Guardian of His servants with what sets them right. That is, they are within Our sight; We manage them as We will.

﴿According to a measure﴾: according to a determination from Us, ﴿known﴾ [al-Hijr: 4], neither increasing nor decreasing, in accordance with the needs of creation and their interests.

﴿Then We caused it to settle in the earth﴾: that is, We made its place of residence in the earth. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas: Allah sent down from Paradise five rivers: the Jayhun, the Sayhun, the Dijla, the Furat and the Nile. In His saying ﴿We caused it to settle in the earth﴾ there is evidence that the resting place of what descends from the heaven is in the earth. From it come the rivers, the springs and the wells. And just as He sent it down by His power, He is able to remove it.

al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿on a going away with it﴾ is among the most indefinite and most incisive of indefinite nouns for the joint (of meaning). The meaning is: upon a way of the ways of going away with it, and a path of its paths. [End of quotation.] ﴿Dhahāb﴾ is the verbal noun of dhahaba, and the bāʾ in (bihi) is causative, equivalent to the hamza (of causation), as in His saying: ﴿would have taken away their hearing﴾ [al-Baqara: 20], that is, would have removed their hearing. In this there is a warning and a threat: that is, it is within Our power to remove it, and you and your livestock would perish of thirst. This is more emphatic in warning than His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunk, then who would bring you flowing water?﴾ [al-Mulk: 30].

Mujahid said: there is no water on the earth except that it comes from the heaven. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this may be restricted to punishment; otherwise, salty water is established in the earth even during drought, and sweet water diminishes during drought. Moreover, the traditions indicate the water that existed before the creation of the heavens and the earth, and there is no doubt that Allah placed water in the earth and sent down water from the heaven. [End of quotation.]

It is also said: what descends from the heaven originally comes from the sea. He, the Exalted, raised it by His subtlety and excellent measure from the sea to the heaven, until it became pure through that lifting and ascent. Then He sent it down to the earth so that it could be benefited from, for had it remained in its state, it would not have been benefited from because of its saltiness.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned the blessing of water, He mentioned what arises from it, saying: ﴿Then We produced for you thereby gardens﴾. He singled out these three kinds: the palm, the grape and the olive, because they are the noblest of trees and the most comprehensive of benefits. He described the palm and the grape with His saying ﴿for you therein﴾ and so on, because their fruit combines two matters: it is a fruit by which one enjoys oneself, and a food eaten fresh and dry: fresh dates and grapes, and dried dates and raisins. As for the olive, its oil is suitable both for lighting and for seasoning (condiment) together. It is possible that His saying ﴿and from them you eat﴾ is from the expression of people: "So-and-so eats from a craft that he practises, from a trade that he pursues, from a commerce by which he profits," meaning that it is his livelihood and the source from which he obtains his provision. As if He said: these gardens are the means of your sustenance and livelihood; from them you derive your provision and your living. This was stated by al-Zamakhshari. Al-Tabari said: He mentioned the palm and the grapes because they are the fruit of the Hijaz, at al-Ta'if, al-Madina and elsewhere. The pronoun in (wa-lakum fīhā) refers to the gardens, and it is more general, including all other fruits. It is also permissible that it refers to the palms and the grapes.

He coordinated ﴿and a tree﴾ with "gardens" (jannāt). It is the olive tree, which is abundant in al-Sham. The majority said ﴿Sinā'﴾ is the name of the mountain, as you say "Mount Uhud," an instance of the general being attributed to the specific. Mujahid said: the meaning of ﴿Sinā'﴾ is "blessed." Qatada said: its meaning is "the beautiful." Both opinions are from Ibn ʿAbbas. It is said: "beautiful" in Abyssinian. It is said: in Nabatean. Maʿmar reported from a group that its meaning is "possessor of trees." It is said: ﴿Sinā'﴾ is the name of a particular stone, and the mountain was attributed to it because it is found near it; this was also stated by Mujahid.

al-Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr) and al-Hasan read Sīn with a kasra (Sina'), which is a dialect of the Banu Kinana. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and the rest of the seven read it with a fatḥa, which is the dialect of the rest of the Arabs. One reading is Sayna (with a shortened vowel) with a fatḥa on the sīn. The more correct view is that ﴿Sinā'﴾ is the name of a place and that it is not derived from al-sanā' (brilliance), because the roots differ, on the assumption that Sinā' is of Arabic origin, since the nūn of al-sanā' is a radical letter, while the ʿayn of Sinā' is a yāʾ.

The majority read ﴿tanbutu﴾ with a fatḥa on the tāʾ and a ḍamma on the bāʾ. The bāʾ in ﴿bil-duhni﴾ on this reading is the bāʾ of ḥāl (circumstance), meaning ﴿tanbutu﴾ accompanied by ﴿bil-duhni﴾, that is, with the oil along with it. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Salam, Sahl, Ruways and al-Jahdari read it with a ḍamma on the tāʾ and a kasra on the bāʾ. It is said: ﴿bil-duhni﴾ is the object, and the bāʾ is extra, the meaning being "it produces oil." It is said: the object is omitted, that is, "it produces its fruit," and ﴿bil-duhni﴾ is in the position of ḥāl from the omitted object, that is, "it produces its fruit with the oil." It is said: anbata is intransitive like nabata, so the bāʾ is for ḥāl. al-Asmaʿi used to deny this and accused the one who narrated Zuhayr's verse with the word anbata:

*qaṭīnan bihā ḥattā idhā anbata al-baqlu*

(They dwelt there until, when the herbage sprouted...)

al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and Ibn Hurmuz read it with a ḍamma on the tāʾ and a fatḥa on the bāʾ, in the passive voice, with (bil-duhni) as a ḥāl. Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh read it with a ḍamma on the tāʾ and a kasra on the bāʾ, with al-duhna in the accusative. Sulayman ibn ʿAbd al-Malik and al-Ashhab read bil-dihan, with an alif. What is narrated from ʿAbd Allah's reading "yakhruju al-duhnu" (the oil comes out) and Ubayy's reading "tuthmiru bil-duhni" (it bears fruit with the oil) is taken as explanation, because it contradicts the consensual written text of the codex, and because the established narration from them is like the reading of the majority.

The ṣibgh means dipping and condiment (accompaniment to bread).

Muqatil said: ṣibgh is the olive, and al-duhn is the oil; He placed in this tree both a condiment and oil. al-Kirmani said: by analogy, ṣibgh should be other than duhn, because the conjoined is other than that to which it is conjoined. al-Aʿmash read wa-ṣibghan with the accusative. ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd Allah read wa-ṣibāgin with an alif. The accusative is coordinated with the position of bil-duhni, whether it was in the position of ḥāl or in the position of the object. Ṣibāgh is like dabgh and dibāgh. This is in the book of Ibn ʿAṭiyya. ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd Qays read wa-matāʿan lil-ākilīn (and a provision for the eaters), as if he intended it to explain ṣibgh.

He, the Exalted, mentioned the nobility of the place where this tree is, which is the mountain where Allah spoke to His confidant Musa, peace be upon him. Then He mentioned what it contains of oil and condiment, and described it with blessing in His saying: ﴿from a blessed tree, an olive﴾ [al-Nur: 35]. It is said: it was the first tree to grow after the flood.

﴿And indeed in the livestock is a lesson for you; We give you drink from what is in their bellies﴾: the explanation of the parallel of this sentence has preceded in al-Nahl.

﴿And for you therein are many benefits﴾: from carrying, riding, ploughing, and benefiting from their skins and wool. He drew attention to the abundance of their benefits and their necessities, namely drinking and eating, and included the rest of the benefits in His saying ﴿and for you therein are many benefits﴾. Then He mentioned what some livestock almost exclusively possess, namely being carried upon them, and He paired it with the ship, because they are the ships of the land, just as the ﴿ships﴾ are the ships of the sea. Dhu al-Rumma said:

*safīnatu barrin taḥta khaddī zimāmuhā*
(a ship of the land, its reins beneath my cheek)

He means the she-camel of Ṣaydaḥ, his she-camel.

When He first mentioned the beginning of human creation and its development through those stages, and the favour He bestowed by making it the means of their lives and of their attaining their purposes, He mentioned examples for the disbelievers of Quraysh from earlier nations who denied that God sends messengers and who rejected what the prophets brought from God. He began with the story of Noah, because he is the second father of mankind, just as He first mentioned Adam in His words: ﴿from an extract of clay﴾ (Al-Mu'minun 23:12). The story also connects with what precedes it, since before it comes ﴿and on the ships you are carried﴾ (Al-Mu'minun 23:22). So He mentioned the story of the one who built the ship first, and that he was the cause of the salvation of those who believed, and that those who were not in the ship were destroyed, having turned away from God's blessing. All these stories serve to warn Quraysh of God's punishments and to remind them of His blessings.

﴿What god have you other than Him?﴾ is a resumptive clause (jumlah mustanifah) that draws attention to the fact that worship should be devoted solely to the One who alone is God. It is thus a justification (ta'lil) for His words: ﴿Worship God﴾. ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾ means: will you not fear His punishment if you worship other than Him?

﴿The chiefs (al-mala')﴾ means the great and leading men of the people, and they are the ones who are most disobedient and most distant from accepting what is good.

﴿This is only a human being like yourselves﴾ means: one equal to you in humanity. ﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ (Yunus 10:34) pertains to his being specially chosen for the message.

﴿He wants to make himself superior over you﴾ means: he seeks superiority over you and wishes to lead you, as in His words: ﴿and that greatness on earth should be yours﴾ (Yunus 10:78). ﴿Had God willed, He would have sent down angels﴾: this indicates that they acknowledged angels, and this is the habit and custom of Quraysh in deeming it unlikely that God would send a human being. The reference in this may be to Noah, peace be upon him, or to what he taught them of the command to worship God and to reject their idols, or to what he brought, namely that he is a messenger of God while being a human being. How strange is the misguidance of these people, who deem the message of a human being unlikely while believing in the divinity of a stone. Their words ﴿We did not hear of this among our earlier fathers﴾ apparently show that they were being obstinate, for the time between the prophethood of Idris and Adam and themselves was not so long that it could be forgotten. They therefore resisted the truth with whatever means of resistance they could find. For this reason they said: ﴿He is only a man possessed by madness﴾, though it was well known to them that he was not mad.

﴿So wait for him﴾ means: wait and watch his condition until his matter becomes clear and the outcome of his affair is made manifest.

So he called upon his Lord, may He be exalted, to help him and grant him victory over them because of their denial of him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "bi-dal ma kadhdhabun" (in return for what they denied me) is like saying "this in exchange for that," meaning: replace for me the grief of their denial with the consolation of victory over them. Or: help me by fulfilling what You promised them of punishment, which is what they denied when he said to them: ﴿I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:59). End of quotation.

Abu Ja'far and Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿qala rabbi﴾ with a damma on the letter ba' (rabbu). Its explanation has been given in His words ﴿He said: My Lord, judge﴾ (Al-Anbiya' 21:112), also with a damma on the ba'. The explanation of most of the words of this verse has already been discussed in Surah Hud. God forbade him to address Him concerning his people with a plea for their salvation or anything else, and He explained the reason for the prohibition: that He had already decreed their drowning.
