﴿وأتْرَفْناهُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (and We gave them luxury) means: We extended to them their hopes and provisions, and We made them live in comfort. This clause may be coordinated with the relative clause of *alladhina* (those who), and the coordination would indicate that denial and disbelief were prevalent, meaning: what drove them to that was that We had given them comfort and done good to them, whereas the matter should have been otherwise, and they should have met Our blessing with faith and with affirming the one whom We sent to them. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: while ﴿وأتْرَفْناهُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (We had given them luxury), ﴿وكَذَّبُوا﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (they denied) in this condition. This meaning returns to the first meaning, namely: they denied in the condition of Our good to them, and they should not have disbelieved, and should have thanked the blessing with faith and affirmation of My messengers.

His saying ﴿يَأْكُلُ مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (who eats of what you eat) is an affirmation of humanity and a judgment of equality between him and them, and that he has no superiority over them. Apparently *ma* (what) in ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you drink) is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and the returning pronoun (a'id) is omitted, its estimate being: ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you drink) *from it*, because the conditions for omission are present, namely the unity of the governing and governed elements, as in his saying: "I passed by the one you passed by." What makes this omission good and preferable is that ﴿تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (you drink) is a verse-ending (fasila), and the indication of ﴿مِنهُ﴾ (from it) in ﴿مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you eat from it) points to it. This is in al-Tahrir.

Al-Farra' claimed that the meaning of His saying ﴿ويَشْرَبُ مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (and drinks of what you drink) is on the basis of an omission, meaning: ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] *from it*. This is not permissible according to the Basran grammarians, and no omission at all is needed, because when *ma* is a verbal noun (masdar), it does not need a returning pronoun. If you make it mean *alladhi* (which), you omit the object and do not need to supply *min*. (End quote.) He means that the estimate becomes: "of what you drink it", so the omitted element is a attached pronoun, and the conditions for permitting its omission are present in it. This is an analysis according to the rule of the Basrans, except that it loses the eloquence of the balance of the structure. Do you not see that he said: ﴿مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you eat of it), so he governed it with the partitive *min*? The balance requires that the estimate be ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] *from it*. Had the structure been "of what you drink it", the estimate "you drink it" would have been the preferable one.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun has been omitted, and the meaning is "of your drink", or *minhu* has been omitted because what precedes it indicates it. (End quote.) So his saying "the pronoun has been omitted" means "of what you drink it", and he explained it by his saying "of your drink", because what you drink is your drink.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "*idha*" (when) falls within the apodosis of the condition and is the answer to those among their people who spoke against them, meaning: you lose your minds and are cheated about your fathers. (End quote.) But *idha* does not fall within the apodosis of the condition; rather it falls between ﴿إنَّكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34] (that you) and the predicate, and the predicate is not the apodosis of the condition. Rather, that clause is the answer of the omitted oath before the *inna* of affirmation (al-muwattia). Had ﴿إنَّكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34] (that you) and the predicate been the answer to the condition, the *fa'* (then) would have been required before ﴿إنَّكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34]. Indeed, even if it were with *fa'* in a structure other than the Qur'an, that structure would not be permissible except according to al-Farra'; the Basrans do not permit it, and for them it is an error.

The grammarians differed about the analysis of the second *innakum*. What is related from Sibawayh is that the second *innakum* is a substitute (badal) for the first, and there is in it the sense of emphasis, and the predicate of the first *innakum* is omitted, because the predicate of the second indicates it. Its estimate is: "that you [will be] resurrected when you die." This omitted predicate is what governs *idha* (when). Al-Farra', al-Jarmi and al-Mubarrad held that the second *innakum* was repeated for emphasis, because the speech had been lengthened, and repetition is good in such a case. According to this, ﴿مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (brought forth) is the predicate of the first *innakum*, and what governs *idha* is this predicate. Al-Mubarrad rejected the substitution because it is not from a future tense, since the predicate of the first *inna* was not mentioned.

Al-Akhfash held that ﴿أنَّكم مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (that you will be brought forth) is estimated as a verbal noun (masdar) in the nominative, governed by an omitted verb, its estimate being: "your bringing forth occurs." According to this estimate, the conditional clause may be the predicate of *annakum*, and the answer of *idha* is that omitted verb. It may also be that this omitted verb is the predicate of *innakum* and governs *idha*.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned al-Mubarrad's view, beginning with it, and said: he repeated *innakum* for emphasis, and the separation between the first and second by the adverbial phrase made the repetition good, and ﴿مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] is the predicate of the first. This is the view of al-Mubarrad. Al-Zamakhshari said: or he made ﴿أنَّكم مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿إذا مِتُّمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (when you die) the predicate, meaning: your bringing forth when you die, and then he informed about *annakum* by the whole clause. (End quote.) This is an easy analysis with no artificiality. He said: or he raised ﴿أنَّكم مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] by a verb which is the apodosis of the condition, as if it were said: "when you die, your bringing forth occurs." (End quote.) This is the view of al-Akhfash, except that he insisted that the conditional clause be the predicate of *annakum*. We permitted in al-Akhfash's view this possibility, and that the predicate of *annakum* be that omitted verb, which governs *idha*.

In the reading of ʿAbd Allah: ﴿أيَعِدُكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (does he promise you), ﴿إذا مِتُّمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (when you die), with the first *anna* omitted.

The majority read ﴿هَيْهاتَ هَيْهاتَ﴾ with both *ta'* (final) pronounced with a fatha, and this is the dialect of the Hijaz. Harun, from Abu 'Amr, read both with fatha and with tanwin, and Ibn 'Atiyya attributed it to Khalid ibn Ilyas. Abu Haywa read both with damma without tanwin, and from him, from al-Ahmar, with damma and tanwin; he agreed with him, Abu al-Simak, in the first and disagreed with him in the second. Abu Ja'far and Shayba read both with kasra without tanwin, and this was related from ʿIsa; it is in the dialect of Tamim and Asad. From him also, and from Khalid ibn Ilyas, both with kasra and tanwin. Kharija ibn Mus'ab, from Abu 'Amr, al-A'raj and ʿIsa also, read both with sukun. This word has been manipulated by the Arabs to a great degree by deletion, substitution, tanwin and other means, and in *al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil* I mentioned about forty dialectal forms. What I choose is that when it is with tanwin and kasra, or with kasra and without tanwin, it is not a plural of *hayhat*. Sibawayh's view is that it is a plural of *hayhat*, and its correct form for him would have been ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36], except that its weakness did not require the *ya'* to appear. Sibawayh said: it is like *bay-hat* (plural of *baydah*), meaning that it is a plural. Some grammarians understood that he meant it agrees with the singular, and said: the singular of *hayhat* is *hayha*. The full treatment of this is mentioned in the science of grammar.

This word is generally not used except repeated, but it came unrepeated in the verse of Jarir:

*"Hayhat, a friend in al-ʿAqiq whom we keep company with"*

and in the verse of Ru'ba:

*"Hayhat, from one who has torn apart, his cry of distance"*

﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36] is a verbal particle (ism fi'l), which does not govern an apparent or implied subject. Here the structure is ﴿هَيْهاتَ هَيْهاتَ لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36], and the subject does not appear, so it must be held that there is an implied pronoun, its estimate being *huwa*, namely "your bringing forth." The *lam* came for clarification, meaning: "I mean, for what you are promised," as it is after *suqya laka* (water for you), so it is connected to an omitted element. I made what is far-fetched come after the verbal particle indicating distance, as it came in ﴿هَيْتَ لَكَ﴾ [Yusuf: 23] (come, I am yours), for the clarification of what it refers to. Al-Zajjaj said: the distance is "for what you are promised," or "a distance for what you are promised." His statement should be taken as an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis, because the verbal-noun status of ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ is not established. Al-Zamakhshari's statement, "whoever gave it tanwin treated it as occupying the place of a verbal noun," is not clear, because they did put tanwin on verbal particles, and we do not say that when it has tanwin it occupies the place of a verbal noun.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: at times it is followed directly by the subject without *lam*, as one says: "hayhat, the coming of Zayd," meaning: he was far. At other times the subject is omitted, and this is with the *lam*, as in this verse, the estimate being: "after existence, for what you are promised." (End quote.) This is not good, because it involves omitting the subject, and it involves a verbal noun whose governed element is retained while it is omitted; the Basrans permit none of this.

Ibn 'Atiyya also said, regarding the reading of the one who read with damma and tanwin, that it is a declinable independent noun, and its predicate is ﴿لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36], meaning: distance is for your promise, just as you say: "success is for your effort." (End quote.)

The author of *al-Lawami'* said: as for the one who said ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36] with a nominative and tanwin, these two may be independent declinable nouns raised as subjects (mubtada'), and what follows them is their predicate, with prepositions, in the sense of distance, ﴿لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36]. The repetition is for emphasis. It is also permissible that the two be verbal particles, and the damma is for indeclinability, like *hawb* in the driving of camels, but it was given tanwin because it is indefinite. (End quote.)

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿هَيْهاتَ هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36] *ma tu'aduna* without *lam*, with *ma* as the subject of *hayhat*. This is a clear reading.

And they said: "There is no life but this [ʾin hiya]." This pronoun is explained by the context of the speech, because previously they had denied the Resurrection, saying: ﴿Does he promise you that when you are dead and have become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 35], and so they asked in a manner of disapproval, reproach and mockery. Thus it implied that there is no life except their life. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is a pronoun whose meaning cannot be known except through the explanation that follows it. Its origin is: in al-ḥayatu ("there is no life") ﴿except our life﴾ of this world, then he placed (hiya, "it") in the position of "the life," because the predicate indicates it and clarifies it. From this comes the expression: hiya al-nafs tataḥammalu mā ḥummilat ("the soul bears what it is burdened with"), and the Arabs say: mā shāʾat ("whatever she wills"). The meaning is: there is no life except this worldly life, because the second ʾin (not) entered upon hiya, which has the sense of "life" indicating the genus, and so negated it, and it corresponded to the lā which negates what follows it as a negation of the genus."

﴿We die and we live﴾, meaning: some die and some are born; one generation passes away and another comes. End of quotation. Then they emphasised what they had restricted, that there is no life except their life, and they affirmed with certainty the non-existence of their being raised from their graves for recompense. This is the disbelief of the Dahriyya (materialists who attribute everything to time). Then they attributed to him the fabrication of a lie against God, in that He informed him, sent him to us, and told him that we would be resurrected.

﴿And we are not believers in him﴾, meaning: we do not confirm (him). When he despaired of their faith and saw their persistence in disbelief, he invoked against them and asked for their punishment for their denial. ﴿He said: "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ Meaning: after a little time. The ʿamma (mā) is an emphasis on the smallness (of the time), and qalīl is an adjective of an omitted noun, "time," and its meaning is close to this. It was said: that is, after death you will become regretful. And it was said: ﴿in a little while﴾ means the time of the descent of the punishment in this world, the appearance of its signs, and regret for abandoning acceptance of what their messenger brought them, at a time when return is of no benefit. The lām in ﴿they will surely become regretful﴾ is the lām of oath (lām al-qasam), and ﴿in a little while﴾ is connected to what follows the lām, either to the verb "they will become" or to "regretful." This is permissible because it is a prepositional phrase, and more latitude is allowed with prepositional phrases and adverbials than with other elements. Do you not see that if it were a direct object it would not be permissible to front it? If you say: la-aḍribanna Zaydan ("I will surely strike Zayd"), it is not permissible to say: Zaydan la-aḍribanna. What we have established, that ﴿in a little while﴾ is connected to what follows the lām of oath, is the view of some of our companions, but the majority hold that the lām of oath does not allow any of the complements of what follows it to precede it, whether it is an adverbial, a prepositional phrase or otherwise. According to the view of the majority, ﴿in a little while﴾ is not connected to what follows, but to an omitted element indicated by what precedes it, its estimated form being: ﴿in a little while you will be helped﴾, because before it he said: ﴿My Lord, help me﴾. Al-Farraʾ and Abu ʿUbayda held that the complement of what follows this lām may precede it in all cases. In al-Lawamih, from some of them, it is recorded: la-tuṣbiḥunna with a tāʾ, in the second person address. So if someone were to say that the speech is from the Messenger to the disbelievers after his supplication had been answered, it would be permissible, and God knows best.

﴿So the Cry seized them﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the cry of Jibril, upon him be peace; he cried out against them and so destroyed them.

﴿in truth﴾: with what is due, because they had deserved destruction; or with justice from God, from your saying: "So-and-so judges with truth" when he is just in his judgments. He likened them, in their destruction, to the debris (ghuthāʾ), which is what the torrent carries away of leaves and sticks that have decayed and turned black. End of quotation. From Ibn ʿAbbas: al-ṣayḥa is al-rajfa (the violent quake). It was said: it is the very punishment and death. It was said: the punishment that uproots. The poet said:

*The age cried out against the family of Zayd with a cry,*
*so that they fell upon their chins from its violence.*

Al-Mufaḍḍal said: ﴿in truth﴾ means by what cannot be repelled, like His saying: ﴿And the agony of death came in truth﴾ [Qaf: 19]. The word bʿdan ("away") is in the accusative, governed by a verb that is omitted from being expressed, meaning: they were distanced, a distancing; that is, they perished. It is said: baʿida buʿdan and baʿadan, like rashida rushdan and rashadan. Al-Ḥawfi said: ﴿for the people﴾ is connected to bʿdan. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿for the people, the wrongdoers﴾ is an explanation of the one against whom the distancing was invoked, like ﴿Come, I am ready for you﴾ [Yusuf: 23] and ﴿for what you are promised﴾. End of quotation. So it is not connected to bʿdan but to an omitted element.

﴿Then We produced after them another generation.﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 31] ﴿Then We sent among them a messenger from themselves, (saying): "Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be wary?"﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 32] ﴿The chiefs of his people, who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, and whom We had given luxury in the worldly life, said: "This is none but a human being like you, who eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink."﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] ﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves, you will then surely be losers.﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34] ﴿Does he promise you that when you die and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] ﴿Far, far is what you are promised!﴾ ﴿It is only our life of this world: we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected.﴾ ﴿He is only a man who has fabricated a lie against Allah, and we are not going to believe him.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, help me, for they have denied me."﴾ ﴿He said: "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ ﴿So the Cry seized them in truth, and We made them debris. So away with the wrongdoing people!﴾

Mentioning this story after the story of Noah shows that these people are the people of Hud, and the messenger is Hud, peace be upon him, and this is the view of most scholars. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and al-Tabari said: they were Thamud, and the messenger was Salih, peace be upon him, and they were destroyed by the Cry. At the end of the story there is: ﴿So the Cry seized them﴾, but it has not been reported that the people of Hud were destroyed by the Cry. The story of the people of Hud came in al-A'raf, in Hud, and in al-Shu'ara', directly after the story of the people of Noah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [Al-A'raf: 69].

The original usage of arsala (to send) is that it is transitive with ila (to), like its counterparts wajjaha (to direct), anfadha (to dispatch) and ba'atha (to send forth). Here it is transitive with fi (in), as the community is treated as the place of sending, as Ru'ba said:

*You sent into it Mus'ab, a man of great intrusion.*

Ba'atha also occurs in this way, in His saying: ﴿And on the Day when We raise up from every community﴾ [An-Nahl: 89], and ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised up in every town a warner﴾ [Al-Furqan: 51].

The ﴿أنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 32] (that worship Allah) — the *an* here may be explanatory (mufassira) or verbal (masdariyya, "to worship Allah"). Here the phrase ﴿وقالَ المَلَأُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (and the chiefs said) comes with a conjunction, *wa*. In al-A'raf and in the Surah of Hud, in his story, it comes without a *wa*. With *wa*, the intent is coordination with what he said, meaning that his statement, which is true, and their statement, which is false, were brought together, as if it were an informing of the contrast between the two situations. The one without *wa* is intended as a fresh start (isti'naf), as if it were an answer to an implied question, meaning: what was their reply to him? He said, and they said such-and-such.

(بِلِقاءِ الآخِرَةِ) (the meeting of the Hereafter) means the meeting with the recompense of reward and punishment in it.

﴿وأتْرَفْناهُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (and We gave them luxury) means: We extended to them their hopes and provisions, and We made them live in comfort. This clause may be coordinated with the relative clause of *alladhina* (those who), and the coordination would indicate that denial and disbelief were prevalent, meaning: what drove them to that was that We had given them comfort and done good to them, whereas the matter should have been otherwise, and they should have met Our blessing with faith and with affirming the one whom We sent to them. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: while ﴿وأتْرَفْناهُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (We had given them luxury), ﴿وكَذَّبُوا﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (they denied) in this condition. This meaning returns to the first meaning, namely: they denied in the condition of Our good to them, and they should not have disbelieved, and should have thanked the blessing with faith and affirmation of My messengers.

His saying ﴿يَأْكُلُ مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (who eats of what you eat) is an affirmation of humanity and a judgment of equality between him and them, and that he has no superiority over them. Apparently *ma* (what) in ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you drink) is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and the returning pronoun (a'id) is omitted, its estimate being: ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you drink) *from it*, because the conditions for omission are present, namely the unity of the governing and governed elements, as in his saying: "I passed by the one you passed by." What makes this omission good and preferable is that ﴿تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (you drink) is a verse-ending (fasila), and the indication of ﴿مِنهُ﴾ (from it) in ﴿مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you eat from it) points to it. This is in al-Tahrir.

Al-Farra' claimed that the meaning of His saying ﴿ويَشْرَبُ مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (and drinks of what you drink) is on the basis of an omission, meaning: ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] *from it*. This is not permissible according to the Basran grammarians, and no omission at all is needed, because when *ma* is a verbal noun (masdar), it does not need a returning pronoun. If you make it mean *alladhi* (which), you omit the object and do not need to supply *min*. (End quote.) He means that the estimate becomes: "of what you drink it", so the omitted element is a attached pronoun, and the conditions for permitting its omission are present in it. This is an analysis according to the rule of the Basrans, except that it loses the eloquence of the balance of the structure. Do you not see that he said: ﴿مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you eat of it), so he governed it with the partitive *min*? The balance requires that the estimate be ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] *from it*. Had the structure been "of what you drink it", the estimate "you drink it" would have been the preferable one.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun has been omitted, and the meaning is "of your drink", or *minhu* has been omitted because what precedes it indicates it. (End quote.) So his saying "the pronoun has been omitted" means "of what you drink it", and he explained it by his saying "of your drink", because what you drink is your drink.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "*idha*" (when) falls within the apodosis of the condition and is the answer to those among their people who spoke against them, meaning: you lose your minds and are cheated about your fathers. (End quote.) But *idha* does not fall within the apodosis of the condition; rather it falls between ﴿إنَّكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34] (that you) and the predicate, and the predicate is not the apodosis of the condition. Rather, that clause is the answer of the omitted oath before the *inna* of affirmation (al-muwattia). Had ﴿إنَّكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34] (that you) and the predicate been the answer to the condition, the *fa'* (then) would have been required before ﴿إنَّكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34]. Indeed, even if it were with *fa'* in a structure other than the Qur'an, that structure would not be permissible except according to al-Farra'; the Basrans do not permit it, and for them it is an error.

The grammarians differed about the analysis of the second *innakum*. What is related from Sibawayh is that the second *innakum* is a substitute (badal) for the first, and there is in it the sense of emphasis, and the predicate of the first *innakum* is omitted, because the predicate of the second indicates it. Its estimate is: "that you [will be] resurrected when you die." This omitted predicate is what governs *idha* (when). Al-Farra', al-Jarmi and al-Mubarrad held that the second *innakum* was repeated for emphasis, because the speech had been lengthened, and repetition is good in such a case. According to this, ﴿مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (brought forth) is the predicate of the first *innakum*, and what governs *idha* is this predicate. Al-Mubarrad rejected the substitution because it is not from a future tense, since the predicate of the first *inna* was not mentioned.

Al-Akhfash held that ﴿أنَّكم مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (that you will be brought forth) is estimated as a verbal noun (masdar) in the nominative, governed by an omitted verb, its estimate being: "your bringing forth occurs." According to this estimate, the conditional clause may be the predicate of *annakum*, and the answer of *idha* is that omitted verb. It may also be that this omitted verb is the predicate of *innakum* and governs *idha*.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned al-Mubarrad's view, beginning with it, and said: he repeated *innakum* for emphasis, and the separation between the first and second by the adverbial phrase made the repetition good, and ﴿مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] is the predicate of the first. This is the view of al-Mubarrad. Al-Zamakhshari said: or he made ﴿أنَّكم مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿إذا مِتُّمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (when you die) the predicate, meaning: your bringing forth when you die, and then he informed about *annakum* by the whole clause. (End quote.) This is an easy analysis with no artificiality. He said: or he raised ﴿أنَّكم مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] by a verb which is the apodosis of the condition, as if it were said: "when you die, your bringing forth occurs." (End quote.) This is the view of al-Akhfash, except that he insisted that the conditional clause be the predicate of *annakum*. We permitted in al-Akhfash's view this possibility, and that the predicate of *annakum* be that omitted verb, which governs *idha*.

In the reading of ʿAbd Allah: ﴿أيَعِدُكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (does he promise you), ﴿إذا مِتُّمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (when you die), with the first *anna* omitted.

The majority read ﴿هَيْهاتَ هَيْهاتَ﴾ with both *ta'* (final) pronounced with a fatha, and this is the dialect of the Hijaz. Harun, from Abu 'Amr, read both with fatha and with tanwin, and Ibn 'Atiyya attributed it to Khalid ibn Ilyas. Abu Haywa read both with damma without tanwin, and from him, from al-Ahmar, with damma and tanwin; he agreed with him, Abu al-Simak, in the first and disagreed with him in the second. Abu Ja'far and Shayba read both with kasra without tanwin, and this was related from ʿIsa; it is in the dialect of Tamim and Asad. From him also, and from Khalid ibn Ilyas, both with kasra and tanwin. Kharija ibn Mus'ab, from Abu 'Amr, al-A'raj and ʿIsa also, read both with sukun. This word has been manipulated by the Arabs to a great degree by deletion, substitution, tanwin and other means, and in *al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil* I mentioned about forty dialectal forms. What I choose is that when it is with tanwin and kasra, or with kasra and without tanwin, it is not a plural of *hayhat*. Sibawayh's view is that it is a plural of *hayhat*, and its correct form for him would have been ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36], except that its weakness did not require the *ya'* to appear. Sibawayh said: it is like *bay-hat* (plural of *baydah*), meaning that it is a plural. Some grammarians understood that he meant it agrees with the singular, and said: the singular of *hayhat* is *hayha*. The full treatment of this is mentioned in the science of grammar.

This word is generally not used except repeated, but it came unrepeated in the verse of Jarir:

*"Hayhat, a friend in al-ʿAqiq whom we keep company with"*

and in the verse of Ru'ba:

*"Hayhat, from one who has torn apart, his cry of distance"*

﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36] is a verbal particle (ism fi'l), which does not govern an apparent or implied subject. Here the structure is ﴿هَيْهاتَ هَيْهاتَ لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36], and the subject does not appear, so it must be held that there is an implied pronoun, its estimate being *huwa*, namely "your bringing forth." The *lam* came for clarification, meaning: "I mean, for what you are promised," as it is after *suqya laka* (water for you), so it is connected to an omitted element. I made what is far-fetched come after the verbal particle indicating distance, as it came in ﴿هَيْتَ لَكَ﴾ [Yusuf: 23] (come, I am yours), for the clarification of what it refers to. Al-Zajjaj said: the distance is "for what you are promised," or "a distance for what you are promised." His statement should be taken as an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis, because the verbal-noun status of ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ is not established. Al-Zamakhshari's statement, "whoever gave it tanwin treated it as occupying the place of a verbal noun," is not clear, because they did put tanwin on verbal particles, and we do not say that when it has tanwin it occupies the place of a verbal noun.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: at times it is followed directly by the subject without *lam*, as one says: "hayhat, the coming of Zayd," meaning: he was far. At other times the subject is omitted, and this is with the *lam*, as in this verse, the estimate being: "after existence, for what you are promised." (End quote.) This is not good, because it involves omitting the subject, and it involves a verbal noun whose governed element is retained while it is omitted; the Basrans permit none of this.

Ibn 'Atiyya also said, regarding the reading of the one who read with damma and tanwin, that it is a declinable independent noun, and its predicate is ﴿لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36], meaning: distance is for your promise, just as you say: "success is for your effort." (End quote.)

The author of *al-Lawami'* said: as for the one who said ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36] with a nominative and tanwin, these two may be independent declinable nouns raised as subjects (mubtada'), and what follows them is their predicate, with prepositions, in the sense of distance, ﴿لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36]. The repetition is for emphasis. It is also permissible that the two be verbal particles, and the damma is for indeclinability, like *hawb* in the driving of camels, but it was given tanwin because it is indefinite. (End quote.)

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿هَيْهاتَ هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36] *ma tu'aduna* without *lam*, with *ma* as the subject of *hayhat*. This is a clear reading.

And they said: "There is no life but this [ʾin hiya]." This pronoun is explained by the context of the speech, because previously they had denied the Resurrection, saying: ﴿Does he promise you that when you are dead and have become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 35], and so they asked in a manner of disapproval, reproach and mockery. Thus it implied that there is no life except their life. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is a pronoun whose meaning cannot be known except through the explanation that follows it. Its origin is: in al-ḥayatu ("there is no life") ﴿except our life﴾ of this world, then he placed (hiya, "it") in the position of "the life," because the predicate indicates it and clarifies it. From this comes the expression: hiya al-nafs tataḥammalu mā ḥummilat ("the soul bears what it is burdened with"), and the Arabs say: mā shāʾat ("whatever she wills"). The meaning is: there is no life except this worldly life, because the second ʾin (not) entered upon hiya, which has the sense of "life" indicating the genus, and so negated it, and it corresponded to the lā which negates what follows it as a negation of the genus."

﴿We die and we live﴾, meaning: some die and some are born; one generation passes away and another comes. End of quotation. Then they emphasised what they had restricted, that there is no life except their life, and they affirmed with certainty the non-existence of their being raised from their graves for recompense. This is the disbelief of the Dahriyya (materialists who attribute everything to time). Then they attributed to him the fabrication of a lie against God, in that He informed him, sent him to us, and told him that we would be resurrected.

﴿And we are not believers in him﴾, meaning: we do not confirm (him). When he despaired of their faith and saw their persistence in disbelief, he invoked against them and asked for their punishment for their denial. ﴿He said: "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ Meaning: after a little time. The ʿamma (mā) is an emphasis on the smallness (of the time), and qalīl is an adjective of an omitted noun, "time," and its meaning is close to this. It was said: that is, after death you will become regretful. And it was said: ﴿in a little while﴾ means the time of the descent of the punishment in this world, the appearance of its signs, and regret for abandoning acceptance of what their messenger brought them, at a time when return is of no benefit. The lām in ﴿they will surely become regretful﴾ is the lām of oath (lām al-qasam), and ﴿in a little while﴾ is connected to what follows the lām, either to the verb "they will become" or to "regretful." This is permissible because it is a prepositional phrase, and more latitude is allowed with prepositional phrases and adverbials than with other elements. Do you not see that if it were a direct object it would not be permissible to front it? If you say: la-aḍribanna Zaydan ("I will surely strike Zayd"), it is not permissible to say: Zaydan la-aḍribanna. What we have established, that ﴿in a little while﴾ is connected to what follows the lām of oath, is the view of some of our companions, but the majority hold that the lām of oath does not allow any of the complements of what follows it to precede it, whether it is an adverbial, a prepositional phrase or otherwise. According to the view of the majority, ﴿in a little while﴾ is not connected to what follows, but to an omitted element indicated by what precedes it, its estimated form being: ﴿in a little while you will be helped﴾, because before it he said: ﴿My Lord, help me﴾. Al-Farraʾ and Abu ʿUbayda held that the complement of what follows this lām may precede it in all cases. In al-Lawamih, from some of them, it is recorded: la-tuṣbiḥunna with a tāʾ, in the second person address. So if someone were to say that the speech is from the Messenger to the disbelievers after his supplication had been answered, it would be permissible, and God knows best.

﴿So the Cry seized them﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the cry of Jibril, upon him be peace; he cried out against them and so destroyed them.

﴿in truth﴾: with what is due, because they had deserved destruction; or with justice from God, from your saying: "So-and-so judges with truth" when he is just in his judgments. He likened them, in their destruction, to the debris (ghuthāʾ), which is what the torrent carries away of leaves and sticks that have decayed and turned black. End of quotation. From Ibn ʿAbbas: al-ṣayḥa is al-rajfa (the violent quake). It was said: it is the very punishment and death. It was said: the punishment that uproots. The poet said:

*The age cried out against the family of Zayd with a cry,*
*so that they fell upon their chins from its violence.*

Al-Mufaḍḍal said: ﴿in truth﴾ means by what cannot be repelled, like His saying: ﴿And the agony of death came in truth﴾ [Qaf: 19]. The word bʿdan ("away") is in the accusative, governed by a verb that is omitted from being expressed, meaning: they were distanced, a distancing; that is, they perished. It is said: baʿida buʿdan and baʿadan, like rashida rushdan and rashadan. Al-Ḥawfi said: ﴿for the people﴾ is connected to bʿdan. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿for the people, the wrongdoers﴾ is an explanation of the one against whom the distancing was invoked, like ﴿Come, I am ready for you﴾ [Yusuf: 23] and ﴿for what you are promised﴾. End of quotation. So it is not connected to bʿdan but to an omitted element.

﴿Then We produced after them another generation.﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 31] ﴿Then We sent among them a messenger from themselves, (saying): "Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be wary?"﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 32] ﴿The chiefs of his people, who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, and whom We had given luxury in the worldly life, said: "This is none but a human being like you, who eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink."﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] ﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves, you will then surely be losers.﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34] ﴿Does he promise you that when you die and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] ﴿Far, far is what you are promised!﴾ ﴿It is only our life of this world: we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected.﴾ ﴿He is only a man who has fabricated a lie against Allah, and we are not going to believe him.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, help me, for they have denied me."﴾ ﴿He said: "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ ﴿So the Cry seized them in truth, and We made them debris. So away with the wrongdoing people!﴾

Mentioning this story after the story of Noah shows that these people are the people of Hud, and the messenger is Hud, peace be upon him, and this is the view of most scholars. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and al-Tabari said: they were Thamud, and the messenger was Salih, peace be upon him, and they were destroyed by the Cry. At the end of the story there is: ﴿So the Cry seized them﴾, but it has not been reported that the people of Hud were destroyed by the Cry. The story of the people of Hud came in al-A'raf, in Hud, and in al-Shu'ara', directly after the story of the people of Noah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [Al-A'raf: 69].

The original usage of arsala (to send) is that it is transitive with ila (to), like its counterparts wajjaha (to direct), anfadha (to dispatch) and ba'atha (to send forth). Here it is transitive with fi (in), as the community is treated as the place of sending, as Ru'ba said:

*You sent into it Mus'ab, a man of great intrusion.*

Ba'atha also occurs in this way, in His saying: ﴿And on the Day when We raise up from every community﴾ [An-Nahl: 89], and ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised up in every town a warner﴾ [Al-Furqan: 51].

The ﴿أنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 32] (that worship Allah) — the *an* here may be explanatory (mufassira) or verbal (masdariyya, "to worship Allah"). Here the phrase ﴿وقالَ المَلَأُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (and the chiefs said) comes with a conjunction, *wa*. In al-A'raf and in the Surah of Hud, in his story, it comes without a *wa*. With *wa*, the intent is coordination with what he said, meaning that his statement, which is true, and their statement, which is false, were brought together, as if it were an informing of the contrast between the two situations. The one without *wa* is intended as a fresh start (isti'naf), as if it were an answer to an implied question, meaning: what was their reply to him? He said, and they said such-and-such.

(بِلِقاءِ الآخِرَةِ) (the meeting of the Hereafter) means the meeting with the recompense of reward and punishment in it.

﴿وأتْرَفْناهُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (and We gave them luxury) means: We extended to them their hopes and provisions, and We made them live in comfort. This clause may be coordinated with the relative clause of *alladhina* (those who), and the coordination would indicate that denial and disbelief were prevalent, meaning: what drove them to that was that We had given them comfort and done good to them, whereas the matter should have been otherwise, and they should have met Our blessing with faith and with affirming the one whom We sent to them. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: while ﴿وأتْرَفْناهُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (We had given them luxury), ﴿وكَذَّبُوا﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (they denied) in this condition. This meaning returns to the first meaning, namely: they denied in the condition of Our good to them, and they should not have disbelieved, and should have thanked the blessing with faith and affirmation of My messengers.

His saying ﴿يَأْكُلُ مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (who eats of what you eat) is an affirmation of humanity and a judgment of equality between him and them, and that he has no superiority over them. Apparently *ma* (what) in ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you drink) is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and the returning pronoun (a'id) is omitted, its estimate being: ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you drink) *from it*, because the conditions for omission are present, namely the unity of the governing and governed elements, as in his saying: "I passed by the one you passed by." What makes this omission good and preferable is that ﴿تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (you drink) is a verse-ending (fasila), and the indication of ﴿مِنهُ﴾ (from it) in ﴿مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you eat from it) points to it. This is in al-Tahrir.

Al-Farra' claimed that the meaning of His saying ﴿ويَشْرَبُ مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (and drinks of what you drink) is on the basis of an omission, meaning: ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] *from it*. This is not permissible according to the Basran grammarians, and no omission at all is needed, because when *ma* is a verbal noun (masdar), it does not need a returning pronoun. If you make it mean *alladhi* (which), you omit the object and do not need to supply *min*. (End quote.) He means that the estimate becomes: "of what you drink it", so the omitted element is a attached pronoun, and the conditions for permitting its omission are present in it. This is an analysis according to the rule of the Basrans, except that it loses the eloquence of the balance of the structure. Do you not see that he said: ﴿مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you eat of it), so he governed it with the partitive *min*? The balance requires that the estimate be ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] *from it*. Had the structure been "of what you drink it", the estimate "you drink it" would have been the preferable one.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun has been omitted, and the meaning is "of your drink", or *minhu* has been omitted because what precedes it indicates it. (End quote.) So his saying "the pronoun has been omitted" means "of what you drink it", and he explained it by his saying "of your drink", because what you drink is your drink.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "*idha*" (when) falls within the apodosis of the condition and is the answer to those among their people who spoke against them, meaning: you lose your minds and are cheated about your fathers. (End quote.) But *idha* does not fall within the apodosis of the condition; rather it falls between ﴿إنَّكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34] (that you) and the predicate, and the predicate is not the apodosis of the condition. Rather, that clause is the answer of the omitted oath before the *inna* of affirmation (al-muwattia). Had ﴿إنَّكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34] (that you) and the predicate been the answer to the condition, the *fa'* (then) would have been required before ﴿إنَّكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34]. Indeed, even if it were with *fa'* in a structure other than the Qur'an, that structure would not be permissible except according to al-Farra'; the Basrans do not permit it, and for them it is an error.

The grammarians differed about the analysis of the second *innakum*. What is related from Sibawayh is that the second *innakum* is a substitute (badal) for the first, and there is in it the sense of emphasis, and the predicate of the first *innakum* is omitted, because the predicate of the second indicates it. Its estimate is: "that you [will be] resurrected when you die." This omitted predicate is what governs *idha* (when). Al-Farra', al-Jarmi and al-Mubarrad held that the second *innakum* was repeated for emphasis, because the speech had been lengthened, and repetition is good in such a case. According to this, ﴿مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (brought forth) is the predicate of the first *innakum*, and what governs *idha* is this predicate. Al-Mubarrad rejected the substitution because it is not from a future tense, since the predicate of the first *inna* was not mentioned.

Al-Akhfash held that ﴿أنَّكم مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (that you will be brought forth) is estimated as a verbal noun (masdar) in the nominative, governed by an omitted verb, its estimate being: "your bringing forth occurs." According to this estimate, the conditional clause may be the predicate of *annakum*, and the answer of *idha* is that omitted verb. It may also be that this omitted verb is the predicate of *innakum* and governs *idha*.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned al-Mubarrad's view, beginning with it, and said: he repeated *innakum* for emphasis, and the separation between the first and second by the adverbial phrase made the repetition good, and ﴿مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] is the predicate of the first. This is the view of al-Mubarrad. Al-Zamakhshari said: or he made ﴿أنَّكم مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿إذا مِتُّمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (when you die) the predicate, meaning: your bringing forth when you die, and then he informed about *annakum* by the whole clause. (End quote.) This is an easy analysis with no artificiality. He said: or he raised ﴿أنَّكم مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] by a verb which is the apodosis of the condition, as if it were said: "when you die, your bringing forth occurs." (End quote.) This is the view of al-Akhfash, except that he insisted that the conditional clause be the predicate of *annakum*. We permitted in al-Akhfash's view this possibility, and that the predicate of *annakum* be that omitted verb, which governs *idha*.

In the reading of ʿAbd Allah: ﴿أيَعِدُكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (does he promise you), ﴿إذا مِتُّمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (when you die), with the first *anna* omitted.

At other times the subject is omitted, and this is with the *lam*, as in this verse, the estimate being: "after existence, for what you are promised." (End quote.) This is not good, because it involves omitting the subject, and it involves a verbal noun whose governed element is retained while it is omitted; the Basrans permit none of this.

Ibn 'Atiyya also said, regarding the reading of the one who read with damma and tanwin, that it is a declinable independent noun, and its predicate is ﴿لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36], meaning: distance is for your promise, just as you say: "success is for your effort." (End quote.)

The author of *al-Lawami'* said: as for the one who said ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36] with a nominative and tanwin, these two may be independent declinable nouns raised as subjects (mubtada'), and what follows them is their predicate, with prepositions, in the sense of distance, ﴿لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36]. The repetition is for emphasis. It is also permissible that the two be verbal particles, and the damma is for indeclinability, like *hawb* in the driving of camels, but it was given tanwin because it is indefinite. (End quote.)

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿هَيْهاتَ هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36] *ma tu'aduna* without *lam*, with *ma* as the subject of *hayhat*. This is a clear reading.

And they said: "There is no life but this [ʾin hiya]." This pronoun is explained by the context of the speech, because previously they had denied the Resurrection, saying: ﴿Does he promise you that when you are dead and have become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 35], and so they asked in a manner of disapproval, reproach and mockery. Thus it implied that there is no life except their life. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is a pronoun whose meaning cannot be known except through the explanation that follows it. Its origin is: in al-ḥayatu ("there is no life") ﴿except our life﴾ of this world, then he placed (hiya, "it") in the position of "the life," because the predicate indicates it and clarifies it. From this comes the expression: hiya al-nafs tataḥammalu mā ḥummilat ("the soul bears what it is burdened with"), and the Arabs say: mā shāʾat ("whatever she wills"). The meaning is: there is no life except this worldly life, because the second ʾin (not) entered upon hiya, which has the sense of "life" indicating the genus, and so negated it, and it corresponded to the lā which negates what follows it as a negation of the genus."

﴿We die and we live﴾, meaning: some die and some are born; one generation passes away and another comes. End of quotation. Then they emphasised what they had restricted, that there is no life except their life, and they affirmed with certainty the non-existence of their being raised from their graves for recompense. This is the disbelief of the Dahriyya (materialists who attribute everything to time). Then they attributed to him the fabrication of a lie against God, in that He informed him, sent him to us, and told him that we would be resurrected.

﴿And we are not believers in him﴾, meaning: we do not confirm (him). When he despaired of their faith and saw their persistence in disbelief, he invoked against them and asked for their punishment for their denial. ﴿He said: "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ Meaning: after a little time. The ʿamma (mā) is an emphasis on the smallness (of the time), and qalīl is an adjective of an omitted noun, "time," and its meaning is close to this. It was said: that is, after death you will become regretful. And it was said: ﴿in a little while﴾ means the time of the descent of the punishment in this world, the appearance of its signs, and regret for abandoning acceptance of what their messenger brought them, at a time when return is of no benefit. The lām in ﴿they will surely become regretful﴾ is the lām of oath (lām al-qasam), and ﴿in a little while﴾ is connected to what follows the lām, either to the verb "they will become" or to "regretful." This is permissible because it is a prepositional phrase, and more latitude is allowed with prepositional phrases and adverbials than with other elements. Do you not see that if it were a direct object it would not be permissible to front it? If you say: la-aḍribanna Zaydan ("I will surely strike Zayd"), it is not permissible to say: Zaydan la-aḍribanna. What we have established, that ﴿in a little while﴾ is connected to what follows the lām of oath, is the view of some of our companions, but the majority hold that the lām of oath does not allow any of the complements of what follows it to precede it, whether it is an adverbial, a prepositional phrase or otherwise. According to the view of the majority, ﴿in a little while﴾ is not connected to what follows, but to an omitted element indicated by what precedes it, its estimated form being: ﴿in a little while you will be helped﴾, because before it he said: ﴿My Lord, help me﴾. Al-Farraʾ and Abu ʿUbayda held that the complement of what follows this lām may precede it in all cases. In al-Lawamih, from some of them, it is recorded: la-tuṣbiḥunna with a tāʾ, in the second person address. So if someone were to say that the speech is from the Messenger to the disbelievers after his supplication had been answered, it would be permissible, and God knows best.

﴿So the Cry seized them﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the cry of Jibril, upon him be peace; he cried out against them and so destroyed them.

﴿in truth﴾: with what is due, because they had deserved destruction; or with justice from God, from your saying: "So-and-so judges with truth" when he is just in his judgments. He likened them, in their destruction, to the debris (ghuthāʾ), which is what the torrent carries away of leaves and sticks that have decayed and turned black. End of quotation. From Ibn ʿAbbas: al-ṣayḥa is al-rajfa (the violent quake). It was said: it is the very punishment and death. It was said: the punishment that uproots. The poet said:

*The age cried out against the family of Zayd with a cry,*
*so that they fell upon their chins from its violence.*

Al-Mufaḍḍal said: ﴿in truth﴾ means by what cannot be repelled, like His saying: ﴿And the agony of death came in truth﴾ [Qaf: 19]. The word bʿdan ("away") is in the accusative, governed by a verb that is omitted from being expressed, meaning: they were distanced, a distancing; that is, they perished. It is said: baʿida buʿdan and baʿadan, like rashida rushdan and rashadan. Al-Ḥawfi said: ﴿for the people﴾ is connected to bʿdan. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿for the people, the wrongdoers﴾ is an explanation of the one against whom the distancing was invoked, like ﴿Come, I am ready for you﴾ [Yusuf: 23] and ﴿for what you are promised﴾. End of quotation. So it is not connected to bʿdan but to an omitted element.

﴿Then We produced after them another generation.﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 31] ﴿Then We sent among them a messenger from themselves, (saying): "Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be wary?"﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 32] ﴿The chiefs of his people, who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, and whom We had given luxury in the worldly life, said: "This is none but a human being like you, who eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink."﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] ﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves, you will then surely be losers.﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34] ﴿Does he promise you that when you die and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] ﴿Far, far is what you are promised!﴾ ﴿It is only our life of this world: we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected.﴾ ﴿He is only a man who has fabricated a lie against Allah, and we are not going to believe him.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, help me, for they have denied me."﴾ ﴿He said: "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ ﴿So the Cry seized them in truth, and We made them debris. So away with the wrongdoing people!﴾

Mentioning this story after the story of Noah shows that these people are the people of Hud, and the messenger is Hud, peace be upon him, and this is the view of most scholars. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and al-Tabari said: they were Thamud, and the messenger was Salih, peace be upon him, and they were destroyed by the Cry. At the end of the story there is: ﴿So the Cry seized them﴾, but it has not been reported that the people of Hud were destroyed by the Cry. The story of the people of Hud came in al-A'raf, in Hud, and in al-Shu'ara', directly after the story of the people of Noah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [Al-A'raf: 69].

The original usage of arsala (to send) is that it is transitive with ila (to), like its counterparts wajjaha (to direct), anfadha (to dispatch) and ba'atha (to send forth). Here it is transitive with fi (in), as the community is treated as the place of sending, as Ru'ba said:

*You sent into it Mus'ab, a man of great intrusion.*

Ba'atha also occurs in this way, in His saying: ﴿And on the Day when We raise up from every community﴾ [An-Nahl: 89], and ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised up in every town a warner﴾ [Al-Furqan: 51].

The ﴿أنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 32] (that worship Allah) — the *an* here may be explanatory (mufassira) or verbal (masdariyya, "to worship Allah"). Here the phrase ﴿وقالَ المَلَأُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (and the chiefs said) comes with a conjunction, *wa*. In al-A'raf and in the Surah of Hud, in his story, it comes without a *wa*. With *wa*, the intent is coordination with what he said, meaning that his statement, which is true, and their statement, which is false, were brought together, as if it were an informing of the contrast between the two situations. The one without *wa* is intended as a fresh start (isti'naf), as if it were an answer to an implied question, meaning: what was their reply to him? He said, and they said such-and-such.

(بِلِقاءِ الآخِرَةِ) (the meeting of the Hereafter) means the meeting with the recompense of reward and punishment in it.

﴿وأتْرَفْناهُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (and We gave them luxury) means: We extended to them their hopes and provisions, and We made them live in comfort. This clause may be coordinated with the relative clause of *alladhina* (those who), and the coordination would indicate that denial and disbelief were prevalent, meaning: what drove them to that was that We had given them comfort and done good to them, whereas the matter should have been otherwise, and they should have met Our blessing with faith and with affirming the one whom We sent to them. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: while ﴿وأتْرَفْناهُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (We had given them luxury), ﴿وكَذَّبُوا﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (they denied) in this condition. This meaning returns to the first meaning, namely: they denied in the condition of Our good to them, and they should not have disbelieved, and should have thanked the blessing with faith and affirmation of My messengers.

His saying ﴿يَأْكُلُ مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (who eats of what you eat) is an affirmation of humanity and a judgment of equality between him and them, and that he has no superiority over them. Apparently *ma* (what) in ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you drink) is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and the returning pronoun (a'id) is omitted, its estimate being: ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you drink) *from it*, because the conditions for omission are present, namely the unity of the governing and governed elements, as in his saying: "I passed by the one you passed by." What makes this omission good and preferable is that ﴿تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (you drink) is a verse-ending (fasila), and the indication of ﴿مِنهُ﴾ (from it) in ﴿مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you eat from it) points to it. This is in al-Tahrir.

Al-Farra' claimed that the meaning of His saying ﴿ويَشْرَبُ مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (and drinks of what you drink) is on the basis of an omission, meaning: ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] *from it*. This is not permissible according to the Basran grammarians, and no omission at all is needed, because when *ma* is a verbal noun (masdar), it does not need a returning pronoun. If you make it mean *alladhi* (which), you omit the object and do not need to supply *min*. (End quote.) He means that the estimate becomes: "of what you drink it", so the omitted element is a attached pronoun, and the conditions for permitting its omission are present in it. This is an analysis according to the rule of the Basrans, except that it loses the eloquence of the balance of the structure. Do you not see that he said: ﴿مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] (of what you eat of it), so he governed it with the partitive *min*? The balance requires that the estimate be ﴿مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 33] *from it*. Had the structure been "of what you drink it", the estimate "you drink it" would have been the preferable one.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun has been omitted, and the meaning is "of your drink", or *minhu* has been omitted because what precedes it indicates it. (End quote.) So his saying "the pronoun has been omitted" means "of what you drink it", and he explained it by his saying "of your drink", because what you drink is your drink.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "*idha*" (when) falls within the apodosis of the condition and is the answer to those among their people who spoke against them, meaning: you lose your minds and are cheated about your fathers. (End quote.) But *idha* does not fall within the apodosis of the condition; rather it falls between ﴿إنَّكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34] (that you) and the predicate, and the predicate is not the apodosis of the condition. Rather, that clause is the answer of the omitted oath before the *inna* of affirmation (al-muwattia). Had ﴿إنَّكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34] (that you) and the predicate been the answer to the condition, the *fa'* (then) would have been required before ﴿إنَّكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 34]. Indeed, even if it were with *fa'* in a structure other than the Qur'an, that structure would not be permissible except according to al-Farra'; the Basrans do not permit it, and for them it is an error.

The grammarians differed about the analysis of the second *innakum*. What is related from Sibawayh is that the second *innakum* is a substitute (badal) for the first, and there is in it the sense of emphasis, and the predicate of the first *innakum* is omitted, because the predicate of the second indicates it. Its estimate is: "that you [will be] resurrected when you die." This omitted predicate is what governs *idha* (when). Al-Farra', al-Jarmi and al-Mubarrad held that the second *innakum* was repeated for emphasis, because the speech had been lengthened, and repetition is good in such a case. According to this, ﴿مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (brought forth) is the predicate of the first *innakum*, and what governs *idha* is this predicate. Al-Mubarrad rejected the substitution because it is not from a future tense, since the predicate of the first *inna* was not mentioned.

Al-Akhfash held that ﴿أنَّكم مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (that you will be brought forth) is estimated as a verbal noun (masdar) in the nominative, governed by an omitted verb, its estimate being: "your bringing forth occurs." According to this estimate, the conditional clause may be the predicate of *annakum*, and the answer of *idha* is that omitted verb. It may also be that this omitted verb is the predicate of *innakum* and governs *idha*.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned al-Mubarrad's view, beginning with it, and said: he repeated *innakum* for emphasis, and the separation between the first and second by the adverbial phrase made the repetition good, and ﴿مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] is the predicate of the first. This is the view of al-Mubarrad. Al-Zamakhshari said: or he made ﴿أنَّكم مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿إذا مِتُّمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (when you die) the predicate, meaning: your bringing forth when you die, and then he informed about *annakum* by the whole clause. (End quote.) This is an easy analysis with no artificiality. He said: or he raised ﴿أنَّكم مُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] by a verb which is the apodosis of the condition, as if it were said: "when you die, your bringing forth occurs." (End quote.) This is the view of al-Akhfash, except that he insisted that the conditional clause be the predicate of *annakum*. We permitted in al-Akhfash's view this possibility, and that the predicate of *annakum* be that omitted verb, which governs *idha*.

In the reading of ʿAbd Allah: ﴿أيَعِدُكُمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (does he promise you), ﴿إذا مِتُّمْ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 35] (when you die), with the first *anna* omitted.

The majority read ﴿هَيْهاتَ هَيْهاتَ﴾ with both *ta'* (final) pronounced with a fatha, and this is the dialect of the Hijaz. Harun, from Abu 'Amr, read both with fatha and with tanwin, and Ibn 'Atiyya attributed it to Khalid ibn Ilyas. Abu Haywa read both with damma without tanwin, and from him, from al-Ahmar, with damma and tanwin; he agreed with him, Abu al-Simak, in the first and disagreed with him in the second. Abu Ja'far and Shayba read both with kasra without tanwin, and this was related from ʿIsa; it is in the dialect of Tamim and Asad. From him also, and from Khalid ibn Ilyas, both with kasra and tanwin. Kharija ibn Mus'ab, from Abu 'Amr, al-A'raj and ʿIsa also, read both with sukun. This word has been manipulated by the Arabs to a great degree by deletion, substitution, tanwin and other means, and in *al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil* I mentioned about forty dialectal forms. What I choose is that when it is with tanwin and kasra, or with kasra and without tanwin, it is not a plural of *hayhat*. Sibawayh's view is that it is a plural of *hayhat*, and its correct form for him would have been ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36], except that its weakness did not require the *ya'* to appear. Sibawayh said: it is like *bay-hat* (plural of *baydah*), meaning that it is a plural. Some grammarians understood that he meant it agrees with the singular, and said: the singular of *hayhat* is *hayha*. The full treatment of this is mentioned in the science of grammar.

This word is generally not used except repeated, but it came unrepeated in the verse of Jarir:

*"Hayhat, a friend in al-ʿAqiq whom we keep company with"*

and in the verse of Ru'ba:

*"Hayhat, from one who has torn apart, his cry of distance"*

﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36] is a verbal particle (ism fi'l), which does not govern an apparent or implied subject. Here the structure is ﴿هَيْهاتَ هَيْهاتَ لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36], and the subject does not appear, so it must be held that there is an implied pronoun, its estimate being *huwa*, namely "your bringing forth." The *lam* came for clarification, meaning: "I mean, for what you are promised," as it is after *suqya laka* (water for you), so it is connected to an omitted element. I made what is far-fetched come after the verbal particle indicating distance, as it came in ﴿هَيْتَ لَكَ﴾ [Yusuf: 23] (come, I am yours), for the clarification of what it refers to. Al-Zajjaj said: the distance is "for what you are promised," or "a distance for what you are promised." His statement should be taken as an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis, because the verbal-noun status of ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ is not established. Al-Zamakhshari's statement, "whoever gave it tanwin treated it as occupying the place of a verbal noun," is not clear, because they did put tanwin on verbal particles, and we do not say that when it has tanwin it occupies the place of a verbal noun.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: at times it is followed directly by the subject without *lam*, as one says: "hayhat, the coming of Zayd," meaning: he was far. At other times the subject is omitted, and this is with the *lam*, as in this verse, the estimate being: "after existence, for what you are promised." (End quote.) This is not good, because it involves omitting the subject, and it involves a verbal noun whose governed element is retained while it is omitted; the Basrans permit none of this.

Ibn 'Atiyya also said, regarding the reading of the one who read with damma and tanwin, that it is a declinable independent noun, and its predicate is ﴿لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36], meaning: distance is for your promise, just as you say: "success is for your effort." (End quote.)

The author of *al-Lawami'* said: as for the one who said ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36] with a nominative and tanwin, these two may be independent declinable nouns raised as subjects (mubtada'), and what follows them is their predicate, with prepositions, in the sense of distance, ﴿لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36]. The repetition is for emphasis. It is also permissible that the two be verbal particles, and the damma is for indeclinability, like *hawb* in the driving of camels, but it was given tanwin because it is indefinite. (End quote.)

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿هَيْهاتَ هَيْهاتَ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 36] *ma tu'aduna* without *lam*, with *ma* as the subject of *hayhat*. This is a clear reading.

And they said: "There is no life but this [ʾin hiya]." This pronoun is explained by the context of the speech, because previously they had denied the Resurrection, saying: ﴿Does he promise you that when you are dead and have become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 35], and so they asked in a manner of disapproval, reproach and mockery. Its origin is: in al-ḥayatu ("there is no life") ﴿except our life﴾ of this world, then he placed (hiya, "it") in the position of "the life," because the predicate indicates it and clarifies it. ﴿We die and we live﴾, meaning: some die and some are born; one generation passes away and another comes. End of quotation. Then they emphasised what they had restricted, that there is no life except their life, and they affirmed with certainty the non-existence of their being raised from their graves for recompense. This is the disbelief of the Dahriyya (materialists who attribute everything to time). Then they attributed to him the fabrication of a lie against God, in that He informed him, sent him to us, and told him that we would be resurrected.

﴿And we are not believers in him﴾, meaning: we do not confirm (him). When he despaired of their faith and saw their persistence in disbelief, he invoked against them and asked for their punishment for their denial. ﴿He said: "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ Meaning: after a little time. The ʿamma (mā) is an emphasis on the smallness (of the time), and qalīl is an adjective of an omitted noun, "time," and its meaning is close to this. It was said: that is, after death you will become regretful. And it was said: ﴿in a little while﴾ means the time of the descent of the punishment in this world, the appearance of its signs, and regret for abandoning acceptance of what their messenger brought them, at a time when return is of no benefit. The lām in ﴿they will surely become regretful﴾ is the lām of oath (lām al-qasam), and ﴿in a little while﴾ is connected to what follows the lām, either to the verb "they will become" or to "regretful." This is permissible because it is a prepositional phrase, and more latitude is allowed with prepositional phrases and adverbials than with other elements. Do you not see that if it were a direct object it would not be permissible to front it? If you say: la-aḍribanna Zaydan ("I will surely strike Zayd"), it is not permissible to say: Zaydan la-aḍribanna. What we have established, that ﴿in a little while﴾ is connected to what follows the lām of oath, is the view of some of our companions, but the majority hold that the lām of oath does not allow any of the complements of what follows it to precede it, whether it is an adverbial, a prepositional phrase or otherwise. According to the view of the majority, ﴿in a little while﴾ is not connected to what follows, but to an omitted element indicated by what precedes it, its estimated form being: ﴿in a little while you will be helped﴾, because before it he said: ﴿My Lord, help me﴾. Al-Farraʾ and Abu ʿUbayda held that the complement of what follows this lām may precede it in all cases. In al-Lawamih, from some of them, it is recorded: la-tuṣbiḥunna with a tāʾ, in the second person address. So if someone were to say that the speech is from the Messenger to the disbelievers after his supplication had been answered, it would be permissible, and God knows best.

﴿So the Cry seized them﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the cry of Jibril, upon him be peace; he cried out against them and so destroyed them.

﴿in truth﴾: with what is due, because they had deserved destruction; or with justice from God, from your saying: "So-and-so judges with truth" when he is just in his judgments. He likened them, in their destruction, to the debris (ghuthāʾ), which is what the torrent carries away of leaves and sticks that have decayed and turned black. End of quotation. From Ibn ʿAbbas: al-ṣayḥa is al-rajfa (the violent quake). It was said: it is the very punishment and death. It was said: the punishment that uproots. The poet said:

*The age cried out against the family of Zayd with a cry,*
*so that they fell upon their chins from its violence.*

﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother﴾: i.e., their story. It is a great sign (*āyah*) as a whole, and they are signs when considered in detail. It is also possible that *āyah* was omitted from the first clause because the second clause indicates it, so that the sense is: "And We made the son of Mary a sign, and his mother a sign." As for *al-Rabwah* here, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Musayyib said it is al-Ghūṭah in Damascus, and its description is that it is ﴿a [land] of firm settlement and flowing water﴾ in the fullest sense. Abu Hurayrah said it is the plain of Ramlah in Palestine. Qatadah and Ka'b said it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Ka'b claimed that the Torah says Bayt al-Maqdis is the nearest part of the earth to the sky, and that it rises eighteen miles above the highest part of the earth. Ibn Zayd and Wahb said al-Rabwah is in the land of Egypt, and the reason for this sheltering was that the king of that time had resolved to kill 'Isa, so his mother fled with him to one of these places mentioned by the exegetes.

The majority (*al-Jumhūr*) read *rabwah* with a *ḍammah* on the *rā'*, and this is the dialect of Quraysh (*lughat Quraysh*). Al-Ḥasan, Abu 'Abd al-Raḥmān, 'Āṣim and Ibn 'Āmir read it with a *fatḥah*. Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i read it with a *kasrah*. Ibn Abi Ishaq read *rubāwah* with a *ḍammah* on the *rā'* and an *alif*. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, al-Farazdaq, and al-Sulami, as transmitted by the author of *al-Lawāmiḥ*, read it with a *fatḥah* and an *alif*. It has also been read with a *kasrah* and an *alif*.

﴿Of firm settlement﴾: i.e., level, such that one can settle there for ploughing and planting. The meaning is that it is among the good lands. It is reported from Qatadah: "Possessing fruits and water," meaning that because of its fruits its inhabitants settle there.

The address ﴿O Messengers﴾ and its speaking to them is taken to mean the calling and address of each one of them in his own time, since they did not all gather in one time to be called and addressed together. The plural form was used so that the listener would believe that a command was addressed to all the Messengers and that they were enjoined with it, and that it is therefore fitting that it be affirmed and acted upon. It was also said: the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and it came in the plural form because he stands in the position of ﴿the Messengers﴾. It was also said: so that one would understand from this that this is the method of every messenger, just as you would address a merchant by saying, "O merchants, beware of usury." Al-Ṭabarī said: the address is to 'Isa. It is related that he used to eat from the spinning of his mother, and the well-known [food] was the herbs of the wilderness. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is also possible that this announcement occurred at the time 'Isa and Mary were given shelter in al-Rabwah, and so it was mentioned by way of narration, meaning: ﴿And We sheltered them both﴾, and We said to them this that We informed them, that all the Messengers were addressed with this: ﴿And eat of the good things We have provided for you, and do righteous deeds﴾, following the example of the Messengers. "The good things" (*al-ṭayyibāt*) means the lawful, whether delicious or not. It was also said: it means what is found agreeable and pleasant of foods and fruits, and ﴿of firm settlement and flowing water﴾ supports this. He placed eating of the good things before righteous deeds to indicate that a deed cannot be righteous unless it is preceded by eating what is lawful.

﴿Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾: this is a warning on the surface, while the intended meaning is that they should follow them. ﴿And indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾ (23:52): the explanation of its like has already been given at the end of al-Anbiya'. The Kufans read *wa-inna* with a *kasrah* on the *hamzah* and with shaddah, as a new sentence (*isti'nāf*). The two Ḥaramīs (Makkah and Madinah) and Abu 'Amr read it with a *fatḥah* and shaddah, meaning (p. 409) "and because." Ibn 'Āmir read it with a *fatḥah* and without shaddah, and this is the lightened form of the heavy (*al-mukhaffafah min al-thaqīlah*). That the call to the Messengers was addressed to each of them in his own time is shown by His saying: ﴿And indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾.

His saying ﴿then they cut their affairs among themselves into sects﴾ (23:53). Here it comes with ﴿And I am your Lord, so fear Me﴾ (23:52), and this is more forceful in frightening and warning than His saying in al-Anbiya': ﴿so worship Me﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:25). This is because the former came after the destruction of many peoples, from the people of Noah and the nations after them; and in al-Anbiya', although the story of Noah and what preceded it also came before, what followed it was a sign of complete kindness and gentleness in the stories of Job, Jonah, Zechariah and Mary. Thus it was fitting to command worship of One whose attribute is such. Here it comes as ﴿then they cut [their affairs]﴾ with the particle *fa* (then), indicating that the cutting followed the command to piety, and this is an intensification of their refusal and their aversion from the Oneness of God and His worship. In al-Anbiya' it came with *wa* (and), which may carry the sense of *fa*, and may also carry the sense that their cutting came later than the command to worship. The joy of every party in what it has is evidence of [its] being in error, and that it is the thing which ought to be believed; and as if there were no doubt for them that it is the truth.

When He, exalted, mentioned those He mentioned of the nations and the outcome of their affair in destruction, when they denied the Messengers, this was an example for Quraysh. So He addressed His Messenger concerning them with His saying: ﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time﴾ (23:54). This is a threat against them, since they were divided over the affair of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): one says he is a poet, another says he is a sorcerer, another says he has madness, just as those before them had divided. As He said: ﴿Did they charge one another with it? Rather, they are a transgressing people﴾ (al-Dhariyat 51:53). Al-Kalbī said: ﴿in their confusion﴾ means in their ignorance. Ibn Bahr said: in their bewilderment. Ibn Salam said: in their heedlessness. It was also said: in their error. ﴿For a time﴾: until death comes upon them. It was said: until what they were promised of punishment comes. It was said: it is the day of Badr. It was said: it is abrogated (*mansūkhah*) by the verse of the sword.

The majority read ﴿in their confusion﴾ (*ghamratihim*, singular). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Ḥaywah and al-Sulami read *fī ghamarātihim* (plural), because each one has his own *ghamrah*. According to the reading of the majority, *ghamrah* is general when it is annexed to a general noun. Al-Zamakhsharī said: *al-ghamrah* is the water that covers a man up to his height, and so it is used as a metaphor for what they are submerged in from their ignorance and blindness; or they were likened to players in the flood of water, because of the falsehood they were upon. The poet said:

*"As if I were a striker in a flood, a player."*

He consoled the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with this, and forbade him to hasten their punishment and to be distressed at its delay. End of quotation.
