*"As if I were a striker in a flood, a player."*

He consoled the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with this, and forbade him to hasten their punishment and to be distressed at its delay. End of quotation.

Then He, exalted, made them stand before the error of their opinion that God's blessing upon them in wealth and the like was only because of His pleasure with their condition. This is a threat against them, since they were divided over the affair of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): one says he is a poet, another says he is a sorcerer, another says he has madness, just as those before them had divided. As He said: ﴿Did they charge one another with it? Rather, they are a transgressing people﴾ (al-Dhariyat 51:53). Al-Kalbī said: ﴿in their confusion﴾ means in their ignorance. Ibn Bahr said: in their bewilderment. Ibn Salam said: in their heedlessness. It was also said: in their error. ﴿For a time﴾: until death comes upon them. It was said: until what they were promised of punishment comes. It was said: it is the day of Badr. It was said: it is abrogated (*mansūkhah*) by the verse of the sword.

The majority read ﴿in their confusion﴾ (*ghamratihim*, singular). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Ḥaywah and al-Sulami read *fī ghamarātihim* (plural), because each one has his own *ghamrah*. According to the reading of the majority, *ghamrah* is general when it is annexed to a general noun. Al-Zamakhsharī said: *al-ghamrah* is the water that covers a man up to his height, and so it is used as a metaphor for what they are submerged in from their ignorance and blindness; or they were likened to players in the flood of water, because of the falsehood they were upon. The poet said:

*"As if I were a striker in a flood, a player."*

He consoled the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with this, and forbade him to hasten their punishment and to be distressed at its delay. End of quotation.

Then He, exalted, made them stand before the error of their opinion that God's blessing upon them in wealth and the like was only because of His pleasure with their condition. God, exalted, explained that this was only a respite (*imlā'*) and a drawing-on (*istidrāj*) toward sins and a dragging toward increase in sin, while they think it is hastening for them toward good things and speed in kindness.

Ibn Thabbāth read ﴿indeed We give them respite﴾ (*innamā numiddu-hum*) with a *kasrah* on the *hamzah*. Ibn Kathīr, in one transmission, read *yumiddu-hum* with *yā'*. The *mā* in *innamā* is either in the sense of *alladhī* (which), or verbal-noun (*maṣdariyyah*), or a *kāffah muhayyi'ah* (a particle that prevents the government of *inna*). If it is in the sense of *alladhī*, its relative clause is what follows it, and the predicate of *inna* is the sentence ﴿We hasten for them in the good things﴾. The link to this sentence is a deleted pronoun understood from the meaning, its estimate being: "We hasten for them by it in the good things." Its deletion is made acceptable by the length of the speech with the absence of ambiguity. Its like was mentioned in His saying: ﴿that what We give them as respite by it﴾ (23:55, as above). Hisham ibn Ma'unah said: the linking pronoun is the apparent one, which is ﴿in the good things﴾, and the original sense was: "We hasten for them in it," and then it was made apparent, saying: ﴿in the good things﴾; so there is no deletion according to this estimate. This follows the view of al-Akhfash in permitting such constructions as: "Zayd stood, Abu 'Abd Allah," when Abu 'Abd Allah is a *kunyah* (honorific by-name) for Zayd. So the "good things" in meaning are that with which they were given respite of wealth and sons. If *mā* is verbal-noun, then what is formed from it and what follows it is the verbal-noun of *inna*'s noun, and the predicate of *inna* is ﴿We hasten﴾, on the estimate of a hastening (*musāra'ah*), so the original would be "that We hasten (*an nusāri'a*)", then *an* was deleted and the verb became *marfū'* (nominative). The estimate: "Do they think that Our giving them respite with wealth and sons is a hastening for them in the good things?" If *mā* is a *kāffah muhayyi'ah*, this is the view of al-Kisā'ī regarding it here, so there is no need for a pronoun or a deletion. It is permissible to pause at ﴿and sons﴾, as you would say, "I thought indeed a man would stand," and "I thought that you are departing"; this is allowed because what follows *ḥasiba* (thought) has become a predicate and subject in meaning, though in the estimate it is a single item, since it forms from *an* and what follows it a verbal-noun.

Al-Sulamī and 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Abi Bakrah read *yusāri'u* with *yā'* and a *kasrah* on the *rā'*. If the subject of ﴿nusāri'u﴾ is a pronoun returning to *mā* in the sense of *alladhī*, or to the verbal-noun formed from *mā numiddu*, then ﴿nusāri'u﴾ is the predicate of *inna*, with no pronoun or deletion; the estimate being: "that which gives respite hastens, i.e., the one who gives respite hastens," or "it, i.e., Our giving respite, hastens." It is reported from Ibn Abi Bakrah, the same, with *yā'* and a *fatḥah* on the *rā'*, in the passive voice. Al-Ḥurr al-Naḥwī read *nusri'u* with *nūn*, present tense of *asra'a* (to hasten).

﴿Nay, they do not perceive﴾: this is a turning away from His saying ﴿Do they think?﴾, meaning: nay, they are like the beasts; they have no shrewdness or perception, so that they might consider and reflect whether it is respite and drawing-on or hastening in good. In this is a threat and warning.

﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother﴾: i.e., their story. It is a great sign (*āyah*) as a whole, and they are signs when considered in detail. It is also possible that *āyah* was omitted from the first clause because the second clause indicates it, so that the sense is: "And We made the son of Mary a sign, and his mother a sign." As for *al-Rabwah* here, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Musayyib said it is al-Ghūṭah in Damascus, and its description is that it is ﴿a [land] of firm settlement and flowing water﴾ in the fullest sense. Abu Hurayrah said it is the plain of Ramlah in Palestine. Qatadah and Ka'b said it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Ka'b claimed that the Torah says Bayt al-Maqdis is the nearest part of the earth to the sky, and that it rises eighteen miles above the highest part of the earth. Ibn Zayd and Wahb said al-Rabwah is in the land of Egypt, and the reason for this sheltering was that the king of that time had resolved to kill 'Isa, so his mother fled with him to one of these places mentioned by the exegetes.

The majority (*al-Jumhūr*) read *rabwah* with a *ḍammah* on the *rā'*, and this is the dialect of Quraysh (*lughat Quraysh*). Al-Ḥasan, Abu 'Abd al-Raḥmān, 'Āṣim and Ibn 'Āmir read it with a *fatḥah*. Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i read it with a *kasrah*. Ibn Abi Ishaq read *rubāwah* with a *ḍammah* on the *rā'* and an *alif*. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, al-Farazdaq, and al-Sulami, as transmitted by the author of *al-Lawāmiḥ*, read it with a *fatḥah* and an *alif*. It has also been read with a *kasrah* and an *alif*.

﴿Of firm settlement﴾: i.e., level, such that one can settle there for ploughing and planting. The meaning is that it is among the good lands. It is reported from Qatadah: "Possessing fruits and water," meaning that because of its fruits its inhabitants settle there.

The address ﴿O Messengers﴾ and its speaking to them is taken to mean the calling and address of each one of them in his own time, since they did not all gather in one time to be called and addressed together. The plural form was used so that the listener would believe that a command was addressed to all the Messengers and that they were enjoined with it, and that it is therefore fitting that it be affirmed and acted upon. It was also said: the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and it came in the plural form because he stands in the position of ﴿the Messengers﴾. It was also said: so that one would understand from this that this is the method of every messenger, just as you would address a merchant by saying, "O merchants, beware of usury." Al-Ṭabarī said: the address is to 'Isa. It is related that he used to eat from the spinning of his mother, and the well-known [food] was the herbs of the wilderness. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is also possible that this announcement occurred at the time 'Isa and Mary were given shelter in al-Rabwah, and so it was mentioned by way of narration, meaning: ﴿And We sheltered them both﴾, and We said to them this that We informed them, that all the Messengers were addressed with this: ﴿And eat of the good things We have provided for you, and do righteous deeds﴾, following the example of the Messengers. "The good things" (*al-ṭayyibāt*) means the lawful, whether delicious or not. It was also said: it means what is found agreeable and pleasant of foods and fruits, and ﴿of firm settlement and flowing water﴾ supports this. He placed eating of the good things before righteous deeds to indicate that a deed cannot be righteous unless it is preceded by eating what is lawful.

﴿Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾: this is a warning on the surface, while the intended meaning is that they should follow them. ﴿And indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾ (23:52): the explanation of its like has already been given at the end of al-Anbiya'. The Kufans read *wa-inna* with a *kasrah* on the *hamzah* and with shaddah, as a new sentence (*isti'nāf*). The two Ḥaramīs (Makkah and Madinah) and Abu 'Amr read it with a *fatḥah* and shaddah, meaning (p. 409) "and because." Ibn 'Āmir read it with a *fatḥah* and without shaddah, and this is the lightened form of the heavy (*al-mukhaffafah min al-thaqīlah*). That the call to the Messengers was addressed to each of them in his own time is shown by His saying: ﴿And indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾.

His saying ﴿then they cut their affairs among themselves into sects﴾ (23:53). Here it comes with ﴿And I am your Lord, so fear Me﴾ (23:52), and this is more forceful in frightening and warning than His saying in al-Anbiya': ﴿so worship Me﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:25). This is because the former came after the destruction of many peoples, from the people of Noah and the nations after them; and in al-Anbiya', although the story of Noah and what preceded it also came before, what followed it was a sign of complete kindness and gentleness in the stories of Job, Jonah, Zechariah and Mary. Thus it was fitting to command worship of One whose attribute is such. Here it comes as ﴿then they cut [their affairs]﴾ with the particle *fa* (then), indicating that the cutting followed the command to piety, and this is an intensification of their refusal and their aversion from the Oneness of God and His worship. In al-Anbiya' it came with *wa* (and), which may carry the sense of *fa*, and may also carry the sense that their cutting came later than the command to worship. The joy of every party in what it has is evidence of [its] being in error, and that it is the thing which ought to be believed; and as if there were no doubt for them that it is the truth.

When he finished speaking about the disbelievers and warned them, he followed that with mention of the believers, promised them, and described them with their most eloquent attributes. Al-ishfaq (apprehension) is a stronger form of expectation and fear. Then he mentioned the negation of shirk, which is their worship of their gods, which are the idols. The majority read ﴿yu'tuna ma ataw﴾, meaning they give what they have given, namely of zakat and charities.

﴿And their hearts are fearful﴾, that is, fearful that it will not be accepted from them because of their shortcomings; ﴿that they﴾, that is, fearful on account of their return to God, that is, fearful because of what they expect of meeting the recompense. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: this is general to all acts of righteousness, as if he said: those who do of their own selves in obedience to God whatever their effort reaches. 'A'ishah, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-A'mash, al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i read ﴿ya'tuna ma ataw﴾, meaning from the coming, that is, they do what they did. 'A'ishah said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Is it the one who commits adultery, steals and drinks wine, and while he is like that he fears God?" He said: "No, O daughter of al-Siddiq, rather it is the one who prays, fasts and gives charity, and while he is like that he fears God that it may not be accepted." It has been said: the fear of the knower regarding his obedience is greater than his fear regarding his disobedience, because disobedience is erased by repentance, while obedience requires correction. Al-Hasan said: the believer combines good deeds and compassion, while the hypocrite combines wrongdoing and a sense of security. al-A'mash read ﴿innahum﴾ with a kasrah. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the arrangement of these attributes is at the peak of excellence, because the first indicates the presence of intense fear which necessitates caution; the second indicates the attainment of belief in God; the third indicates abandoning showing off in obedience; and the fourth indicates that one who combines these three attributes performs acts of obedience together with fear of falling short, and this is the highest station of the Siddiqin (the truthful ones), end of quote.

﴿Those hasten to good things﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 61]: the clause is in the position of the predicate of inna. Ibn Zayd said: ﴿al-khayrat﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 61] means secret devotion, faith, and refraining from shirk. al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿yusari'una fi al-khayrat﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 61] may have two meanings: one is that they desire acts of obedience with the utmost desire and so hasten to them; the second is that they hasten to worldly benefits and the forms of honour, as He said: ﴿So God gave them the reward of this world and the goodly reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 148], and ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world, and in the Hereafter he is surely among the righteous﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 27]; because when these things are hastened to them, they have hastened to attain them and to seize them early. It is said: "asra'tu ila al-shay'" and "sra'tu ilayhi" with one meaning. As for al-musara'ah (hastening), it is competition, that is, they hasten ahead of others. al-Zajjaj said: ﴿yusari'una﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 61] is more intensive than ﴿yusri'una﴾, end of quote. ﴿And their hearts are fearful﴾, that is, fearful that it will not be accepted from them because of their shortcomings; ﴿that they﴾, that is, fearful on account of their return to God, that is, fearful because of what they expect of meeting the recompense. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: this is general to all acts of righteousness, as if he said: those who do of their own selves in obedience to God whatever their effort reaches. 'A'ishah, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-A'mash, al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i read ﴿ya'tuna ma ataw﴾, meaning from the coming, that is, they do what they did. 'A'ishah said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Is it the one who commits adultery, steals and drinks wine, and while he is like that he fears God?" He said: "No, O daughter of al-Siddiq, rather it is the one who prays, fasts and gives charity, and while he is like that he fears God that it may not be accepted." It is said: "asra'tu ila al-shay'" and "sra'tu ilayhi" with one meaning. As for al-musara'ah (hastening), it is competition, that is, they hasten ahead of others. al-Zajjaj said: ﴿yusari'una﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 61] is more intensive than ﴿yusri'una﴾, end of quote. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 23, verses 61–67:**

﴿And they race toward them (al-khayrat), and they are foremost in them.﴾ The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *lahā* ("for it" / "toward it") refers to *al-khayrat* (the good deeds), meaning *sabiqūna ilayhā* ("they outstrip others to them"). One says *sabaqtu li-kadha* and *sabaqtu ilā kadha* ("I preceded toward such a thing"). The object of *sābiqūn* is omitted, meaning *sābiqūna al-nās* ("outstripping the people"). The sentence then serves as an emphasis on the preceding one, indicating the renewal of the action through the words *yusāri'ūn* ("they hasten") and its firmness through *sābiqūn*. It has also been said that the *lām* is causal, meaning "for their sake they outstrip the people toward the pleasure of God." Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Lahā sābiqūn* means they are doers of outstripping for its sake, or they outstrip the people for its sake," end quote. In my view, these two statements amount to one and the same meaning. He also said: "Or *iyyāhā sābiqūn*, meaning they attain it before the Hereafter, since it was hastened for them in this world," end quote. The words *lahā sābiqūn* do not indicate this interpretation, because the outstripping of one thing by another indicates the precedence of the one who outstrips over the one who is outstripped. How, then, could it be said to them, while they are outstripping the good deeds, that this is not valid? Al-Zamakhshari also said: "It is permissible that *lahā sābiqūn* be a predicate after a predicate, and the meaning of *wa-hum lahā* is like the meaning of His saying *anta lahā* ('you are for it')," end quote. This is related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The meaning is that happiness preceded for them in eternity, so they are for it." Al-Tabari preferred this, on the grounds that the *lām* is firmly established in meaning. The apparent meaning, however, is the first view, and the rest is forced and an imposition on the wording beyond its apparent sense. It has also been said that the pronoun in *lahā* refers to Paradise, and it has been said that it refers to the nations.

﴿And We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity.﴾ The discussion of the like of this sentence has already passed at the end of al-Baqarah. ﴿And with Us is a Book that speaks with the truth.﴾ That is, it is a Book in which the deeds of creation are counted, pointing to the pages from which they will read what has been recorded for them in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). It has been said that it is the Qur'an.

﴿But their hearts are in confusion about this.﴾ That is, the hearts of the disbelievers are in misguidance, which has overwhelmed them as water overwhelms. *Min hadha* ("about this") means: about this work with which the believers were described, or about the Book that is with Us, or about the Qur'an. The meaning is: from abandoning this and leaving it. Or it points to the religion in its entirety, or to Muhammad. There are five opinions.

﴿And they have deeds other than that.﴾ That is, other than the overwhelming confusion and misguidance that encompasses them. The meaning is that they are astray and turn away from the truth, and yet along with that they have efforts of corruption. God, exalted is He, described them with two evil states. Qatadah and Abu al-Aliyah said this. According to this interpretation, the statement is about what has already passed of their deeds and what they are in. It has been said that the reference of *bi-dhālika* ("other than that") is to *min hadha*, as if He said to them: they have deeds other than the truth, or other than the Qur'an and the like. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: He only informed by His saying *wa-lahum a'mālun* about what will be started of their deeds, meaning that they have deeds of corruption. From Ibn Abbas: *a'mālun* ("deeds") are evil deeds short of polytheism. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Wa-lahum a'mālun* means deeds that exceed and transgress that, meaning: for what the believers were described with, they are habituated to them, harmed by them, and not weaned from them until God seizes them with punishment. This *ḥattā* is the one after which speech begins, and the speech is the conditional clause," end quote. It has also been said that the pronoun in His saying *bal qulūbuhum* ("but their hearts") refers to the believers who are fearful, *fī ghamratin min hadhā* ("in confusion about this"), a description of them as bewildered, as if He said: "they" with that fear and dread are like those bewildered about their deeds: are they accepted or rejected?

﴿And they have deeds other than that.﴾ That is, of the supererogatory acts and forms of righteousness, apart from what they are upon. By the first *a'māl* he means the obligatory duties, and by the second the supererogatory acts.

﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones...﴾ This is a return to the description of the disbelievers. Abu Muslim said this. Abu Abd Allah al-Razi said: "This is preferable, because when it is possible to refer the speech to what is connected with it, it is better than referring it to what comes after it, especially since it encourages a person to good by mentioning that their deeds are preserved, just as it warns against evil by this, and it describes intense thought about the matter of the Hereafter, that their heart is in confusion, and is meant that thought has taken hold of it about its acceptance or rejection, and about whether one has discharged it as required or fallen short." If it is asked: what is meant by His saying *min hadhā* ("about this")? We say: it is a reference to their fear and dread between the dominance of that over their hearts," end quote. Al-Zamakhshari's statement about *ḥattā* was mentioned before: that it is the one after which speech begins, and that it is the end point of what precedes it. This was refuted by the fact that they are habituated to them until God seizes them with punishment. Al-Hawfi said: "*Ḥattā* is an end point and it is conjunctive; *idhā* is an adverb that is attached to what follows it and carries the meaning of a condition; the second *idhā* stands in the position of the answer to the first. The meaning of the sentence governs *idhā*, and the estimate is *ja'arū* ('they cried out'), so *ja'arū* is the governing word of the first *idhā*, and *akhadhnā* ('We seized') is the governing word of the second," end quote. This is speech that is confused and does not deserve to be answered. Ibn Atiyyah said: "*Ḥattā* is only a particle of beginning, and the second *idhā*, which is the answer, prevents *ḥattā* from being an end point for *'āmilūna* ('doing')," end quote. Makki said: "That is, for the disbelievers of Quraysh there are deeds of evil apart from the deeds of the people of righteousness."

﴿They are doing them...﴾ until God seizes the people of blessing and insolence among them.

﴿With punishment, when they...﴾ cry out and implore. *Al-mutrafūn* are those given luxury, the wealthy and the leaders. The punishment was famine for seven years and hunger, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) invoked against them, saying: "O God, press Your foot down hard upon Mudar, and make it upon them as years like the years of Joseph." So God tested them with famine until they ate carrion, dogs, burnt bones, cured hide, and children. It has been said that the punishment was their killing on the Day of Badr. It has been said that it is the punishment of the Hereafter. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *idhā hum* refers to *mutrafīhim*, since they are the ones spoken of, who cried out when punishment descended upon them. It has been said that it refers to those remaining after those who were punished. Ibn Juraij said: "Those punished are the dead of Badr, and those who *yaj'arūna* ('cry out') are the people of Makkah, because they wailed and implored."

﴿Do not cry out today...﴾ That is, it will be said to them, either literally, the angels saying this to them, or figuratively, meaning the tongue of the situation says this. This is if those who cry out are the ones punished. According to the view of Ibn Juraij, the speaker is not the angels. Qatadah said: "*Yaj'arūna* means they cry out in repentance, but nothing is accepted from them." Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "*Tajarūn* means you lament (tajza'ūn)," expressing crying out by lamentation, since lamentation is its cause.

﴿Indeed, from Us you will not be helped.﴾ That is, you will not be protected from Our punishment, or there will be no help for you from Our side. So the neighbourhood (of the sacred house) will not benefit you, nor will it avail you.

﴿My signs were recited to you...﴾ *Āyātī* ("My signs") are the verses of the Qur'an. *Tankiṣūna* ("you turned back") means you return, a metaphor for turning away from the truth. Ali ibn Abi Talib read *tankuṣūna* with a *ḍamma* on the *kāf*. The pronoun in *bihi* ("by it") refers to the verbal noun indicated by *tankiṣūna*, meaning by the backing away and distancing from hearing the signs. Or it refers to the signs, since they carry the meaning of the Book. *Mustakbirīn* ("arrogant") was made to carry the meaning of "denying," so it takes *bi-* as complement. Or the *bā'* indicates cause, meaning arrogance and defiance arise in you because of hearing it. The majority hold that the pronoun in *bihi* refers to the Sacred Precinct and the Mosque, even though no mention of it has preceded, and what justified this implicit reference was that they were well known for their arrogance regarding the House, and that they had no miracle except that they were its custodians and those who maintained it. Munthir ibn Sa'id mentioned that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and what strengthens this is that in His saying *tutlā 'alaykum* ("recited to you") there is an indication of the one who recites, who is the Messenger (peace be upon him). These are views in which *bihi* is attached to *mustakbirīn*. It has also been said that it is attached to *sāmiran* ("conversing by night"), meaning you converse at night, mentioning the Qur'an and disparaging it. They used to gather around the House at night conversing, and most of their nightly conversation was about the Qur'an, calling it sorcery and poetry and reviling the one who brought it.

The majority read *sāmiran*, while Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Abu Haywah, Ibn Muhaysin, Ikrimah, al-Za'farani, and Mahbub from Abu Amr read *sumaran* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn* and a shadda on the *mīm* with a *fatḥa*, the plural of *sāmir*. Also Ibn Abbas, Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Raja', and Abu Nahik read it so, and with an added *alif* between the *mīm* and the *rā'* it is also the plural of *sāmir*. Both are regular plurals in the pattern of *sāmir*.

The majority read *tahjurūna* with a *fatḥa* on the *tā'* and a *ḍamma* on the *jīm*. Ibn Abi Asim transmitted it with a *yā'* as a shift of person (*iltifāt*). Ibn Abbas said: "*Tahjurūna* means you abandon the truth and the remembrance of God, cutting it off, from *al-hajr* (abandonment)." Ibn Zayd and Abu Hatim said: it is from *hajara al-marīḍu* when the sick person raves, meaning they speak idle talk. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Muhaysin, Nafi', and Humayd read it with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'* and a *kasra* on the *jīm*, the present tense of *ahjara*, meaning they say *al-hujr* with a *ḍamma* on the *hā'*, which is foul speech. Ibn Abbas said: "It refers to reviling the Companions and others." Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Zayd ibn Ali, Ikrimah, Abu Nahik, Ibn Muhaysin, and Abu Haywah also read it so, except that they put a *fatḥa* on the *hā'* and a shadda on the *jīm*, which is an intensive form of *hajjara*, the past tense of *al-hajar* with a *fatḥa*, meaning the opposite of connection, or raving, or the past tense of *al-hujr*, which is foul speech. Ibn Jinni said: "If it were said that the meaning is that you are excessive in openly declaring, to the extent that if you were conversing by night, it is as if you were abandoning (the truth) in the midday heat, in exposure, this would be a valid reading."

﴿And they have deeds other than that.﴾ That is, other than the overwhelming confusion and misguidance that encompasses them. The meaning is that they are astray and turn away from the truth, and yet along with that they have efforts of corruption. God, exalted is He, described them with two evil states. Qatadah and Abu al-Aliyah said this. According to this interpretation, the statement is about what has already passed of their deeds and what they are in. It has been said that the reference of *bi-dhālika* ("other than that") is to *min hadha*, as if He said to them: they have deeds other than the truth, or other than the Qur'an and the like. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: He only informed by His saying *wa-lahum a'mālun* about what will be started of their deeds, meaning that they have deeds of corruption. From Ibn Abbas: *a'mālun* ("deeds") are evil deeds short of polytheism. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Wa-lahum a'mālun* means deeds that exceed and transgress that, meaning: for what the believers were described with, they are habituated to them, harmed by them, and not weaned from them until God seizes them with punishment. This *ḥattā* is the one after which speech begins, and the speech is the conditional clause," end quote. It has also been said that the pronoun in His saying *bal qulūbuhum* ("but their hearts") refers to the believers who are fearful, *fī ghamratin min hadhā* ("in confusion about this"), a description of them as bewildered, as if He said: "they" with that fear and dread are like those bewildered about their deeds: are they accepted or rejected?

﴿And they have deeds other than that.﴾ That is, of the supererogatory acts and forms of righteousness, apart from what they are upon. By the first *a'māl* he means the obligatory duties, and by the second the supererogatory acts.

﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones...﴾ This is a return to the description of the disbelievers. Abu Muslim said this. Abu Abd Allah al-Razi said: "This is preferable, because when it is possible to refer the speech to what is connected with it, it is better than referring it to what comes after it, especially since it encourages a person to good by mentioning that their deeds are preserved, just as it warns against evil by this, and it describes intense thought about the matter of the Hereafter, that their heart is in confusion, and is meant that thought has taken hold of it about its acceptance or rejection, and about whether one has discharged it as required or fallen short." If it is asked: what is meant by His saying *min hadhā* ("about this")? We say: it is a reference to their fear and dread between the dominance of that over their hearts," end quote. Al-Zamakhshari's statement about *ḥattā* was mentioned before: that it is the one after which speech begins, and that it is the end point of what precedes it. This was refuted by the fact that they are habituated to them until God seizes them with punishment. Al-Hawfi said: "*Ḥattā* is an end point and it is conjunctive; *idhā* is an adverb that is attached to what follows it and carries the meaning of a condition; the second *idhā* stands in the position of the answer to the first. The meaning of the sentence governs *idhā*, and the estimate is *ja'arū* ('they cried out'), so *ja'arū* is the governing word of the first *idhā*, and *akhadhnā* ('We seized') is the governing word of the second," end quote. This is speech that is confused and does not deserve to be answered. Ibn Atiyyah said: "*Ḥattā* is only a particle of beginning, and the second *idhā*, which is the answer, prevents *ḥattā* from being an end point for *'āmilūna* ('doing')," end quote. Makki said: "That is, for the disbelievers of Quraysh there are deeds of evil apart from the deeds of the people of righteousness."

﴿They are doing them...﴾ until God seizes the people of blessing and insolence among them.

﴿With punishment, when they...﴾ cry out and implore. *Al-mutrafūn* are those given luxury, the wealthy and the leaders. The punishment was famine for seven years and hunger, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) invoked against them, saying: "O God, press Your foot down hard upon Mudar, and make it upon them as years like the years of Joseph." So God tested them with famine until they ate carrion, dogs, burnt bones, cured hide, and children. It has been said that the punishment was their killing on the Day of Badr. It has been said that it is the punishment of the Hereafter. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *idhā hum* refers to *mutrafīhim*, since they are the ones spoken of, who cried out when punishment descended upon them. It has been said that it refers to those remaining after those who were punished. Ibn Juraij said: "Those punished are the dead of Badr, and those who *yaj'arūna* ('cry out') are the people of Makkah, because they wailed and implored."

﴿Do not cry out today...﴾ That is, it will be said to them, either literally, the angels saying this to them, or figuratively, meaning the tongue of the situation says this. This is if those who cry out are the ones punished. According to the view of Ibn Juraij, the speaker is not the angels. Qatadah said: "*Yaj'arūna* means they cry out in repentance, but nothing is accepted from them." Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "*Tajarūn* means you lament (tajza'ūn)," expressing crying out by lamentation, since lamentation is its cause.

﴿Indeed, from Us you will not be helped.﴾ That is, you will not be protected from Our punishment, or there will be no help for you from Our side. So the neighbourhood (of the sacred house) will not benefit you, nor will it avail you.

﴿My signs were recited to you...﴾ *Āyātī* ("My signs") are the verses of the Qur'an. *Tankiṣūna* ("you turned back") means you return, a metaphor for turning away from the truth. Ali ibn Abi Talib read *tankuṣūna* with a *ḍamma* on the *kāf*. The pronoun in *bihi* ("by it") refers to the verbal noun indicated by *tankiṣūna*, meaning by the backing away and distancing from hearing the signs. Or it refers to the signs, since they carry the meaning of the Book. *Mustakbirīn* ("arrogant") was made to carry the meaning of "denying," so it takes *bi-* as complement. Or the *bā'* indicates cause, meaning arrogance and defiance arise in you because of hearing it. The majority hold that the pronoun in *bihi* refers to the Sacred Precinct and the Mosque, even though no mention of it has preceded, and what justified this implicit reference was that they were well known for their arrogance regarding the House, and that they had no miracle except that they were its custodians and those who maintained it. Munthir ibn Sa'id mentioned that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and what strengthens this is that in His saying *tutlā 'alaykum* ("recited to you") there is an indication of the one who recites, who is the Messenger (peace be upon him). These are views in which *bihi* is attached to *mustakbirīn*. It has also been said that it is attached to *sāmiran* ("conversing by night"), meaning you converse at night, mentioning the Qur'an and disparaging it. They used to gather around the House at night conversing, and most of their nightly conversation was about the Qur'an, calling it sorcery and poetry and reviling the one who brought it.

The majority read *sāmiran*, while Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Abu Haywah, Ibn Muhaysin, Ikrimah, al-Za'farani, and Mahbub from Abu Amr read *sumaran* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn* and a shadda on the *mīm* with a *fatḥa*, the plural of *sāmir*. Also Ibn Abbas, Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Raja', and Abu Nahik read it so, and with an added *alif* between the *mīm* and the *rā'* it is also the plural of *sāmir*. Both are regular plurals in the pattern of *sāmir*.

The majority read *tahjurūna* with a *fatḥa* on the *tā'* and a *ḍamma* on the *jīm*. Ibn Abi Asim transmitted it with a *yā'* as a shift of person (*iltifāt*). Ibn Abbas said: "*Tahjurūna* means you abandon the truth and the remembrance of God, cutting it off, from *al-hajr* (abandonment)." Ibn Zayd and Abu Hatim said: it is from *hajara al-marīḍu* when the sick person raves, meaning they speak idle talk. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Muhaysin, Nafi', and Humayd read it with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'* and a *kasra* on the *jīm*, the present tense of *ahjara*, meaning they say *al-hujr* with a *ḍamma* on the *hā'*, which is foul speech. Ibn Abbas said: "It refers to reviling the Companions and others." Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Zayd ibn Ali, Ikrimah, Abu Nahik, Ibn Muhaysin, and Abu Haywah also read it so, except that they put a *fatḥa* on the *hā'* and a shadda on the *jīm*, which is an intensive form of *hajjara*, the past tense of *al-hajar* with a *fatḥa*, meaning the opposite of connection, or raving, or the past tense of *al-hujr*, which is foul speech. Ibn Jinni said: "If it were said that the meaning is that you are excessive in openly declaring, to the extent that if you were conversing by night, it is as if you were abandoning (the truth) in the midday heat, in exposure, this would be a valid reading."

﴿Will they not then reflect upon the Word, or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾ ﴿Or do they not recognise their Messenger, so that they deny him?﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has madness"? No, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.﴾ ﴿Had the truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Rather, We have brought them their reminder, but they turn away from their reminder.﴾ ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment? The payment of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers.﴾ ﴿And indeed you call them to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And indeed those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾ ﴿Even if We had mercy on them and removed the harm that is upon them, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ ﴿We had already seized them with punishment, yet they did not submit to their Lord, nor did they humble themselves.﴾ ﴿Until, when We opened upon them a gate of severe punishment, they were then plunged into despair.﴾

He (exalted is He) reproached them for turning away from following the truth and from the Qur'an that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. That is, "Did they not reflect upon what he brought from Allah, so that they would know that it is the miraculous Book which cannot be opposed, and so that they would believe in it and in the one who brought it?" He rebuked them and made them stand before its contemplation, while they, through their obstinacy and corrupt reasoning, said some of them: "It is sorcery," and some of them said: "It is poetry." Yet it is the greatest of the enduring proofs throughout the ages. He first chided them for failing to benefit from the Qur'an, then secondly that what had come to them had come to their forefathers of old. That is, the sending of messengers is neither novel nor strange; rather, messengers came to the nations before them. They knew this through successive reports (tawatur), through the salvation of those who believed and the annihilation of those who denied. Their forefathers were Isma'il and his descendants from Adnan and Qahtan. It has been narrated: "Do not revile Mudar, nor Rabi'a, nor al-Harith ibn Ka'b, nor Asad ibn Khuzayma, nor Tamim ibn Murra, nor Qiss." He also mentioned that they were Muslims, and that Tubba' was a Muslim, and that Sulayman ibn Dawud was upon his same condition.

[p. 414] Thirdly, He rebuked them by saying that they know Muhammad (ﷺ), his sound lineage, his residence among the clan of Hashim, his trustworthiness, his truthfulness, his nobility, his intellect, and that he was distinguished as the best of the youths of Quraysh. It is sufficient to recall the sermon of Abu Talib when he married Khadija, and that it contained qualities of his which reached the ears of Quraysh, and they denied none of them. That is, his knowledge was already prior, in whole and in detail, so it is not possible to deny any of his attributes.

Fourthly, He rebuked them by saying that they attributed him to the jinn, though they knew that he was the most intelligent of them and the keenest of mind, and that the difference between the wisdom and decisive speech he brought and the speech of one possessed by a jinn is not hidden from anyone who has a measure of sound reason. These four rebukes required that what they were rebuked for should be a cause for their submission to the truth, because contemplating what he brought, considering the histories of those who passed, the sending of messengers to them, knowing the Messenger in his essence and attributes and his freedom from madness, is a guide for whoever Allah has granted success to be guided. But he brought them what came between them and their desires, and did not agree with what they had been raised upon of following falsehood. When they found no way to repel it, because it is the truth, they resorted to slander and relied upon falsehood, attributing to him madness, sorcery and poetry.

﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth﴾: that is, the Qur'an, which includes monotheism, and that by which salvation in the Hereafter and nobility in this world are attained.

﴿But most of them are averse to the truth﴾ indicates that among them are some who do not hate the truth, and these are the ones who abandon faith out of pride and arrogance, lest their people reproach them by saying: "He has turned away (sabi'a) and abandoned the religion of his fathers."

﴿Had the truth followed their desires﴾: Ibn Wathhab recited ﴿Wa-lawu ittaba'a﴾ with a dammah on the waw. The apparent meaning is that "the truth" is the one mentioned earlier in their words: ﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth﴾. That is, if what the Messenger brought of Islam and monotheism were to follow their desires, it would turn into evil, and Allah would bring about the Resurrection and destroy the world without delay. Al-Zamakhshari said this meaning, and some of it in his own words. He also said: "By this He indicates the great importance of the truth; had it followed their desires, it would have turned into falsehood, and what sustains the world would have gone, and nothing would remain standing after it." It has also been said: if what the Messenger brought were to follow the desire of these people, by taking partners and offspring for Allah, and that were true, then Allah would not have the lofty attributes, nor His power as it is, and in that would be the corruption of the heavens and the earth. It has also been said: they saw the truth in taking gods alongside Allah, but if that were correct, corruption would occur in the heavens and the earth, according to what is established in the argument of mutual prevention (dalil al-tamanu') in His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. It has also been said: their opinions were contradictory, so if the truth followed their desires, contradiction would occur and the order of the world would be disrupted. Qatada said: "the truth" here is Allah (exalted is He).

Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is: "Had Allah been following their desires, commanding polytheism and sins, He would not be a god, and He would not be able to hold the heavens and the earth." Ibn 'Atiyya said: whoever says that "the truth" in the verse is Allah (exalted is He), which he attributed to Ibn Jurayj and Abu Salih, the word "followed" becomes problematic for him, and it is hard for him to arrange the corruption mentioned in the verse, because the word "following" is only a metaphor (isti'ara) in the sense that their desires would be established by the truth. We find that Allah has established the disbelief of nations and their desires, and there is no corruption of heavens in that. As for His essence, which is the correct view, if it were in accordance with their desires, everything would be corrupted, so consider it. End.

The majority read with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama), while Ibn Abi Ishaq, Isa ibn Umar and Yunus, from Abu 'Amr, read with the first-person ya'; Ibn Abi Ishaq, Isa also, Abu al-Barahsam, Abu Haywa, al-Jahdari, Ibn Qutayb and Abu Raja read with the second-person ta' addressed to the Messenger (peace be upon him); and Abu 'Amr in one narration read ﴿ataynahum﴾ with the long vowel, meaning "We gave them." The majority read ﴿bi-dhikrihim﴾, meaning "with their admonition and clarification to them," as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Isa read "bi-dhikrahum" with the feminine alif, and Qatada read "nadhkuruhum" with nun, the present tense of dhakara. Attributing the literal bringing to Allah is not valid, and it is only a metaphor (majaz), meaning: rather, Our Book or Our Messenger brought them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿bi-dhikrihim﴾ means "with the Book which is their reminder," that is their admonition, or their renown and pride; or "with the reminder which they used to wish for, saying: ﴿Had we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been the sincere servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat: 168]."

﴿Or do you ask them for a payment?﴾ This is an interrogation of rebuke as well. The meaning is: "Rather, do you ask them for wealth, so that they became averse to you on that account and found you burdensome?" Said by Ibn 'Atiyya. Al-Zamakhshari expressed it most eloquently, saying: "(Or do you ask them) for a little of the gifts of creation in return for your guidance to them, while the abundance of the gifts of the Creator is better?" He has thus imposed the proof upon them in these verses, and cut off their excuses and pretexts by showing that the one sent to them is a man whose affair and condition are well known, whose secret and public life are known, deserving that such a man should be chosen for the message from among them; that he did not come to them until he claimed such a great claim falsely, nor did he make that a ladder to gain from their worldly goods or to beg their wealth; and he called them only to the religion of Islam, which is the straight path, while revealing the hidden of their ailments, which is their neglect of reflection and contemplation, and their frivolous attachment to the religion of misguided forefathers without proof, and their excuse that he is mad after the truth had become manifest and the confirmation from Allah through clear miracles and signs, and their aversion to the truth and their turning away from what holds their share of the reminder. End.

The discussion of ﴿khar'jan fa-kharaju﴾ has preceded in the verse ﴿So shall We make for you a payment?﴾ [al-Kahf: 94] in al-Kahf, both as recitation and meaning. Al-Hasan and Isa read ﴿kharajan fa-kharju﴾, so with this reading four recitations are complete. In both words, ﴿fa-kharaju rabbika﴾ means His reward, because it is lasting, and what is taken from others is perishable. Al-Kalbi said: "His giving, because He gives not out of need, whereas others give out of need." It has also been said: "His provision," and this is supported by ﴿the best of providers﴾. Al-Jubba'i said: "The best of providers" indicates that no one equals Him in bestowing favour on His servants, and it indicates that servants may provide for one another. End. This is the implication of ﴿khayr﴾, the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil), and the implication of ﴿al-raziqin﴾, the plural to which the comparative form is annexed.

When He disproved the path of the disbelievers, He followed this with an explanation of the correctness of what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought, and said: ﴿And indeed you call them to a straight path﴾, which is the religion of Islam. Then He informed that whoever denies the Resurrection is deviating from this path, because one does not travel it except the one who hopes for reward and fears punishment; and these do not believe in the requital, so they are inclining away from it. Those who claimed that the path they deviate from is the path to Paradise in the Hereafter are even further from the truth, and those who claimed that the path in the Hereafter is one they deviate from by turning right and left toward Hell. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿deviating﴾ means "turning away." Al-Hasan said: "abandoning it." Qatada said: "bewildered." Al-Kalbi said: "avoiding." These statements are close in meaning.

﴿Even if We had mercy on them and removed the harm that is upon them﴾: it has been said that the harm is hunger; it has been said it is killing and captivity; it has been said it is the punishment of the Hereafter. That is, they reached such a degree of defiance and obstinacy that if they were returned to the world they would return, because of the intensity of their stubbornness in what they are upon of distance. But this statement is far-fetched; rather, the apparent meaning is that this conditional would be in this world. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿We had already seized them with punishment﴾ up to the end of the verse. He takes as evidence of the severity of their obstinacy in disbelief and stubbornness, on the supposition of His mercy toward them, that He had seized them first with swords, and by what befell them on the day of Badr of the slaying of their chieftains and the capture of their men. Yet after that no submission or humility was found in them, until We opened upon them the gate of hunger, which is harder than captivity and killing, and they were then made despairing and their necks submitted. The apparent meaning from this is that the pronoun refers to the drought and hunger which afflicted them by the supplication of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj.

The occasion of revelation of the verse is evidence of this. It is narrated that when Thumama ibn Uthal al-Hanafi embraced Islam and joined al-Yamama, he prevented the supply of grain from the people of Makkah. So Allah seized them with years of famine until they ate al-'ilhiz (a food made of blood and hair). Then Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said to him: "I adjure you by Allah and by the ties of kinship. Do you not claim that you were sent as a mercy to the worlds?" He said: "Yes." He said: "You killed the fathers by the sword, and the sons by hunger." So the verse was revealed. The meaning is: if Allah had removed this harm from them, which is the emaciation and drought that befell them, and they found fertility, they would have returned to what they were upon of arrogance and enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, and excess in it. It has also been said: the meaning is, if We tested them with every trial of killing and hunger, no submission or compliance would be seen in them, until when they are punished with the fire of Hell they are made despairing, as in His saying ﴿And on the day the Hour comes, the criminals will be in despair﴾ [al-Rum: 12], and ﴿Its punishment will not be lightened for them, and they will be in it in despair﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 75]. According to this view, the opening of the gate of severe punishment is in the Hereafter, whereas according to the first view it was in this world.

[p. 416] The measure of ﴿istakana﴾ is ﴿istaf'ala﴾, meaning it passed from one state to another, just as you say: ﴿istahala﴾ meaning it passed from one condition to another. As for the view of one who claimed that ﴿istakana﴾ is ﴿ifta'ala﴾ from al-sukun (stillness), and that the alif is a weak lengthening of the vowel (ishba')—since lengthening of the vowel belongs to poetry, as in his saying:

I seek refuge in Allah from the scorpions that raise their tails in coils.

And also because lengthening of the vowel does not occur within the inflections of the word; do you not see that whoever lengthens in his saying:

And from blaming the times with one who has been removed.

[The translation of the quoted verse fragments is given as they stand; the second line is incomplete in the source text.]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 23, verse 68–77 (part 2 of 2):

You do not say "intazaha (انْتِزاحَ) yantazihu (يَنْتَزِيحُ), so he is muntazih (مُنْتَزِيحٌ)," whereas you say "istakana (اسْتَكانَ) yastakinu (يَسْتَكِينُ), so he is mustakin (مُسْتَكِينٌ) and mustakan (مُسْتَكانٌ)." The verbal noun of it, istikanah (اسْتِكانَةً), indicates that the verb's pattern is istaf'ala (اسْتَفْعَلَ), like istaqama (اسْتَقامَ) with istiqamah (اسْتِقامَةً). The forms "istakanu (اسْتَكانُوا)" and "yatadarra'una (يَتَضَرَّعُونَ)" differ in form, so they are neither two past verbs nor two present verbs.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Because the meaning is that We afflicted them, yet no submissiveness was found in them immediately after the affliction; and it is not the habit of these people to become submissive and humble themselves until the gate of severe punishment is opened upon them.

Al-mublis (المُبْلِسُ) is the one who has despaired of the evil that has befallen him. Al-Sulami read (مُبْلَسُونَ) with a fatha on the lam.

I seek refuge in Allah from the scorpions that raise their tails in coils.

And also because lengthening of the vowel does not occur within the inflections of the word; do you not see that whoever lengthens in his saying:

And from blaming the times with one who has been removed.

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿deviating﴾ means "turning away." Al-Hasan said: "abandoning it." Qatada said: "bewildered." Al-Kalbi said: "avoiding." These statements are close in meaning.

﴿Even if We had mercy on them and removed the harm that is upon them﴾: it has been said that the harm is hunger; it has been said it is killing and captivity; it has been said it is the punishment of the Hereafter. That is, they reached such a degree of defiance and obstinacy that if they were returned to the world they would return, because of the intensity of their stubbornness in what they are upon of distance. But this statement is far-fetched; rather, the apparent meaning is that this conditional would be in this world. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿We had already seized them with punishment﴾ up to the end of the verse. He takes as evidence of the severity of their obstinacy in disbelief and stubbornness, on the supposition of His mercy toward them, that He had seized them first with swords, and by what befell them on the day of Badr of the slaying of their chieftains and the capture of their men. Yet after that no submission or humility was found in them, until We opened upon them the gate of hunger, which is harder than captivity and killing, and they were then made despairing and their necks submitted. The apparent meaning from this is that the pronoun refers to the drought and hunger which afflicted them by the supplication of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj.

The occasion of revelation of the verse is evidence of this. It is narrated that when Thumama ibn Uthal al-Hanafi embraced Islam and joined al-Yamama, he prevented the supply of grain from the people of Makkah. So Allah seized them with years of famine until they ate al-'ilhiz (a food made of blood and hair). Then Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said to him: "I adjure you by Allah and by the ties of kinship. Do you not claim that you were sent as a mercy to the worlds?" He said: "Yes." He said: "You killed the fathers by the sword, and the sons by hunger." So the verse was revealed. The meaning is: if Allah had removed this harm from them, which is the emaciation and drought that befell them, and they found fertility, they would have returned to what they were upon of arrogance and enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, and excess in it. It has also been said: the meaning is, if We tested them with every trial of killing and hunger, no submission or compliance would be seen in them, until when they are punished with the fire of Hell they are made despairing, as in His saying ﴿And on the day the Hour comes, the criminals will be in despair﴾ [al-Rum: 12], and ﴿Its punishment will not be lightened for them, and they will be in it in despair﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 75]. According to this view, the opening of the gate of severe punishment is in the Hereafter, whereas according to the first view it was in this world.

I seek refuge in Allah from the scorpions that raise their tails in coils.

And also because lengthening of the vowel does not occur within the inflections of the word; do you not see that whoever lengthens in his saying:

And from blaming the times with one who has been removed.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Because the meaning is that We afflicted them, yet no submissiveness was found in them immediately after the affliction; and it is not the habit of these people to become submissive and humble themselves until the gate of severe punishment is opened upon them.

Al-mublis (المُبْلِسُ) is the one who has despaired of the evil that has befallen him. Al-Sulami read (مُبْلَسُونَ) with a fatha on the lam.

﴿Will they not then reflect upon the Word, or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾ ﴿Or do they not recognise their Messenger, so that they deny him?﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has madness"? No, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.﴾ ﴿Had the truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Rather, We have brought them their reminder, but they turn away from their reminder.﴾ ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment? The payment of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers.﴾ ﴿And indeed you call them to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And indeed those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾ ﴿Even if We had mercy on them and removed the harm that is upon them, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ ﴿We had already seized them with punishment, yet they did not submit to their Lord, nor did they humble themselves.﴾ ﴿Until, when We opened upon them a gate of severe punishment, they were then plunged into despair.﴾

He (exalted is He) reproached them for turning away from following the truth and from the Qur'an that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. That is, "Did they not reflect upon what he brought from Allah, so that they would know that it is the miraculous Book which cannot be opposed, and so that they would believe in it and in the one who brought it?" He rebuked them and made them stand before its contemplation, while they, through their obstinacy and corrupt reasoning, said some of them: "It is sorcery," and some of them said: "It is poetry." Yet it is the greatest of the enduring proofs throughout the ages. He first chided them for failing to benefit from the Qur'an, then secondly that what had come to them had come to their forefathers of old. That is, the sending of messengers is neither novel nor strange; rather, messengers came to the nations before them. They knew this through successive reports (tawatur), through the salvation of those who believed and the annihilation of those who denied. Their forefathers were Isma'il and his descendants from Adnan and Qahtan. It has been narrated: "Do not revile Mudar, nor Rabi'a, nor al-Harith ibn Ka'b, nor Asad ibn Khuzayma, nor Tamim ibn Murra, nor Qiss." He also mentioned that they were Muslims, and that Tubba' was a Muslim, and that Sulayman ibn Dawud was upon his same condition.

[p. 414] Thirdly, He rebuked them by saying that they know Muhammad (ﷺ), his sound lineage, his residence among the clan of Hashim, his trustworthiness, his truthfulness, his nobility, his intellect, and that he was distinguished as the best of the youths of Quraysh. It is sufficient to recall the sermon of Abu Talib when he married Khadija, and that it contained qualities of his which reached the ears of Quraysh, and they denied none of them. That is, his knowledge was already prior, in whole and in detail, so it is not possible to deny any of his attributes.

Fourthly, He rebuked them by saying that they attributed him to the jinn, though they knew that he was the most intelligent of them and the keenest of mind, and that the difference between the wisdom and decisive speech he brought and the speech of one possessed by a jinn is not hidden from anyone who has a measure of sound reason. These four rebukes required that what they were rebuked for should be a cause for their submission to the truth, because contemplating what he brought, considering the histories of those who passed, the sending of messengers to them, knowing the Messenger in his essence and attributes and his freedom from madness, is a guide for whoever Allah has granted success to be guided. But he brought them what came between them and their desires, and did not agree with what they had been raised upon of following falsehood. When they found no way to repel it, because it is the truth, they resorted to slander and relied upon falsehood, attributing to him madness, sorcery and poetry.

﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth﴾: that is, the Qur'an, which includes monotheism, and that by which salvation in the Hereafter and nobility in this world are attained.

﴿But most of them are averse to the truth﴾ indicates that among them are some who do not hate the truth, and these are the ones who abandon faith out of pride and arrogance, lest their people reproach them by saying: "He has turned away (sabi'a) and abandoned the religion of his fathers."

﴿Had the truth followed their desires﴾: Ibn Wathhab recited ﴿Wa-lawu ittaba'a﴾ with a dammah on the waw. The apparent meaning is that "the truth" is the one mentioned earlier in their words: ﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth﴾. That is, if what the Messenger brought of Islam and monotheism were to follow their desires, it would turn into evil, and Allah would bring about the Resurrection and destroy the world without delay. Al-Zamakhshari said this meaning, and some of it in his own words. He also said: "By this He indicates the great importance of the truth; had it followed their desires, it would have turned into falsehood, and what sustains the world would have gone, and nothing would remain standing after it." It has also been said: if what the Messenger brought were to follow the desire of these people, by taking partners and offspring for Allah, and that were true, then Allah would not have the lofty attributes, nor His power as it is, and in that would be the corruption of the heavens and the earth. It has also been said: they saw the truth in taking gods alongside Allah, but if that were correct, corruption would occur in the heavens and the earth, according to what is established in the argument of mutual prevention (dalil al-tamanu') in His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. It has also been said: their opinions were contradictory, so if the truth followed their desires, contradiction would occur and the order of the world would be disrupted. Qatada said: "the truth" here is Allah (exalted is He).

Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is: "Had Allah been following their desires, commanding polytheism and sins, He would not be a god, and He would not be able to hold the heavens and the earth." Ibn 'Atiyya said: whoever says that "the truth" in the verse is Allah (exalted is He), which he attributed to Ibn Jurayj and Abu Salih, the word "followed" becomes problematic for him, and it is hard for him to arrange the corruption mentioned in the verse, because the word "following" is only a metaphor (isti'ara) in the sense that their desires would be established by the truth. We find that Allah has established the disbelief of nations and their desires, and there is no corruption of heavens in that. As for His essence, which is the correct view, if it were in accordance with their desires, everything would be corrupted, so consider it. End.

The majority read with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama), while Ibn Abi Ishaq, Isa ibn Umar and Yunus, from Abu 'Amr, read with the first-person ya'; Ibn Abi Ishaq, Isa also, Abu al-Barahsam, Abu Haywa, al-Jahdari, Ibn Qutayb and Abu Raja read with the second-person ta' addressed to the Messenger (peace be upon him); and Abu 'Amr in one narration read ﴿ataynahum﴾ with the long vowel, meaning "We gave them." Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿bi-dhikrihim﴾ means "with the Book which is their reminder," that is their admonition, or their renown and pride; or "with the reminder which they used to wish for, saying: ﴿Had we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been the sincere servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat: 168]."

﴿Or do you ask them for a payment?﴾ This is an interrogation of rebuke as well. The meaning is: "Rather, do you ask them for wealth, so that they became averse to you on that account and found you burdensome?" Said by Ibn 'Atiyya. End.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 23, verses 78–92:**

﴿It is He who brought into being for you hearing, sight and hearts; little is it that you give thanks.﴾ ﴿It is He who scattered you over the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿It is He who gives life and causes death, and His is the alternation of night and day. Will you not reason?﴾ ﴿Rather, they said the like of what the ancients said.﴾ ﴿They said: "When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised again?"﴾ ﴿Indeed we and our fathers were promised this before; this is nothing but the fables of the ancients.﴾ ﴿Say: "To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?"﴾ ﴿They will say: "To God." Say: "Will you not then remember?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Who is Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the Mighty Throne?"﴾ ﴿They will say: "To God." Say: "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ ﴿Say: "In whose hand is the dominion of everything, who protects and is not protected against, if you know?"﴾ ﴿They will say: "To God." Say: "How then are you deluded?"﴾ ﴿Rather, We have brought them the truth, and indeed they are liars.﴾ ﴿God has not taken any son, and there is no god with Him; otherwise each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others. Glory be to God above what they describe.﴾ ﴿Knower of the unseen and the seen; exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ .

The text of the above verses, in the second reading (p. 417–418), has the following. [The following text is the commentary's own word-by-word explanation.]

**Al-Hamz** (al-hamz, prodding): pricking and pushing with the hand or other things; from it comes the spur of the horse-breaker, and the pushing of people with the tongue (i.e. slander). **Al-barzakh**: the barrier between two distances. It is said: a screen between two things preventing one of them from reaching the other. **Al-nasab**: kinship through birth. **Al-lafh**: the fire's touching a thing with its heat and burning. Al-Zajjaj said: al-laftu (the scorching) is stronger in effect than al-laqh (the fertilising wind). **Al-kulooh**: the drawing back of the two lips from the teeth, whence the snarl of the dog and the lion. It is said: al-kulooh is the frowning of the face, its contraction; kalaha al-rajul kulooh and kulaah (the man frowned), and a dahr kalih (a grim age) and bard kalih (severe cold). **Al-abath**: play that is empty of any benefit.

**Commentary on verses 78–92**

*The connection of ﴿It is He who brought into being for you﴾ with what precedes it:* when He explained the disbelievers' aversion to hearing the proofs, seeing the signs, and reflecting on the realities, He addressed the listeners—the believers, and apparently the whole world—alerting them that whoever does not put these organs to use in what God Most High created, and does not reflect on the proofs of His oneness and His manifest power that He placed in them, is like one who lacks these organs. Among those of whom God Most High said: ﴿Their hearing, their sight, and their hearts availed them nothing at all﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 26]. So He who brought these senses into being, and who was the one to whom they were brought into being, who gives life and causes death, and who disposes the alternation of night and day, is capable of resurrection. He singled out these organs for mention because the benefits of religion and of this world are bound up with them: the work of hearing and sight in God's signs, and the use of the heart's reflection to establish God's oneness and attributes. And since their creation is among the most complete blessings upon the servant, He said: ﴿little is it that you give thanks﴾, meaning: you give thanks a little, and *mā* is extra, for emphasis. Among the thanks due for a blessing is acknowledging the Giver of it and denying any rival or partner to Him.

*Commentary on ﴿scattered﴾:* *dhara'akum* means He created you and spread you throughout it. *﴿And to Him﴾*, that is, to His judgement, His decree, and His recompense, *﴿you will be gathered﴾*: it means the resurrection and the assembling in the Hereafter after the dispersal and dissolution of this world.

*Commentary on ﴿and His is the alternation of night and day﴾:* that is, He alone is its owner and its disposer, and He has the power from which that alternation proceeds. *Al-ikhtilaf* here means succession, i.e. this one follows that one. *﴿Will you not reason?﴾*: these are the operations of His power and the effects of His dominion, so that you should affirm His oneness and deny Him partners and equals, since they have no power over any of that. Abu Amr, in one transmission, read *ya'qilun* with the third-person *ya* (yā' of absence), by way of *iltifat* (a shift from address to third person).

*Commentary on ﴿Rather, they said﴾:* *bal* is a turning away, meaning: they have no intellect and no consideration of these signs. *﴿Rather, they said﴾*: the pronoun refers to the people of Mecca and those who follow their course in denying the resurrection, like what their fathers, ʿĀd and Thamūd, and the disbelievers who came after them, said. Since they took other gods besides God Most High and attributed a son to Him, He alerted them to the extreme of their ignorance: they acknowledge that He Most High owns the earth and whoever is in it as sovereign, that He is Lord of the upper world, and that He is the owner of everything; yet despite this they attribute a son to Him and take partners for Him.

Ibn Masʿūd (ʿAbd Allāh), al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Nasr ibn ʿĀṣim, Ibn Wathhab, Abu al-Ashhab, and Abu Amr among the Seven read *sa-yaqūlūna Allāh* (they will say: God), with the second and third instances in the nominative form of the Name of Majesty (Allāh, not li-Llāh). This is also how it is in the codices of the people of the two Ḥarams (Mecca and Medina), Kufa, and Syria. The remaining Seven read *li-Llāh* with the preposition *lām* of the genitive. The first reading has agreement in form and meaning, and the second came according to the sense, because your saying "Whose Lord is this?" and "To whom does this belong?" have one meaning, and there is no disagreement that the first is with *lām*. Ibn Muhaysin read *al-ʿaẓīm* with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm* as an epithet of the Lord. You say *ajartu fulānan ʿalā fulān* when you protect someone from another, i.e., He protects whom He wills from whom He wills, and no one protects anyone from Him. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿if you know﴾, which does not negate their knowledge, and what He relates of their saying "God", because ﴿if you know﴾ does not negate their knowledge of that. Something like this may be said in argument for emphasis on their knowledge. He concluded each question with what suits it: He concluded with "Sovereign of the earth and whoever is in it," which deserves that no part of His creation who is in the earth should be made a partner with Him, a sovereign who has lordship. And He concluded what follows with piety (*taqwā*), which is more eloquent than remembrance (*tadhakkur*), and in it is a severe warning, meaning: will you not fear Him, so that you do not associate anything with Him? He concluded what follows this with His saying ﴿How then are you deluded?﴾, as an intensification of the reproach after their acknowledgement and their commitment to what is incumbent upon them in the argument. *Annā* here means "how", and He established that they are bewitched, and asked them about the condition by which they were bewitched, meaning: how are you deceived away from His oneness and obedience? Magic here is used metaphorically (*isti'āra*), and it is a comparison of what comes from them of confusion and of placing actions and sayings in other than their proper places, to what occurs from one who is bewitched; He expressed it in that way about them.

It is read *bal ātaynāhum* ("Rather, We brought them") with the first-person *tā'* of the speaker, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with the second-person *tā'* of address.

So He who brought these senses into being, and who was the one to whom they were brought into being, who gives life and causes death, and who disposes the alternation of night and day, is capable of resurrection. He singled out these organs for mention because the benefits of religion and of this world are bound up with them: the work of hearing and sight in God's signs, and the use of the heart's reflection to establish God's oneness and attributes. And since their creation is among the most complete blessings upon the servant, He said: ﴿little is it that you give thanks﴾, meaning: you give thanks a little, and *mā* is extra, for emphasis. Among the thanks due for a blessing is acknowledging the Giver of it and denying any rival or partner to Him.

*Commentary on ﴿scattered﴾:* *dhara'akum* means He created you and spread you throughout it. *﴿And to Him﴾*, that is, to His judgement, His decree, and His recompense, *﴿you will be gathered﴾*: it means the resurrection and the assembling in the Hereafter after the dispersal and dissolution of this world.

*Commentary on ﴿and His is the alternation of night and day﴾:* that is, He alone is its owner and its disposer, and He has the power from which that alternation proceeds. *Al-ikhtilaf* here means succession, i.e. this one follows that one. *﴿Will you not reason?﴾*: these are the operations of His power and the effects of His dominion, so that you should affirm His oneness and deny Him partners and equals, since they have no power over any of that. Abu Amr, in one transmission, read *ya'qilun* with the third-person *ya* (yā' of absence), by way of *iltifat* (a shift from address to third person).

*Commentary on ﴿Rather, they said﴾:* *bal* is a turning away, meaning: they have no intellect and no consideration of these signs. *﴿Rather, they said﴾*: the pronoun refers to the people of Mecca and those who follow their course in denying the resurrection, like what their fathers, ʿĀd and Thamūd, and the disbelievers who came after them, said. Since they took other gods besides God Most High and attributed a son to Him, He alerted them to the extreme of their ignorance: they acknowledge that He Most High owns the earth and whoever is in it as sovereign, that He is Lord of the upper world, and that He is the owner of everything; yet despite this they attribute a son to Him and take partners for Him.

Ibn Masʿūd (ʿAbd Allāh), al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Nasr ibn ʿĀṣim, Ibn Wathhab, Abu al-Ashhab, and Abu Amr among the Seven read *sa-yaqūlūna Allāh* (they will say: God), with the second and third instances in the nominative form of the Name of Majesty (Allāh, not li-Llāh). This is also how it is in the codices of the people of the two Ḥarams (Mecca and Medina), Kufa, and Syria. The remaining Seven read *li-Llāh* with the preposition *lām* of the genitive. The first reading has agreement in form and meaning, and the second came according to the sense, because your saying "Whose Lord is this?" and "To whom does this belong?" have one meaning, and there is no disagreement that the first is with *lām*. Ibn Muhaysin read *al-ʿaẓīm* with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm* as an epithet of the Lord. You say *ajartu fulānan ʿalā fulān* when you protect someone from another, i.e., He protects whom He wills from whom He wills, and no one protects anyone from Him. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿if you know﴾, which does not negate their knowledge, and what He relates of their saying "God", because ﴿if you know﴾ does not negate their knowledge of that. Something like this may be said in argument for emphasis on their knowledge. He concluded each question with what suits it: He concluded with "Sovereign of the earth and whoever is in it," which deserves that no part of His creation who is in the earth should be made a partner with Him, a sovereign who has lordship. And He concluded what follows with piety (*taqwā*), which is more eloquent than remembrance (*tadhakkur*), and in it is a severe warning, meaning: will you not fear Him, so that you do not associate anything with Him? He concluded what follows this with His saying ﴿How then are you deluded?﴾, as an intensification of the reproach after their acknowledgement and their commitment to what is incumbent upon them in the argument. *Annā* here means "how", and He established that they are bewitched, and asked them about the condition by which they were bewitched, meaning: how are you deceived away from His oneness and obedience? Magic here is used metaphorically (*isti'āra*), and it is a comparison of what comes from them of confusion and of placing actions and sayings in other than their proper places, to what occurs from one who is bewitched; He expressed it in that way about them.

It is read *bal ātaynāhum* ("Rather, We brought them") with the first-person *tā'* of the speaker, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with the second-person *tā'* of address.

*Commentary on ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾:* in what they attribute to God Most High of taking a son, of taking partners, and other things in which they are liars. Then He denied the taking of a son, which is a denial of impossibility, and He denied a partner with His saying ﴿and there is no god with Him﴾, meaning: there was no partner with Him in creating the world and originating it, nor in anything else that befits Him of the lofty attributes. So the denial of a son is an alert against the one who said "the angels are God's daughters," and the denial of a partner in divinity is an alert against the one who said "the idols are gods." It is possible that what is meant by it is to nullify the saying of the Christians and the Dualists. ﴿From a son﴾ and ﴿from a god﴾ are general negations that convey the totality of the genus, and for this reason He said ﴿otherwise each god would have taken away﴾ and did not say "otherwise the god would have taken away." It was read *ʿammā taṣifūna* ("what you describe") with the second-person *tā'* of address. It is possible that the meaning is: "So I say: ﴿exalted is He above what they associate﴾" [al-Nahl: 3], as a resumed statement (*ikhbār mu'tanaf*). *Al-ghayb* (the unseen) is what is hidden from people, and *al-shahāda* (the seen) is what they have witnessed.
