**Commentary on verses 78–92**

*The connection of ﴿It is He who brought into being for you﴾ with what precedes it:* when He explained the disbelievers' aversion to hearing the proofs, seeing the signs, and reflecting on the realities, He addressed the listeners—the believers, and apparently the whole world—alerting them that whoever does not put these organs to use in what God Most High created, and does not reflect on the proofs of His oneness and His manifest power that He placed in them, is like one who lacks these organs. Among those of whom God Most High said: ﴿Their hearing, their sight, and their hearts availed them nothing at all﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 26]. So He who brought these senses into being, and who was the one to whom they were brought into being, who gives life and causes death, and who disposes the alternation of night and day, is capable of resurrection. He singled out these organs for mention because the benefits of religion and of this world are bound up with them: the work of hearing and sight in God's signs, and the use of the heart's reflection to establish God's oneness and attributes. And since their creation is among the most complete blessings upon the servant, He said: ﴿little is it that you give thanks﴾, meaning: you give thanks a little, and *mā* is extra, for emphasis. Among the thanks due for a blessing is acknowledging the Giver of it and denying any rival or partner to Him.

*Commentary on ﴿scattered﴾:* *dhara'akum* means He created you and spread you throughout it. *﴿And to Him﴾*, that is, to His judgement, His decree, and His recompense, *﴿you will be gathered﴾*: it means the resurrection and the assembling in the Hereafter after the dispersal and dissolution of this world.

*Commentary on ﴿and His is the alternation of night and day﴾:* that is, He alone is its owner and its disposer, and He has the power from which that alternation proceeds. *Al-ikhtilaf* here means succession, i.e. this one follows that one. *﴿Will you not reason?﴾*: these are the operations of His power and the effects of His dominion, so that you should affirm His oneness and deny Him partners and equals, since they have no power over any of that. Abu Amr, in one transmission, read *ya'qilun* with the third-person *ya* (yā' of absence), by way of *iltifat* (a shift from address to third person).

*Commentary on ﴿Rather, they said﴾:* *bal* is a turning away, meaning: they have no intellect and no consideration of these signs. *﴿Rather, they said﴾*: the pronoun refers to the people of Mecca and those who follow their course in denying the resurrection, like what their fathers, ʿĀd and Thamūd, and the disbelievers who came after them, said. Since they took other gods besides God Most High and attributed a son to Him, He alerted them to the extreme of their ignorance: they acknowledge that He Most High owns the earth and whoever is in it as sovereign, that He is Lord of the upper world, and that He is the owner of everything; yet despite this they attribute a son to Him and take partners for Him.

Ibn Masʿūd (ʿAbd Allāh), al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Nasr ibn ʿĀṣim, Ibn Wathhab, Abu al-Ashhab, and Abu Amr among the Seven read *sa-yaqūlūna Allāh* (they will say: God), with the second and third instances in the nominative form of the Name of Majesty (Allāh, not li-Llāh). This is also how it is in the codices of the people of the two Ḥarams (Mecca and Medina), Kufa, and Syria. The remaining Seven read *li-Llāh* with the preposition *lām* of the genitive. The first reading has agreement in form and meaning, and the second came according to the sense, because your saying "Whose Lord is this?" and "To whom does this belong?" have one meaning, and there is no disagreement that the first is with *lām*. Ibn Muhaysin read *al-ʿaẓīm* with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm* as an epithet of the Lord. You say *ajartu fulānan ʿalā fulān* when you protect someone from another, i.e., He protects whom He wills from whom He wills, and no one protects anyone from Him. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿if you know﴾, which does not negate their knowledge, and what He relates of their saying "God", because ﴿if you know﴾ does not negate their knowledge of that. Something like this may be said in argument for emphasis on their knowledge. He concluded each question with what suits it: He concluded with "Sovereign of the earth and whoever is in it," which deserves that no part of His creation who is in the earth should be made a partner with Him, a sovereign who has lordship. And He concluded what follows with piety (*taqwā*), which is more eloquent than remembrance (*tadhakkur*), and in it is a severe warning, meaning: will you not fear Him, so that you do not associate anything with Him? He concluded what follows this with His saying ﴿How then are you deluded?﴾, as an intensification of the reproach after their acknowledgement and their commitment to what is incumbent upon them in the argument. *Annā* here means "how", and He established that they are bewitched, and asked them about the condition by which they were bewitched, meaning: how are you deceived away from His oneness and obedience? Magic here is used metaphorically (*isti'āra*), and it is a comparison of what comes from them of confusion and of placing actions and sayings in other than their proper places, to what occurs from one who is bewitched; He expressed it in that way about them.

It is read *bal ātaynāhum* ("Rather, We brought them") with the first-person *tā'* of the speaker, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with the second-person *tā'* of address.

*Commentary on ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾:* in what they attribute to God Most High of taking a son, of taking partners, and other things in which they are liars. Then He denied the taking of a son, which is a denial of impossibility, and He denied a partner with His saying ﴿and there is no god with Him﴾, meaning: there was no partner with Him in creating the world and originating it, nor in anything else that befits Him of the lofty attributes. So the denial of a son is an alert against the one who said "the angels are God's daughters," and the denial of a partner in divinity is an alert against the one who said "the idols are gods." It is possible that what is meant by it is to nullify the saying of the Christians and the Dualists. ﴿From a son﴾ and ﴿from a god﴾ are general negations that convey the totality of the genus, and for this reason He said ﴿otherwise each god would have taken away﴾ and did not say "otherwise the god would have taken away." The meaning of *la-dhahaba* ("would have taken away") is: each god would have become independent ﴿with what he created﴾, with his own creation, and would have been exclusive in it; the dominion of each one would be distinct from the dominion of the other, and some would have overcome others, as is the condition of the kings of this world. And since separation and mutual domination did not occur, know that He is one God. *Idhan* ("otherwise") was not preceded in the wording by any condition, nor by a questioner's question, nor by a promise, they said. So the condition is elided, its estimated form being: "if there were with Him gods"; and it was elided because His saying ﴿and there was no god with Him﴾ indicates it. This is the view of al-Farra', who claimed that when *lām* follows it, *law* ("if") and what it governs are elided. We have established an explanation of it other than this in His saying ﴿and then they would have taken you as a friend﴾ [al-Isra: 73] in the surah of al-Isra. The apparent reading is that *mā* in ﴿with what He created﴾ means *alladhī* ("that which"), and it is permitted that it be a verbal noun (*maṣdariyya*).

It was read *ʿammā taṣifūna* ("what you describe") with the second-person *tā'* of address. The two Ibns (Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir, the two "sons"), Abu Amr, and Hafs read *ʿĀlimi* ("Knower") in the genitive. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an epithet of God. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is a follow-on (*ittibāʿ*) of the written form. The remaining Seven, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Haywa, and Abu Bahriyya read it in the nominative. Al-Akhfash said: the genitive is better so that the speech is of one aspect. Abu ʿAlī said: the nominative indicates that the speech has been cut off, meaning that it is the predicate of an elided subject, i.e., he is "Knower" ('ālimu). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "In my view the nominative is more excellent." The *fa* in His saying ﴿fa-taʿālā﴾ ("so exalted") is conjunctive, so the meaning is as if He had said: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the seen; so exalted﴾, as you say: "Zayd is brave, so his rank is great," meaning: he was brave and so he became great. It is possible that the meaning is: "So I say: ﴿exalted is He above what they associate﴾" [al-Nahl: 3], as a resumed statement (*ikhbār mu'tanaf*). *Al-ghayb* (the unseen) is what is hidden from people, and *al-shahāda* (the seen) is what they have witnessed. End.

**Commentary on verses 78–92**

*The connection of ﴿It is He who brought into being for you﴾ with what precedes it:* when He explained the disbelievers' aversion to hearing the proofs, seeing the signs, and reflecting on the realities, He addressed the listeners—the believers, and apparently the whole world—alerting them that whoever does not put these organs to use in what God Most High created, and does not reflect on the proofs of His oneness and His manifest power that He placed in them, is like one who lacks these organs. Among those of whom God Most High said: ﴿Their hearing, their sight, and their hearts availed them nothing at all﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 26]. So He who brought these senses into being, and who was the one to whom they were brought into being, who gives life and causes death, and who disposes the alternation of night and day, is capable of resurrection. He singled out these organs for mention because the benefits of religion and of this world are bound up with them: the work of hearing and sight in God's signs, and the use of the heart's reflection to establish God's oneness and attributes. And since their creation is among the most complete blessings upon the servant, He said: ﴿little is it that you give thanks﴾, meaning: you give thanks a little, and *mā* is extra, for emphasis. Among the thanks due for a blessing is acknowledging the Giver of it and denying any rival or partner to Him.

*Commentary on ﴿scattered﴾:* *dhara'akum* means He created you and spread you throughout it. *﴿And to Him﴾*, that is, to His judgement, His decree, and His recompense, *﴿you will be gathered﴾*: it means the resurrection and the assembling in the Hereafter after the dispersal and dissolution of this world.

*Commentary on ﴿and His is the alternation of night and day﴾:* that is, He alone is its owner and its disposer, and He has the power from which that alternation proceeds. *Al-ikhtilaf* here means succession, i.e. this one follows that one. *﴿Will you not reason?﴾*: these are the operations of His power and the effects of His dominion, so that you should affirm His oneness and deny Him partners and equals, since they have no power over any of that. Abu Amr, in one transmission, read *ya'qilun* with the third-person *ya* (yā' of absence), by way of *iltifat* (a shift from address to third person).

*Commentary on ﴿Rather, they said﴾:* *bal* is a turning away, meaning: they have no intellect and no consideration of these signs. *﴿Rather, they said﴾*: the pronoun refers to the people of Mecca and those who follow their course in denying the resurrection, like what their fathers, ʿĀd and Thamūd, and the disbelievers who came after them, said. Since they took other gods besides God Most High and attributed a son to Him, He alerted them to the extreme of their ignorance: they acknowledge that He Most High owns the earth and whoever is in it as sovereign, that He is Lord of the upper world, and that He is the owner of everything; yet despite this they attribute a son to Him and take partners for Him.

Ibn Masʿūd (ʿAbd Allāh), al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Nasr ibn ʿĀṣim, Ibn Wathhab, Abu al-Ashhab, and Abu Amr among the Seven read *sa-yaqūlūna Allāh* (they will say: God), with the second and third instances in the nominative form of the Name of Majesty (Allāh, not li-Llāh). This is also how it is in the codices of the people of the two Ḥarams (Mecca and Medina), Kufa, and Syria. The remaining Seven read *li-Llāh* with the preposition *lām* of the genitive. The first reading has agreement in form and meaning, and the second came according to the sense, because your saying "Whose Lord is this?" and "To whom does this belong?" have one meaning, and there is no disagreement that the first is with *lām*. Ibn Muhaysin read *al-ʿaẓīm* with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm* as an epithet of the Lord. You say *ajartu fulānan ʿalā fulān* when you protect someone from another, i.e., He protects whom He wills from whom He wills, and no one protects anyone from Him. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿if you know﴾, which does not negate their knowledge, and what He relates of their saying "God", because ﴿if you know﴾ does not negate their knowledge of that. Something like this may be said in argument for emphasis on their knowledge. He concluded each question with what suits it: He concluded with "Sovereign of the earth and whoever is in it," which deserves that no part of His creation who is in the earth should be made a partner with Him, a sovereign who has lordship. And He concluded what follows with piety (*taqwā*), which is more eloquent than remembrance (*tadhakkur*), and in it is a severe warning, meaning: will you not fear Him, so that you do not associate anything with Him? He concluded what follows this with His saying ﴿How then are you deluded?﴾, as an intensification of the reproach after their acknowledgement and their commitment to what is incumbent upon them in the argument. *Annā* here means "how", and He established that they are bewitched, and asked them about the condition by which they were bewitched, meaning: how are you deceived away from His oneness and obedience? Magic here is used metaphorically (*isti'āra*), and it is a comparison of what comes from them of confusion and of placing actions and sayings in other than their proper places, to what occurs from one who is bewitched; He expressed it in that way about them.

It is read *bal ātaynāhum* ("Rather, We brought them") with the first-person *tā'* of the speaker, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with the second-person *tā'* of address.

*Commentary on ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾:* in what they attribute to God Most High of taking a son, of taking partners, and other things in which they are liars. Then He denied the taking of a son, which is a denial of impossibility, and He denied a partner with His saying ﴿and there is no god with Him﴾, meaning: there was no partner with Him in creating the world and originating it, nor in anything else that befits Him of the lofty attributes. So the denial of a son is an alert against the one who said "the angels are God's daughters," and the denial of a partner in divinity is an alert against the one who said "the idols are gods." It is possible that what is meant by it is to nullify the saying of the Christians and the Dualists. ﴿From a son﴾ and ﴿from a god﴾ are general negations that convey the totality of the genus, and for this reason He said ﴿otherwise each god would have taken away﴾ and did not say "otherwise the god would have taken away." The meaning of *la-dhahaba* ("would have taken away") is: each god would have become independent ﴿with what he created﴾, with his own creation, and would have been exclusive in it; the dominion of each one would be distinct from the dominion of the other, and some would have overcome others, as is the condition of the kings of this world. And since separation and mutual domination did not occur, know that He is one God. *Idhan* ("otherwise") was not preceded in the wording by any condition, nor by a questioner's question, nor by a promise, they said. So the condition is elided, its estimated form being: "if there were with Him gods"; and it was elided because His saying ﴿and there was no god with Him﴾ indicates it. This is the view of al-Farra', who claimed that when *lām* follows it, *law* ("if") and what it governs are elided. We have established an explanation of it other than this in His saying ﴿and then they would have taken you as a friend﴾ [al-Isra: 73] in the surah of al-Isra. The apparent reading is that *mā* in ﴿with what He created﴾ means *alladhī* ("that which"), and it is permitted that it be a verbal noun (*maṣdariyya*).

Abu ʿAlī said: the nominative indicates that the speech has been cut off, meaning that it is the predicate of an elided subject, i.e., he is "Knower" ('ālimu). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "In my view the nominative is more excellent." The *fa* in His saying ﴿fa-taʿālā﴾ ("so exalted") is conjunctive, so the meaning is as if He had said: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the seen; so exalted﴾, as you say: "Zayd is brave, so his rank is great," meaning: he was brave and so he became great. It is possible that the meaning is: "So I say: ﴿exalted is He above what they associate﴾" [al-Nahl: 3], as a resumed statement (*ikhbār mu'tanaf*). *Al-ghayb* (the unseen) is what is hidden from people, and *al-shahāda* (the seen) is what they have witnessed. End.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 23, verses 93–104:**

﴿Say: "My Lord, if You show me that which they are promised,﴾ ﴿My Lord, then do not place me among the wrongdoing people.﴾ ﴿And indeed, We are able to show you that which We promise them.﴾ ﴿Repel evil with that which is better; We know best what they describe.﴾ ﴿And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils."﴾ ﴿And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me."﴾ ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says: "My Lord, send me back,﴾ ﴿that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind." No! It is only a word he is saying. And before them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected.﴾ ﴿So when the Horn is blown, there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another.﴾ ﴿As for those whose scales are heavy, it is those who will be the successful.﴾ ﴿And as for those whose scales are light, it is those who have lost themselves; in Hell they will abide eternally.﴾ ﴿The Fire will burn their faces, and they therein will be grimacing.﴾

When He mentioned what the disbelievers were upon (p. 420), of claiming a son and a partner for Him, and since Exalted is He had informed His Prophet that He would take vengeance upon them, without specifying at that time whether it would be during his life or after his death, He commanded him to supplicate with this supplication; that is: "If You show me what You promise them as taking effect upon them in this world or in the Hereafter, then do not place me with them." It is known that he, peace be upon him, was protected from anything that would cause him to be placed with them, but He commanded him to supplicate with this in order to demonstrate servitude and humility before God. Likewise, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to seek forgiveness seventy times whenever he rose from his gathering, of this kind. Abu Bakr said: "I have been appointed over you, and I am not the best of you." Al-Hasan said: "He knew that he was the best of them, but the believer belittles himself."

The supplication came with the word "Lord" before the conditional clause and before the response, to intensify the entreaty and supplication to God Exalted, and because the Lord is the Owner, the One who watches over the servant's interests. Al-Dahhak and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read ﴿تُرِئَنِّي﴾ with a hamza in place of the yā' (ي), as it was read in ﴿فَإمّا تَرَئِنَّ﴾ and ﴿وَلَتَرَؤُنَّ﴾ with a hamza. This is a weak substitution (ibdal, replacement of one letter by another). Then Exalted is He informed that He is able to hasten the punishment upon them as they had been asking for it, and this would be during his lifetime, peace and blessings be upon him, but His delay is for a term they will complete. The majority hold that this punishment is in this world. It is said: the Day of Badr. It is said: the conquest of Makkah. It is said: it is the punishment of the Hereafter.

Then Exalted is He commanded him to good conduct, and ﴿that which is better﴾ [al-Isra' 17:53] is the testimony that there is no god but God. "Evil" (al-sayyi'ah) is shirk. Al-Hasan said: it is forgiveness and overlooking. 'Ata' and al-Dahhak said: it is greeting with peace when they become obscene. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 23, verses 93–104:**

﴿Say: "My Lord, if You show me that which they are promised,﴾ ﴿My Lord, then do not place me among the wrongdoing people.﴾ ﴿And indeed, We are able to show you that which We promise them.﴾ ﴿Repel evil with that which is better; We know best what they describe.﴾ ﴿And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils."﴾ ﴿And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me."﴾ ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says: "My Lord, send me back,﴾ ﴿that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind." No! It is only a word he is saying. And before them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected.﴾ ﴿So when the Horn is blown, there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another.﴾ ﴿As for those whose scales are heavy, it is those who will be the successful.﴾ ﴿And as for those whose scales are light, it is those who have lost themselves; in Hell they will abide eternally.﴾ ﴿The Fire will burn their faces, and they therein will be grimacing.﴾

When He mentioned what the disbelievers were upon (p. 420), of claiming a son and a partner for Him, and since Exalted is He had informed His Prophet that He would take vengeance upon them, without specifying at that time whether it would be during his life or after his death, He commanded him to supplicate with this supplication; that is: "If You show me what You promise them as taking effect upon them in this world or in the Hereafter, then do not place me with them." It is known that he, peace be upon him, was protected from anything that would cause him to be placed with them, but He commanded him to supplicate with this in order to demonstrate servitude and humility before God. Likewise, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to seek forgiveness seventy times whenever he rose from his gathering, of this kind. Abu Bakr said: "I have been appointed over you, and I am not the best of you." Al-Hasan said: "He knew that he was the best of them, but the believer belittles himself."

The supplication came with the word "Lord" before the conditional clause and before the response, to intensify the entreaty and supplication to God Exalted, and because the Lord is the Owner, the One who watches over the servant's interests. Al-Dahhak and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read ﴿تُرِئَنِّي﴾ with a hamza in place of the yā' (ي), as it was read in ﴿فَإمّا تَرَئِنَّ﴾ and ﴿وَلَتَرَؤُنَّ﴾ with a hamza. This is a weak substitution (ibdal, replacement of one letter by another). Then Exalted is He informed that He is able to hasten the punishment upon them as they had been asking for it, and this would be during his lifetime, peace and blessings be upon him, but His delay is for a term they will complete. The majority hold that this punishment is in this world. It is said: the Day of Badr. It is said: the conquest of Makkah. It is said: it is the punishment of the Hereafter.

Then Exalted is He commanded him to good conduct, and ﴿that which is better﴾ [al-Isra' 17:53] is the testimony that there is no god but God. "Evil" (al-sayyi'ah) is shirk. Al-Hasan said: it is forgiveness and overlooking. 'Ata' and al-Dahhak said: it is greeting with peace when they become obscene. Al-Mawardi related: "Repel" (idfa') means repelling the wrong with admonition. The better view is generality, both in the good and in what is hurtful. ﴿That which is better﴾ [al-Isra' 17:53] is more emphatic than "good" (hasanah), due to the intensification indicated by the elative form (af'al al-tafdil, comparative/superlative construction), and it came in the relative clause (silah) of "that which" in order to indicate the listener's familiarity with the state which is best. It is said: this verse is abrogated (mansukhah, naskh) by the verse of the sword. It is said: it is decisive (muhkamah), because conciliation (mudarah) is encouraged so long as it does not lead to a breach in religion or a disparagement of one's dignity.

﴿We know best what they describe﴾ implies that this is a verse of truce (muwada'ah, a verse of peaceful disengagement), and the meaning is: "what they mention and describe you with, from things you are not."

Then Exalted commanded him to seek refuge from the pricks (nakhsat) of the devils. The "incitement" (hamz) from the devil is an expression for urging to disobedience and enticing toward it, just as the trainer pricks the animal to make it hurry. Then He commanded him to seek refuge in the violence of anger, in which a person does not control himself. Ibn Zayd said: the incitement of the devil is madness. The apparent meaning is that he was commanded to seek refuge from the presence of the devils at all times. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas that this is at the time of reciting the Qur'an.

﴿Until, when death comes to one of them﴾: al-Zamakhshari said: "until" (hatta) is connected to ﴿yasifun﴾ (they describe), meaning they will not cease in their evil speech until this time, and the verse is inserted between them as a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh) and emphasis for overlooking them, seeking help from God against the devil so that he does not draw him away from forbearance and incite him to avenge himself on them, or it is connected to His saying: ﴿And indeed, they are liars﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:90]. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "until" in this place is a particle of beginning (harf ibtida', a particle introducing a new sentence), and it may be a bare limit (ghayah mujarradah) with an omitted sentence implied. The first is clearer, because what follows it is the thing intended and the purpose of mention. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyyah thus imagined that when "until" is a particle of beginning it cannot be a limit (ghayah), whereas when it is a particle of beginning it never separates from the sense of limit. He also did not specify the omitted implied sentence. Abu al-Baqa' said: "until" is a limit in the sense of coordination ('atf). What appears to me is that before it there is an omitted sentence (p. 421) of which "until" is the limit, indicated by what precedes it. The estimate: "So I will not be like the disbelievers whom the devils incite and who are present with them, until, when death comes to one of them." A parallel to the omission of this sentence is the saying of the poet:

*So how strange, even Kulayb reviles me!*

That is: "people revile me, even Kulayb." What follows "until" indicates the omitted sentence, and in the verse what precedes it indicates it. Al-Qushayri said: Exalted is He argued against them and reminded them of His power, then said: they persist in denial ﴿until, when death comes to one of them﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:18]; he becomes certain of his misguidance, sees the angels, and regrets, but regret does not benefit him. End of quote.

The pronoun in ﴿irji'un﴾ ("send me back") is plural, either addressing Him Exalted with plural address as an honorific, just as He spoke of Himself with the plural "we" in many places. The poet said:

*If you wish, I will forbid women other than you.*

And another said:

*Ah, have mercy on me, O God of Muhammad!*

Or he first sought help from his Lord and addressed the angels of punishment. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ("one of them") refers to the disbelievers, and the context of the verses to the end indicates this. Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever does not pay zakat and does not perform hajj asks for a return. It was said to him that this applies to the disbelievers, so he recited, as evidence for his view, the verse of Surat al-Munafiqun: ﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:10]. Al-Awza'i said: it refers to one who withholds zakat. "Death comes" means it is present and the person sees it, and at that time he asks for a return to the world. In a hadith: "When the believer sees death, the angels say to him: 'Shall we return you?' He says: 'To the house of worries and sorrows? No, rather forward to God.' As for the disbeliever, he says: 'Send me back, that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind.'"

The meaning of ﴿in what I have left behind﴾: in the faith which I abandoned, and the meaning is: "that I may bring what I abandoned of faith and do righteousness in it, as you say: 'I may build on a foundation,' meaning I establish a foundation and build upon it." It is said: ﴿in what I have left behind﴾ refers to wealth, as Ibn 'Abbas explained. ("No!") is a word of deterrence from seeking a return, and of denial and deeming it far-fetched. It is said: it is from God's saying to them. It is said: it is from the words of one who sees death, saying this to himself by way of grief and regret. The meaning of ﴿it is only a word he is saying﴾: he does not remain silent about it nor does he cease, because grief overtakes him; or he finds no benefit in it and his request is not answered nor is he helped. ﴿And before them﴾, that is, the disbelievers, is a barrier (barzakh) between them and returning until the time of resurrection. In this sentence there is an absolute despair that there is any return to the world; rather, the return is to the Hereafter. The word "barzakh" is used metaphorically for the period between a person's death and his resurrection.

Abu Bakr said: "I have been appointed over you, and I am not the best of you." Al-Hasan said: "He knew that he was the best of them, but the believer belittles himself."

This is a weak substitution (ibdal, replacement of one letter by another). Then Exalted is He informed that He is able to hasten the punishment upon them as they had been asking for it, and this would be during his lifetime, peace and blessings be upon him, but His delay is for a term they will complete. The majority hold that this punishment is in this world. It is said: the Day of Badr. It is said: the conquest of Makkah. It is said: it is the punishment of the Hereafter.

Then Exalted is He commanded him to good conduct, and ﴿that which is better﴾ [al-Isra' 17:53] is the testimony that there is no god but God. "Evil" (al-sayyi'ah) is shirk. Al-Hasan said: it is forgiveness and overlooking. 'Ata' and al-Dahhak said: it is greeting with peace when they become obscene. Al-Mawardi related: "Repel" (idfa') means repelling the wrong with admonition. The better view is generality, both in the good and in what is hurtful. ﴿That which is better﴾ [al-Isra' 17:53] is more emphatic than "good" (hasanah), due to the intensification indicated by the elative form (af'al al-tafdil, comparative/superlative construction), and it came in the relative clause (silah) of "that which" in order to indicate the listener's familiarity with the state which is best. It is said: this verse is abrogated (mansukhah, naskh) by the verse of the sword. It is said: it is decisive (muhkamah), because conciliation (mudarah) is encouraged so long as it does not lead to a breach in religion or a disparagement of one's dignity.

﴿We know best what they describe﴾ implies that this is a verse of truce (muwada'ah, a verse of peaceful disengagement), and the meaning is: "what they mention and describe you with, from things you are not."

Then Exalted commanded him to seek refuge from the pricks (nakhsat) of the devils. The "incitement" (hamz) from the devil is an expression for urging to disobedience and enticing toward it, just as the trainer pricks the animal to make it hurry. Then He commanded him to seek refuge in the violence of anger, in which a person does not control himself. Ibn Zayd said: the incitement of the devil is madness. The apparent meaning is that he was commanded to seek refuge from the presence of the devils at all times. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas that this is at the time of reciting the Qur'an.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "until" in this place is a particle of beginning (harf ibtida', a particle introducing a new sentence), and it may be a bare limit (ghayah mujarradah) with an omitted sentence implied. The first is clearer, because what follows it is the thing intended and the purpose of mention. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyyah thus imagined that when "until" is a particle of beginning it cannot be a limit (ghayah), whereas when it is a particle of beginning it never separates from the sense of limit. He also did not specify the omitted implied sentence. Abu al-Baqa' said: "until" is a limit in the sense of coordination ('atf). What appears to me is that before it there is an omitted sentence (p. 421) of which "until" is the limit, indicated by what precedes it. The estimate: "So I will not be like the disbelievers whom the devils incite and who are present with them, until, when death comes to one of them." A parallel to the omission of this sentence is the saying of the poet:

*So how strange, even Kulayb reviles me!*

That is: "people revile me, even Kulayb." What follows "until" indicates the omitted sentence, and in the verse what precedes it indicates it. Al-Qushayri said: Exalted is He argued against them and reminded them of His power, then said: they persist in denial ﴿until, when death comes to one of them﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:18]; he becomes certain of his misguidance, sees the angels, and regrets, but regret does not benefit him. End of quote.

The pronoun in ﴿irji'un﴾ ("send me back") is plural, either addressing Him Exalted with plural address as an honorific, just as He spoke of Himself with the plural "we" in many places. The poet said:

*If you wish, I will forbid women other than you.*

And another said:

*Ah, have mercy on me, O God of Muhammad!*

Or he first sought help from his Lord and addressed the angels of punishment. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ("one of them") refers to the disbelievers, and the context of the verses to the end indicates this. Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever does not pay zakat and does not perform hajj asks for a return. It was said to him that this applies to the disbelievers, so he recited, as evidence for his view, the verse of Surat al-Munafiqun: ﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:10]. Al-Awza'i said: it refers to one who withholds zakat. "Death comes" means it is present and the person sees it, and at that time he asks for a return to the world. In a hadith: "When the believer sees death, the angels say to him: 'Shall we return you?' He says: 'To the house of worries and sorrows? No, rather forward to God.' It is said: it is from God's saying to them. It is said: it is from the words of one who sees death, saying this to himself by way of grief and regret. The meaning of ﴿it is only a word he is saying﴾: he does not remain silent about it nor does he cease, because grief overtakes him; or he finds no benefit in it and his request is not answered nor is he helped. ﴿And before them﴾, that is, the disbelievers, is a barrier (barzakh) between them and returning until the time of resurrection. In this sentence there is an absolute despair that there is any return to the world; rather, the return is to the Hereafter. The word "barzakh" is used metaphorically for the period between a person's death and his resurrection.

The plural of fu'lah with a damma on the fā' according to fi'al with a kasra on the fā' is irregular (shadhdh).

It is related from Qatadah: no one is more hateful to a person on that day than one whom he knows, because he fears that the other has some injustice against him. On that day a person flees from his brother, his mother, his father, his spouse and his children. It is said: ﴿there are no kinships﴾ means there is no connection between them when they are separated toward what has been prepared for them of reward and punishment; connection is only through deeds.

What appears to me is that before it there is an omitted sentence (p. 421) of which "until" is the limit, indicated by what precedes it. The estimate: "So I will not be like the disbelievers whom the devils incite and who are present with them, until, when death comes to one of them." A parallel to the omission of this sentence is the saying of the poet:

*So how strange, even Kulayb reviles me!*

That is: "people revile me, even Kulayb." What follows "until" indicates the omitted sentence, and in the verse what precedes it indicates it. Al-Qushayri said: Exalted is He argued against them and reminded them of His power, then said: they persist in denial ﴿until, when death comes to one of them﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:18]; he becomes certain of his misguidance, sees the angels, and regrets, but regret does not benefit him. End of quote.

The pronoun in ﴿irji'un﴾ ("send me back") is plural, either addressing Him Exalted with plural address as an honorific, just as He spoke of Himself with the plural "we" in many places. The poet said:

*If you wish, I will forbid women other than you.*

And another said:

*Ah, have mercy on me, O God of Muhammad!*

Or he first sought help from his Lord and addressed the angels of punishment. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ("one of them") refers to the disbelievers, and the context of the verses to the end indicates this. Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever does not pay zakat and does not perform hajj asks for a return. It was said to him that this applies to the disbelievers, so he recited, as evidence for his view, the verse of Surat al-Munafiqun: ﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:10]. Al-Awza'i said: it refers to one who withholds zakat. "Death comes" means it is present and the person sees it, and at that time he asks for a return to the world. In a hadith: "When the believer sees death, the angels say to him: 'Shall we return you?' He says: 'To the house of worries and sorrows? No, rather forward to God.' As for the disbeliever, he says: 'Send me back, that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind.'"

The meaning of ﴿in what I have left behind﴾: in the faith which I abandoned, and the meaning is: "that I may bring what I abandoned of faith and do righteousness in it, as you say: 'I may build on a foundation,' meaning I establish a foundation and build upon it." It is said: ﴿in what I have left behind﴾ refers to wealth, as Ibn 'Abbas explained. ("No!") is a word of deterrence from seeking a return, and of denial and deeming it far-fetched. It is said: it is from God's saying to them. It is said: it is from the words of one who sees death, saying this to himself by way of grief and regret. The meaning of ﴿it is only a word he is saying﴾: he does not remain silent about it nor does he cease, because grief overtakes him; or he finds no benefit in it and his request is not answered nor is he helped. ﴿And before them﴾, that is, the disbelievers, is a barrier (barzakh) between them and returning until the time of resurrection. In this sentence there is an absolute despair that there is any return to the world; rather, the return is to the Hereafter. The word "barzakh" is used metaphorically for the period between a person's death and his resurrection.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn 'Iyad read ﴿fi al-sur﴾ with an open wa (و), as the plural of ṣūrah (form). Abu Razin read it with a kasra on the ṣād and an open wa, and likewise ﴿fa-ahsana ṣuwaraku﴾. The plural of fu'lah with a damma on the fā' according to fi'al with a kasra on the fā' is irregular (shadhdh).

﴿Then there are no kinships﴾ is a general negation. Ibn 'Abbas said: at the first blast people die, so there will be no kinship between them at that time while they are dead, and this view removes the terror of the gathering. Ibn Mas'ud and others said: at the rising of people from the graves, because of the terror of the appearance, each person is occupied with himself, the means are cut off, and boasting and mutual help through lineage cease. It is related from Qatadah: no one is more hateful to a person on that day than one whom he knows, because he fears that the other has some injustice against him. On that day a person flees from his brother, his mother, his father, his spouse and his children. It is said: ﴿there are no kinships﴾ means there is no connection between them when they are separated toward what has been prepared for them of reward and punishment; connection is only through deeds.

Abdullah [Ibn Mas'ud] read ﴿wa-la yassa'alun﴾ with a doubled sīn, assimilating the tā' into the sīn, since its original form is ﴿yatasa'alun﴾. There is no contradiction between the negation of questioning here and its affirmation in His saying: ﴿And they will approach one another, questioning each other﴾ [al-Saffat 37:27], because the Day of Resurrection has stations and standing-places, and it is possible that the negation of questioning is at the first blast, while at the second blast questioning occurs.

The discussion of the scales, their heaviness and lightness, has already been covered at the beginning of al-A'raf. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿abiding eternally in Hell﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿they have lost themselves﴾, and there is no place in grammar (mahall i'rab) for the substitute or the substituted, because the relative clause has no place; or it is a predicate after a predicate for ﴿those﴾, or the predicate of an omitted subject. End of quote. He made "in Hell" a substitute for "they lost", and this is a strange substitution. Its reality is that the substitute should be the verb to which "in Hell" is attached, meaning "they settled in Hell," and it seems to be from the type of replacing one thing with another, both referring to one referent by way of metaphor, because whoever loses himself settles in Hell. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿alladhina﴾ ("those who") is an attribute (na't) of ﴿ulaika﴾ ("those"), and the predicate of ﴿ulaika﴾ is ﴿in Hell﴾. The apparent view is that it is the predicate of ﴿ulaika﴾ and not an attribute.

The face was singled out for being burned because it is the most noble part of a human being, and a person protects it from afflictions more than other limbs; so when the most noble is burned, what is below it is also burned. Having mentioned the Fire's reaching the face, He mentioned the grimacing, which is specific to some parts of the face. In al-Tirmidhi: his upper lip contracts until it reaches the middle of his head, and his lower lip relaxes until it strikes his navel. He said: this is a hasan sahih hadith. Abu Haywah, Abu Bahriyyah and Ibn Abi 'Abla read ﴿kalihun﴾ without an alif.

God says to them through whichever of His angels He wills: ﴿Were not My verses recited to you, and did you not deny them?﴾ Those verses are the Qur'an. When they heard this reproach, they submitted and confessed against themselves, saying: ﴿Our wretchedness overcame us﴾. This follows the usage "ghalabani fulan 'ala kadha" (so-and-so overcame me in such-and-such), meaning he took it from you and took possession of it. Al-shaqawa (wretchedness) is the evil outcome. It has been said that al-shiqwa is desire and the pursuit of pleasures, because that leads to wretchedness, so the cause is named by its effect. This is the view of al-Jubba'i (al-Jibda'i). It has also been said that it means what was written against us in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) and what Your knowledge preceded. 

ʿAbd Allah, al-Hasan, Qatada, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim, Aban, al-Za'farani and Ibn Miqsam read "shaqawatuna" on the pattern of "al-sa'ada" (happiness). This is a widespread dialect. Qatada and al-Hasan also read it so, in the narration of Khalid ibn Hawshab from him, except that the shin is kasra. The rest of the Seven and the majority (al-jumhur, the majority of readers) read it with a kasra on the shin and sukun on the qaf, and this is a common dialect in the Hijaz. Al-Farra' said: Abu Thawwan recited to me, and he was eloquent:

"He was overcome by his hardship and his wretchedness, a girl of eighteen years in her marriage."

Shibl, in his own choice of reading, read it with a fatha on the shin and sukun on the qaf.

﴿And we were a people astray﴾, that is, from guidance. Then they moved gradually from confession to desire and supplication. This is because they confessed, and confession of sin is an apology. So they said: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it﴾, that is, out of Hell. ﴿Then if we return﴾, that is, to denial, taking other gods, and worshipping other than You, ﴿then we are indeed wrongdoers﴾, that is, those who exceed the limit in transgression, since they wronged themselves first and were then granted leniency and wronged themselves a second time.

Al-Tabari related a long narrative about a dispute between the disbelievers and Malik, the keeper of the Fire, and then between them and their Lord, may He be glorified and exalted. Its end is: ﴿He said: "Be driven away in it, and do not speak to Me."﴾ He said: Hell will close upon them, despair will set in, and they will remain barking at one another's faces. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: I have abridged that narrative because it is not sound, but its meaning is sound. The meaning of ﴿ukhsa'u﴾ is: be humiliated in it and be restrained as dogs are restrained when they are driven off. It is said: "khasa'tu al-kalb" (I drove the dog away), and "khasa'a" itself is used both transitively and intransitively. And (﴿la tukallimun﴾) means: do not speak concerning the lifting or lightening of the punishment. It has been said that this is the last speech they utter, after which there is no speech, only groaning, wailing and howling like the howling of dogs, without intelligible words.

﴿Indeed there was a party among My servants who said: "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ Ubayy and Harun al-ʿAtaki read "innahu" with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "because it". The majority read it with a kasra, and the hā' is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), which is omitted together with "anna" with a fatha on its hamza. Here "al-fariq" (the party) means the weak among the believers. This verse is among those said to the disbelievers as a rebuke. It was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh together with Suhayb, ʿAmmar, Bilal and their likes. Then it is general in its application to whoever followed their path in earlier times and in the rest of time.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Nafi' read "sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin, and the rest of the Seven with a kasra. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the verbal noun of "sakhira" like "al-sukhr", except that the nisba ya' adds emphasis to the verb, as it is said "al-khususiyya" for "al-khusus". Both mean mockery, according to al-Khalil, Abu Zayd al-Ansari and Sibawayh. Abu ʿUbayda, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the damma on the sin is from "al-sukhra" (servitude and employment), and the kasra is from "al-sakhr", which is ridicule. From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"A report came to me that I do not keep secret, from a high source, neither false nor mocking."

Yunus said: if the intended meaning is service, then only the damma is used; if the intended meaning is ridicule, then both the damma and the kasra may be used. Ibn ʿAtiyya said:

And the companions of ʿAbd Allah, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'raj read every occurrence in the Qur'an with a damma on the sin. Al-Hasan and Abu ʿAmr read with a kasra, except in the one in al-Zukhruf, where they both used a damma on the sin as the people do. The narration ends. Ibn ʿAtiyya had said, from Abu ʿAli (meaning al-Farisi), that the reading with a kasra on the sin is more preferable, because it means ridicule, the kasra is more common in it, and it fits the verse better. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾? The words of Abu ʿAli end here. Then Ibn ʿAtiyya said: Do you not see that the readers agreed on a damma on the sin in His saying: ﴿so that some of them may take others as servants﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32], when the matter was purely about service? The narration ends. What he mentioned about the agreement of the readers on the damma on the sin in al-Zukhruf is not accurate, because Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Muslim read it with a kasra in al-Zukhruf. Abu al-Qasim ibn Jubara al-Hudhali mentioned this in his book al-Kamil.

﴿So you took them as objects of ridicule﴾, that is, you made them a laughing-stock, mocking them.

﴿Until they made you forget My remembrance﴾, that is, by your preoccupation with them you abandoned My remembrance, namely that you should remember Me and thus fear Me regarding My allies. The forgetting is attributed to the party of believers because it was the cause of it.

Zayd ibn ʿAli, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Kharija from Nafi' read "innahum hum" with a kasra on the hamza, and the rest of the Seven read it with a fatha. The second object of ﴿jazaytuhum﴾ is omitted; its estimate is "the Garden" or "My pleasure". Al-Zamakhshari said: In the reading of the one who reads "annahum" with a fatha, it is the second object, that is, ﴿jazaytuhum﴾ (p-424) their success. The narration ends. The apparent sense is that it is a causal clause, that is, ﴿I have rewarded them﴾ because they are...; the kasra is for a new sentence, though it may also be intended as causal, so the kasra has the same meaning as the fatha, though not the same grammatical analysis, since the fatha requires a governing word. "Al-fa'izun" means those who are saved from destruction into blessing.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read "qul kam" (say: how many), and the addressee is an angel who asks them, or some of the people of the Fire. Therefore he said: "express it about the people." The rest of the Seven read "qala" (He said), and the speaker is God, Exalted, or an angel commanded to ask them. Al-Zamakhshari said: In the codices of the people of Kufa it is "qala", and in those of the people of the Two Sanctuaries (Makka and Madina), Basra and Syria it is "qul". Ibn ʿAtiyya said: In the codices it is "qala" in both places, except in the codex of Kufa, where it is "qul" without an alif. The idghaam (assimilation) of the class of "labithtu" was discussed in al-Baqara. He asked them a question seeking exact determination of the period. The majority read ﴿ʿadada sinin﴾ as an idafa (construct phrase). "Kam" is in the accusative position as a time adverb, and its specification is "ʿadad". Al-A'mash and al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim read "ʿadadan" with tanwin. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi, author of al-Lawami', said: "sinin" is accusative as an adverb of time, and "ʿadad" is a verbal noun placed in the position of a noun, so it is a modifier preceding the modified noun. It is also possible that the meaning of "labithtum" is "you counted", and then "ʿadadan" is accusative as a verbal noun, and "sinin" is its substitute. The statement that "labithtum" means "ʿadadtum" is far-fetched.

When they were asked about the period they had spent on the earth, meaning in the life of this world (said by al-Tabari, and al-Zamakhshari followed him), they forgot because of the extreme horror of the punishment, until they said: ﴿a day or part of a day﴾. They answered: ﴿We stayed a day or part of a day﴾. They were uncertain about how long they had stayed. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

It has also been said that by His saying "on the earth" is meant within the depths of the soil, as dead people. This is the view of the majority of commentators. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: This is the most correct, since they denied resurrection and used to say that they would not rise from the dust. It was said to them when they rose: ﴿How long did you stay?﴾ His last statement: ﴿and that you will not be returned to Us﴾ supports what we have said. The narration ends.

﴿So ask those who count﴾ is addressed to the one who questioned them. Mujahid said: ﴿those who count﴾ are the angels, that is, those who guard the deeds of the children of Adam and count their hours. Qatada said: they are the people of reckoning. The apparent sense is that whoever has this attribute is an angel or someone else, since the sleeper and the dead do not count, so time cannot be measured for them. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is that we do not know the number of those years except that we consider it little, and we reckon it as a day or part of a day, because of what we are suffering. There is no one among us who could count how long they remained. Ask someone who can count, and who can direct his thought to him. The narration ends. Al-Hasan and al-Kisa'i, in one narration, read ﴿al-'adin﴾ with a light dal, meaning "the wrongdoers", since they speak as you speak. Ibn Khalawayh said: Another dialect is "al-ʿadiyyin", with a doubled ya', meaning the plural of "ʿadiyy", that is, of the ancients. Al-Zamakhshari said: It has been read as "al-ʿadiyyin", that is, the ancient long-lived ones, for they consider it short, so how about those less than them.

The two brothers (al-Akhawan, Hamza and al-Kisa'i) read ﴿Say: if you stayed﴾ as an imperative, while the rest of the Seven read it as a statement, and "in" is negating, meaning: you did not stay except a little, that is, of little measure compared to what you are punished in, whether the stay was in the world or in the graves. I said: every coming thing is near, but you denied it, since you did not know, that is, you did not desire knowledge and guidance. The word ﴿ʿabathan﴾ is accusative as a state (ḥāl), meaning playing, or as an object of purpose. The meaning of this is: We did not create you for play; We created you only for obligation and worship. The two brothers read ﴿la turja'un﴾ with the active voice, and the rest of the Seven with the passive voice. The apparent sense is that "wa annakum" is coordinated with "annama", so it falls within the reckoning.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It may be that it is "for play", that is, for play and for your being left unreturned.

﴿So exalted is God﴾, that is, He is magnified and exempted from consorts, offspring, partners, play and all deficiencies. Rather, He is ﴿the King, the Truth﴾, whose existence and supreme attributes are established. ﴿The Noble﴾ is an attribute of the Throne, because the good comes down from it, or because it is attributed to the Most Noble of the noble. Aban ibn Taghlib, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Ja'far and Isma'il, from Ibn Kathir, read "al-karimu" with a damma, as an attribute of "the Lord of the Throne", or of "the Throne", and it is coordinated with the sense of praise.

"Man" is conditional, and its answer is "fa-innama". ﴿There is no proof for him concerning it﴾ is a necessary attribute, not to exclude the possibility that there is another god for whom a proof exists. It is therefore an emphatic attribute, like His saying: ﴿flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. It may also be a parenthetical clause, since it contains emphasis and reinforcement, so it has no place in the grammar, as when you say: "Whoever wrongs you has no right to the wrong, so wrong him." Whoever holds that the answer of the conditional is ﴿There is no proof for him concerning it﴾, in flight from the implication (dalil al-khitab) that there might be another god for whom a proof exists, is wrong, since it would require omitting the "fa" in the answer of the conditional, which is permitted only in poetry. We have explained it as a necessary attribute or as a parenthesis, and both are sound explanations. Al-Hasan and Qatada read "annahu la yuflihu" with a fatha on the hamza, meaning: he, so the disbelievers were placed where the pronoun would be, taking account of the sense of "man". The majority read it with a kasra on the hamza, and the predicate of "hisabuhu" is the adverbial phrase, and "annahu" begins a new sentence. Al-Hasan read "yuflahu" with fatha on the ya' and the lam.

He opened the sūra with His saying: ﴿The believers have certainly succeeded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1], and He closed it with ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾. Consider the difference between the opening and the closing. Then He commanded His Messenger, peace be upon him, to supplicate for forgiveness and mercy. Ibn Muhaysin read "Rabbu" with a damma on the ba'.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Nafi' read "sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin, and the rest of the Seven with a kasra. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the verbal noun of "sakhira" like "al-sukhr", except that the nisba ya' adds emphasis to the verb, as it is said "al-khususiyya" for "al-khusus". Both mean mockery, according to al-Khalil, Abu Zayd al-Ansari and Sibawayh. Abu ʿUbayda, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the damma on the sin is from "al-sukhra" (servitude and employment), and the kasra is from "al-sakhr", which is ridicule. From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"A report came to me that I do not keep secret, from a high source, neither false nor mocking."

Yunus said: if the intended meaning is service, then only the damma is used; if the intended meaning is ridicule, then both the damma and the kasra may be used. Ibn ʿAtiyya said:

And the companions of ʿAbd Allah, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'raj read every occurrence in the Qur'an with a damma on the sin. Al-Hasan and Abu ʿAmr read with a kasra, except in the one in al-Zukhruf, where they both used a damma on the sin as the people do. The narration ends. Ibn ʿAtiyya had said, from Abu ʿAli (meaning al-Farisi), that the reading with a kasra on the sin is more preferable, because it means ridicule, the kasra is more common in it, and it fits the verse better. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾? The words of Abu ʿAli end here. Then Ibn ʿAtiyya said: Do you not see that the readers agreed on a damma on the sin in His saying: ﴿so that some of them may take others as servants﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32], when the matter was purely about service? The narration ends. What he mentioned about the agreement of the readers on the damma on the sin in al-Zukhruf is not accurate, because Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Muslim read it with a kasra in al-Zukhruf. Abu al-Qasim ibn Jubara al-Hudhali mentioned this in his book al-Kamil.

﴿So you took them as objects of ridicule﴾, that is, you made them a laughing-stock, mocking them.

﴿Until they made you forget My remembrance﴾, that is, by your preoccupation with them you abandoned My remembrance, namely that you should remember Me and thus fear Me regarding My allies. The forgetting is attributed to the party of believers because it was the cause of it.

Zayd ibn ʿAli, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Kharija from Nafi' read "innahum hum" with a kasra on the hamza, and the rest of the Seven read it with a fatha. The second object of ﴿jazaytuhum﴾ is omitted; its estimate is "the Garden" or "My pleasure". Al-Zamakhshari said: In the reading of the one who reads "annahum" with a fatha, it is the second object, that is, ﴿jazaytuhum﴾ (p-424) their success. The narration ends. The apparent sense is that it is a causal clause, that is, ﴿I have rewarded them﴾ because they are...; the kasra is for a new sentence, though it may also be intended as causal, so the kasra has the same meaning as the fatha, though not the same grammatical analysis, since the fatha requires a governing word. "Al-fa'izun" means those who are saved from destruction into blessing.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read "qul kam" (say: how many), and the addressee is an angel who asks them, or some of the people of the Fire. Therefore he said: "express it about the people." The rest of the Seven read "qala" (He said), and the speaker is God, Exalted, or an angel commanded to ask them. Al-Zamakhshari said: In the codices of the people of Kufa it is "qala", and in those of the people of the Two Sanctuaries (Makka and Madina), Basra and Syria it is "qul". Ibn ʿAtiyya said: In the codices it is "qala" in both places, except in the codex of Kufa, where it is "qul" without an alif. The idghaam (assimilation) of the class of "labithtu" was discussed in al-Baqara. He asked them a question seeking exact determination of the period. The majority read ﴿ʿadada sinin﴾ as an idafa (construct phrase). "Kam" is in the accusative position as a time adverb, and its specification is "ʿadad". Al-A'mash and al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim read "ʿadadan" with tanwin. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi, author of al-Lawami', said: "sinin" is accusative as an adverb of time, and "ʿadad" is a verbal noun placed in the position of a noun, so it is a modifier preceding the modified noun. It is also possible that the meaning of "labithtum" is "you counted", and then "ʿadadan" is accusative as a verbal noun, and "sinin" is its substitute. The statement that "labithtum" means "ʿadadtum" is far-fetched.

When they were asked about the period they had spent on the earth, meaning in the life of this world (said by al-Tabari, and al-Zamakhshari followed him), they forgot because of the extreme horror of the punishment, until they said: ﴿a day or part of a day﴾. They answered: ﴿We stayed a day or part of a day﴾. They were uncertain about how long they had stayed. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

It has also been said that by His saying "on the earth" is meant within the depths of the soil, as dead people. This is the view of the majority of commentators. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: This is the most correct, since they denied resurrection and used to say that they would not rise from the dust. It was said to them when they rose: ﴿How long did you stay?﴾ His last statement: ﴿and that you will not be returned to Us﴾ supports what we have said. The narration ends.

﴿So ask those who count﴾ is addressed to the one who questioned them. Mujahid said: ﴿those who count﴾ are the angels, that is, those who guard the deeds of the children of Adam and count their hours. Qatada said: they are the people of reckoning. The apparent sense is that whoever has this attribute is an angel or someone else, since the sleeper and the dead do not count, so time cannot be measured for them. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is that we do not know the number of those years except that we consider it little, and we reckon it as a day or part of a day, because of what we are suffering. There is no one among us who could count how long they remained. Ask someone who can count, and who can direct his thought to him. The narration ends. Al-Hasan and al-Kisa'i, in one narration, read ﴿al-'adin﴾ with a light dal, meaning "the wrongdoers", since they speak as you speak. Ibn Khalawayh said: Another dialect is "al-ʿadiyyin", with a doubled ya', meaning the plural of "ʿadiyy", that is, of the ancients. Al-Zamakhshari said: It has been read as "al-ʿadiyyin", that is, the ancient long-lived ones, for they consider it short, so how about those less than them.

The two brothers (al-Akhawan, Hamza and al-Kisa'i) read ﴿Say: if you stayed﴾ as an imperative, while the rest of the Seven read it as a statement, and "in" is negating, meaning: you did not stay except a little, that is, of little measure compared to what you are punished in, whether the stay was in the world or in the graves. I said: every coming thing is near, but you denied it, since you did not know, that is, you did not desire knowledge and guidance. The word ﴿ʿabathan﴾ is accusative as a state (ḥāl), meaning playing, or as an object of purpose. The meaning of this is: We did not create you for play; We created you only for obligation and worship. The two brothers read ﴿la turja'un﴾ with the active voice, and the rest of the Seven with the passive voice. The apparent sense is that "wa annakum" is coordinated with "annama", so it falls within the reckoning.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It may be that it is "for play", that is, for play and for your being left unreturned.

﴿So exalted is God﴾, that is, He is magnified and exempted from consorts, offspring, partners, play and all deficiencies. Rather, He is ﴿the King, the Truth﴾, whose existence and supreme attributes are established. ﴿The Noble﴾ is an attribute of the Throne, because the good comes down from it, or because it is attributed to the Most Noble of the noble. Aban ibn Taghlib, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Ja'far and Isma'il, from Ibn Kathir, read "al-karimu" with a damma, as an attribute of "the Lord of the Throne", or of "the Throne", and it is coordinated with the sense of praise.

"Man" is conditional, and its answer is "fa-innama". ﴿There is no proof for him concerning it﴾ is a necessary attribute, not to exclude the possibility that there is another god for whom a proof exists. It is therefore an emphatic attribute, like His saying: ﴿flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. It may also be a parenthetical clause, since it contains emphasis and reinforcement, so it has no place in the grammar, as when you say: "Whoever wrongs you has no right to the wrong, so wrong him." Whoever holds that the answer of the conditional is ﴿There is no proof for him concerning it﴾, in flight from the implication (dalil al-khitab) that there might be another god for whom a proof exists, is wrong, since it would require omitting the "fa" in the answer of the conditional, which is permitted only in poetry. We have explained it as a necessary attribute or as a parenthesis, and both are sound explanations. Al-Hasan and Qatada read "annahu la yuflihu" with a fatha on the hamza, meaning: he, so the disbelievers were placed where the pronoun would be, taking account of the sense of "man". The majority read it with a kasra on the hamza, and the predicate of "hisabuhu" is the adverbial phrase, and "annahu" begins a new sentence. Al-Hasan read "yuflahu" with fatha on the ya' and the lam.

He opened the sūra with His saying: ﴿The believers have certainly succeeded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1], and He closed it with ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾. Consider the difference between the opening and the closing. Then He commanded His Messenger, peace be upon him, to supplicate for forgiveness and mercy. Ibn Muhaysin read "Rabbu" with a damma on the ba'.
